AND coach_id = e.owner_id)` — one clause, but it hands every client the coach's entire private library including drafts and exercises meant for other people. Snapshotting the exercise name into the plan item and rendering that — the plan lists correctly but the player loses the media, the muscle map and the instructions, which is the whole feature.

keyDecisions.decision: Every plan and log read/write uses `coach_clients.status = 'active'`, resolving the split with the roster's `status <> 'archived'`.
keyDecisions.rationale: An 'invited' link is a person who has not accepted the relationship. A coach must not be able to prescribe to, or read logs of, someone who has not consented — that is data the client never agreed to. 'active' is also the stricter predicate already used for the only existing cross-user data read (onboarding/routes.js:261). The roster's looser predicate is correct FOR THE ROSTER: you must see pending invites to manage them. The inconsistency is only apparent — one is a management surface, the other is data access.
keyDecisions.rejected: `status <> 'archived'` everywhere for uniformity, which would let a coach author a full programme against an invited-but-never-accepted email address.

keyDecisions.decision: Scheduling is materialised into `plan_schedule` — one row per planned session — rather than computed from a recurrence rule on the assignment.
keyDecisions.rationale: Coaches move individual sessions constantly. With a rule, every move becomes an exception row, which is a second data model bolted onto the first, and the two disagree at every edge. With materialised rows, a move is one guarded UPDATE, the calendar week is a range scan on `plan_schedule_today_idx`, the Home 'today' card is a point lookup on the same index, ICS is one VEVENT per row, and adherence is a LEFT JOIN to workout_logs. The materialisation is bounded by `repeat_cycles BETWEEN 1 AND 52`.
keyDecisions.rejected: RRULE-style computation (compact, but 'push Thursday to Friday' needs an override table anyway, and the Home card then has to evaluate a recurrence in SQL or fetch-and-filter in JS). A hybrid rule-plus-exceptions — the worst of both, since every read must apply both.

keyDecisions.decision: Fan-out to a team is N sequential `clonePlanToClient` calls at the route layer, capped at 50 per request — NOT one transaction.
keyDecisions.rationale: A 200-member team at 7 days x 8 items is ~11 000 inserts. One IMMEDIATE transaction holding SQLite's single write lock for that long pushes every other writer past `busy_timeout = 5000` into SQLITE_BUSY. The pool sizing note is explicit: keep named transactions short. Partial failure is also the right failure mode for a bulk op — the clones that succeeded are visible in the coach's list, and the retry is over the remainder.
keyDecisions.rejected: A single `clonePlanToTeam` named transaction (atomic and appealing, but it is a self-inflicted lock storm and an all-or-nothing failure over work the coach can see partially succeeded).

keyDecisions.decision: New enum codes are snake_case. Codes that mirror an existing enum keep that enum's spelling, including kebab.
keyDecisions.rationale: The ground truth is right that casing has drifted and that a call must be made. snake_case matches the two most recent structural enums ('pending_review', 'team_code'). But `workout_plans.goal` and `.experience` deliberately reuse onboarding_profiles' vocabulary verbatim — 'fat-loss' kebab included — because the suggestion matcher is then an equality join rather than a translation table between two spellings of one concept. Same for `body_area_muscle_map.body_area`, which must match onboarding_limitations exactly.
keyDecisions.rejected: Kebab everywhere (matches the slug convention, but breaks with 'pending_review' and reads badly in JS). Renaming the onboarding codes to snake_case for consistency — a migration and a frontend i18n key change to fix a cosmetic inconsistency, at the cost of breaking every stored draft profile.

keyDecisions.decision: Index naming is the SUFFIX form: `*_idx`, `*_unique`. Triggers use the PREFIX form `trg_*` and the 008 WHEN-guarded body.
keyDecisions.rationale: Both forms are live and one must win. `*_idx` is the majority of the schema (001–006, ~20 indexes vs ~3), and it sorts each index next to its table in a schema dump. Triggers go the other way because the 008 form is not just newer, it is SAFER: `WHEN NEW.updated_at = OLD.updated_at` cannot recurse through its own UPDATE and does not silently clobber an updated_at set deliberately by a backfill. The 001-style unguarded touch trigger is only non-recursive by accident — `PRAGMA recursive_triggers` is never set in worker.js, and turning it on would infinite-loop six existing tables.
keyDecisions.rejected: The `idx_*` prefix form of 007–008 (newest, but a 3-vs-20 minority). Copying the 001-style trigger for consistency with the majority — consistency with a latent bug.

designs.idempotency:
THE SET ROW IS ITS OWN IDEMPOTENCY KEY. "Set checked" is modelled as an assertion about the state of set N of exercise M in workout W, not as an event to append — so `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX workout_log_sets_slot_unique ON workout_log_sets (log_item_id, set_index)` is the natural key, and the write is an UPSERT. No idempotency_keys table, no TTL sweeper, no stored response bodies.

The whole path is ONE named worker transaction, `recordSet` (worker.js export + `export const recordSet = (a) => pool.run(a, { name: 'recordSet' })` in index.js). writeTx cannot do it: it cannot inspect the record-upsert's changes count and therefore cannot decide the PR. In strict order — and every read that can produce an error runs BEFORE the first write, per ADR-0005:

STEP 0 — ownership and state, read-only:
  SELECT li.id, li.exercise_id, l.status
    FROM workout_log_items li JOIN workout_logs l ON l.id = li.log_id
   WHERE li.id = ? AND li.client_id = ? AND l.status = 'in_progress';
  A miss throws NOT_FOUND (route → 404, never 403). A log already 'completed' throws CONFLICT → 409.

STEP 1 — the set, upserted on the natural key:
  INSERT INTO workout_log_sets
    (log_item_id, log_id, set_index, set_kind, weight_kg, reps, seconds, distance_m, rpe,
     rest_taken_seconds, completed_at, target_reps, target_weight_kg, target_rpe)
  VALUES (?,?,?,?,?,?,?,?,?,?, unixepoch(), ?,?,?)
  ON CONFLICT (log_item_id, set_index) DO UPDATE SET
    weight_kg  = excluded.weight_kg,
    reps       = excluded.reps,
    seconds    = excluded.seconds,
    distance_m = excluded.distance_m,
    rpe        = excluded.rpe,
    rest_taken_seconds = excluded.rest_taken_seconds,
    completed_at = COALESCE(workout_log_sets.completed_at, excluded.completed_at),
    updated_at   = unixepoch();
  A replay rewrites the same row with the same values: one row, not two. `completed_at` is COALESCEd so the first check's timestamp is the true one. `is_pr` is DELIBERATELY ABSENT from the DO UPDATE list — a replay must neither clear a badge already earned nor grant one it did not.

STEP 2 — the set's id, read after the write (reads after writes are fine; only a conditional error RETURN after a write is forbidden, because better-sqlite3 commits on return):
  SELECT id, is_pr FROM workout_log_sets WHERE log_item_id = ? AND set_index = ?;
  last_insert_rowid() is NOT used here — it is meaningless when the ON CONFLICT branch fired.

STEP 3 — the PR, with the comparison INSIDE the UPDATE. Once per metric (max_e1rm, max_weight, max_reps, max_volume_set, max_duration, max_distance), values computed in the worker from the set's own numbers, Epley in JS, never from anything the client sent:
  INSERT INTO exercise_records
    (user_id, exercise_id, metric, value, reps, weight_kg, source_set_id, achieved_on, previous_value)
  VALUES (?,?,?,?,?,?,?,?, NULL)
  ON CONFLICT (user_id, exercise_id, metric) DO UPDATE SET
    previous_value = exercise_records.value,
    value          = excluded.value,
    reps           = excluded.reps,
    weight_kg      = excluded.weight_kg,
    source_set_id  = excluded.source_set_id,
    achieved_on    = excluded.achieved_on,
    achieved_at    = unixepoch(),
    updated_at     = unixepoch()
  WHERE excluded.value > exercise_records.value;

  THIS IS THE LOAD-BEARING LINE. changes === 1 means, and can only mean, a genuinely new best. On a replay the row already exists holding exactly this set's value, so `excluded.value > exercise_records.value` is FALSE, changes === 0, and no PR is awarded. There is no preceding SELECT to race against and no window between check and write — the guard is the UPDATE. Two concurrent replays serialise on SQLite's single write lock and the second one still sees changes === 0.

STEP 4 — the badge, only if step 3 actually moved a record:
  UPDATE workout_log_sets SET is_pr = 1 WHERE id = ? AND is_pr = 0;

STEP 5 — totals, RECOMPUTED not incremented (this is what stops a replay inflating volume):
  UPDATE workout_logs SET
    total_sets   = (SELECT COUNT(*)                     FROM workout_log_sets WHERE log_id = ? AND completed_at IS NOT NULL),
    total_reps   = (SELECT COALESCE(SUM(reps),0)        FROM workout_log_sets WHERE log_id = ? AND completed_at IS NOT NULL),
    total_volume_kg = (SELECT COALESCE(SUM(COALESCE(weight_kg,0) * COALESCE(reps,0)),0)
                         FROM workout_log_sets WHERE log_id = ? AND completed_at IS NOT NULL)
  WHERE id = ?;
  Bounded to ~40 rows by workout_log_sets_log_idx. `SET x = (SELECT SUM(...))` is idempotent; `SET x = x + ?` is not, and no column in this schema uses the second form except the `rev` counters, which are deliberately allowed to over-count.

THE FUTURE COIN REWARD (T2.10.3, Phase-7) inherits all of this without inventing the economy: the ledger will be `reward_ledger(..., source_type TEXT, source_id INTEGER, UNIQUE(source_type, source_id))` and the award is `INSERT OR IGNORE ... VALUES ('workout_set', <set id>, ...)`. That is double-award-proof precisely BECAUSE step 1 upserts on a natural key — the set's `id` is stable across every replay, so the second attempt collides on the unique index and inserts nothing.

TWO MORE REPLAY SURFACES CLOSED THE SAME WAY:
- Starting a workout: `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX workout_logs_schedule_unique ON workout_logs (schedule_id) WHERE schedule_id IS NOT NULL AND status <> 'abandoned'`. A double-tapped Start hits the conflict, and `startWorkout` returns the existing log instead of a twin. 'Already started' is not an error here, exactly as onboarding/routes.js:237 returns `{ ok: true, alreadyComplete }` rather than a 409.
- Materialising a schedule: `plan_schedule_slot_unique (assignment_id, cycle_index, plan_day_id)` means a re-run after a crash inserts nothing new rather than doubling every session.

CORRECTIONS: editing or deleting an already-logged set can invalidate a record it holds. `exercise_records.source_set_id` is the pointer that makes that detectable, and `recomputeExerciseRecord` (a separate named tx) rebuilds that one (user, exercise, metric) row by full aggregate over `workout_log_items_history_idx`. Recompute-by-aggregate again — a decrement would be as wrong here as it is anywhere else.
designs.ownership:
THE PROOF OF ENTITLEMENT IS ALWAYS THE LINK ID, NEVER THE CLIENT'S USER ID. Every coach-facing plan/log route is keyed `/api/v1/clients/:linkId/...`, following onboarding/routes.js:255-265 verbatim. A route keyed on the client's user id would break the property that archiving ends access immediately, because a user id stays valid forever while a link's status does not. Every miss is 404 with the generic 'not found' body — never 403, which would confirm the id is real and let a coach enumerate another coach's roster. (Role gates are the documented exception and DO return 403: requireCoach, requireAuth.)

PER TABLE, THE EXACT PREDICATE:

workout_plans — COACH WRITE (and coach read of an instance):
  WHERE p.id = ?
    AND p.owner_user_id = ?                       -- the coach authored it
    AND p.archived_at IS NULL
    AND p.scope IN ('template', 'client')
    AND (p.client_link_id IS NULL OR EXISTS (
          SELECT 1 FROM coach_clients cc
           WHERE cc.id = p.client_link_id AND cc.coach_id = ? AND cc.status = 'active'))
  `owner_user_id = ?` alone is NOT sufficient — it would let an archived coach keep editing a plan they still own. The EXISTS is what makes archiving take effect on the very next request with the same token. Note that for scope='client' the owner is the COACH, which is exactly what makes "the client may read their plan but may never edit it" a one-column fact rather than a route-level convention.

workout_plans — CLIENT READ:
  WHERE p.archived_at IS NULL AND (
        (p.scope = 'personal' AND p.owner_user_id = ?)
     OR (p.scope = 'client' AND p.published_at IS NOT NULL AND EXISTS (
           SELECT 1 FROM coach_clients cc
            WHERE cc.id = p.client_link_id AND cc.client_id = ? AND cc.status = 'active'))
     OR p.scope = 'system')
  `published_at IS NOT NULL` keeps a half-built week invisible. A coach's template is never in this set.

workout_plan_days / _groups / _items / _item_sets — never queried by their own id alone. Always reached through their plan, and the ownership predicate is applied to the PLAN in the same statement:
  UPDATE workout_plan_items SET ... 
   WHERE id = ? AND day_id = ?
     AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM workout_plan_days d JOIN workout_plans p ON p.id = d.plan_id
                  WHERE d.id = ? AND p.owner_user_id = ?
                    AND (p.client_link_id IS NULL OR EXISTS (
                          SELECT 1 FROM coach_clients cc WHERE cc.id = p.client_link_id
                            AND cc.coach_id = ? AND cc.status = 'active')));
  The ownership check is INSIDE the UPDATE, never a preceding SELECT. changes === 0 → 404.

plan_assignments / plan_schedule — dual-keyed. Coach: `AND client_link_id = ? AND EXISTS (coach_clients WHERE id = ? AND coach_id = ? AND status='active')`. Client: `AND client_id = ?` directly (the denormalised column exists for exactly this, and it is the only predicate a personal plan can use since it has no link).

workout_logs / workout_log_items / workout_log_sets — the CLIENT owns their log outright: `AND client_id = ?` on every read and write, and `workout_log_items.client_id` / `workout_log_sets.log_id` carry it so no query ever has to climb two levels to find the owner. A COACH reads a client's logs only through the link:
  WHERE l.client_id = (SELECT client_id FROM coach_clients
                        WHERE id = ? AND coach_id = ? AND status = 'active')
  A subquery returning NULL matches nothing, so an archived link yields an empty result rather than an error — the miss and the denial are indistinguishable. A coach never WRITES a client's log; there is no route for it.

exercise_records — `AND user_id = ?` for the owner. A coach reads them through the same link subquery as logs.

client_exercise_prefs — keyed on client_link_id, so `AND EXISTS (coach_clients WHERE id = ? AND coach_id = ? AND status='active')`. It dies with the link and never leaks one coach's clinical judgement into another coach's suggestions for the same person.

HOW AN ARCHIVED coach_clients LINK ENDS ACCESS, EXACTLY:
coaching/routes.js:137 sets `status='archived'` (and archived_at) in one guarded UPDATE. From that commit onward:
1. Every coach-side predicate above contains `cc.status = 'active'`. The subquery/EXISTS matches zero rows, so the coach's very next request — with the SAME unexpired JWT — returns 404. There is no claim in the token to expire and therefore no stale grant. This is why the link and not a role claim is the key.
2. The client's own read of the plan fails the same EXISTS, so the plan disappears from their app too. Their LOGS do not: `workout_logs.client_id` is the client's own user id and owes nothing to the link. History survives the relationship, which is correct — they did those workouts.
3. Exercise visibility contracts automatically. The prescribed-to-me EXISTS in the client-side visibility predicate joins `coach_clients ... AND cc.status = 'active'`, so the coach's private exercises stop resolving for that client at the same instant. The performed-by-me EXISTS still holds, so an exercise they actually did stays readable in their history forever — the correct asymmetry.
4. The ICS feed dies with it: `coach_clients.ics_token` is on the link row, and the feed route resolves it with `WHERE ics_token = ? AND status = 'active'`. No separate revocation step, no orphaned calendar subscription still leaking next week's sessions.
5. Nothing is deleted. `plan_assignments.client_link_id` and the plans still reference the archived link, so un-archiving (the ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE at coaching/routes.js:275 sets status='active', archived_at=NULL) restores the whole relationship intact rather than requiring the coach to rebuild it.
weaknesses: COPY-ON-ASSIGN HAS NO PROPAGATION PATH, AND THAT HURTS WEEKLY. A coach running 40 clients on one programme who spots a bad rep range fixes it in the template and then has to re-clone 40 plans — losing every per-client tweak in the process. `source_plan_id` makes a bulk re-clone *possible* and previewable, but I did not design the diff/merge that would make it safe, and without one the honest answer to 'I changed my mind about week 3' is 'edit it 40 times'. This is the single biggest cost of the central decision, and I would take it again for the history-integrity reason, but it is a real, recurring tax.

PLAN_SCHEDULE MATERIALISATION HAS NO REPAIR PATH. `plan_schedule.plan_day_id REFERENCES workout_plan_days ON DELETE CASCADE` means a coach deleting a day silently deletes every future scheduled session that pointed at it — the client's calendar loses entries with no notification and no audit row. Adding a day after assignment materialises nothing. An open-ended assignment needs a horizon top-up job I did not design. The whole class of 'the plan changed after it was assigned' is unhandled, and it is not rare.

THE BODY_AREA → MUSCLE_GROUP BRIDGE IS A BLUNT HEURISTIC. 'Avoid knee' excluding everything quad-dominant kills leg extensions (right), leg press (arguable) and hip thrusts (wrong). Proper modelling needs joint-action tags per exercise — knee flexion under load, shoulder abduction above 90° — which neither wger nor free-exercise-db provides. `client_exercise_prefs` is the escape hatch that makes it shippable, but it puts the correction work on the coach, one exercise at a time, and a coach who trusts the filter will prescribe something they should not have.

THE TWO-PASS POSITION PARKING (+1000000) IS VISIBLE IN THE DDL AS A MISSING UPPER BOUND. `CHECK (position >= 0)` with no ceiling exists only because pass 1 needs somewhere to park. If a future named transaction writes pass 1 and then throws for an unrelated reason, WAL rolls it back — but a *logic* bug between the two passes inside a committing transaction would leave rows at 1000000+ and no constraint would catch it. The invariant `max(position) = count(*) - 1` is checkable but nothing checks it. A periodic integrity query, or a deferred check I cannot express in SQLite, is missing.

EIGHT NEW NAMED WORKER TRANSACTIONS IN A CODEBASE WITH ZERO EXISTING EXAMPLES. savePlanDayOrder, copyPlanDays, clonePlanToClient, assignPlan, startWorkout, recordSet, finishWorkout, recomputeExerciseRecord. The Piscina `{ name }` mechanism is proven only by `migrate`, and every one of these depends on details the design asserts rather than demonstrates: that a throw inside `.immediate()` rolls back cleanly through the structured-clone boundary, that a typed error survives it with enough information for the route to map 404 vs 409 vs 500 (worker.js's rethrow flattens everything into a message string and a SQLite code — it has no place to put an application error code, so I am assuming a convention that does not exist yet).

NO IDEMPOTENCY FOR THE BULK OPERATIONS. Set-checking is replay-proof; 'assign this plan to 30 clients' is not. A request that times out client-side after committing 18 clones, then retried, produces 18 duplicate plans. I gestured at an `assignment_batch_id` client-supplied key and then did not put it in the schema. The same gap applies to copy-week: a retried copy of week 1 into week 2 hits `workout_plan_days_slot_unique` and aborts — which is at least loud — but copy-week into 'the next free index' would silently duplicate.

DENORMALISED COLUMNS PROTECTED ONLY ON INSERT. `workout_log_items.client_id` has a BEFORE INSERT coherence trigger; `workout_log_items.performed_on` has none, and neither has an UPDATE twin. If a log's `performed_on` is ever corrected (a client logging yesterday's session today), the items' copies drift and `workout_log_items_history_idx` — the index behind PREVIOUS-performance, the progress graph and PR recomputation — silently orders history wrongly. I chose the denormalisation for a genuinely hot read and then under-defended it.

PER-SET OVERRIDES CREATE ORPHANS NOTHING CLEANS UP. A coach who writes four `workout_plan_item_sets` rows and then lowers `target_sets` from 4 to 3 leaves a row at set_index 3 that the player will never show and no constraint forbids. There is no cross-row CHECK that could catch it, no trigger written for it, and the copy/clone transactions will faithfully duplicate the orphan forever. It also doubles the id-remapping work in every copy transaction, which is where copy bugs will live.

EXERCISE_RECORDS ARE PER-USER AND GLOBAL, WITH NO COACH ERA. Correct for the athlete — your PRs are yours across coaches — but a coach cannot ask 'what has this client PR'd since I started with them' without a date filter the UI must remember to apply, and `previous_value` holds only one step of history, so the progress narrative a coach wants ('+15 kg in eight weeks') has to be reconstructed from the log rather than read.

YYYYMMDD CIVIL DATES WILL SURPRISE THE NEXT READER. They are INTEGERs and they sort, but they are not epoch seconds and every grep for `unixepoch()` will miss them. Date arithmetic in SQL is impossible on them — 'the week containing today' and 'seven days later' must round-trip through JS — so a careless `scheduled_on + 7` produces 20260833. Nothing in the schema prevents that; only a lib/date.js that does not exist yet would.

DAY-LEVEL REORDERING IS UNDER-SPECIFIED RELATIVE TO ITEM-LEVEL. `workout_plan_days_slot_unique (plan_id, week_index, day_index)` has exactly the same permutation-collision problem as item positions, and I specified the two-pass solution only for items. Days move rarely — usually you rename them — but 'rarely' is not 'never', and the first coach to drag Wednesday before Tuesday will hit a UNIQUE violation surfacing as a 500.

designs.name: 009_workouts — history-integrity schema for plans, execution, records and analytics
designs.thesis: A workout log is a historical fact, not a view of current state: every measurement is frozen at the database level once checked, every derived value is either provably immutable (stored) or a single index seek away (never stored), and the only mutation the log path permits is a void that leaves a tombstone.

tables.name: workout_plans
tables.purpose: The plan document. Doubles as the coach's template library (is_template=1, no client) and as an assigned plan (is_template=0, client + coach_clients link). Carries the scheduling rule (cycle_days + starts_on) rather than materialised dates, a monotonically bumped `revision` that logs snapshot, and `source_plan_id`/`source_revision` so 'which template produces adherence' is answerable. Ownership is the coach_clients LINK id, not the client's user id, so archiving the link ends coach access on the next read.
tables.ddl:
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS workout_plans (
  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  owner_user_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  -- Who authored it. 'system' is reserved for a future product-shipped starter library, which is
  -- the only case that will ever need a workout_plan_translations table; coach- and client-authored
  -- names are the author's own prose and are never translated, exactly like onboarding notes.
  origin TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'coach' CHECK (origin IN ('coach', 'client', 'system')),
  is_template INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 CHECK (is_template IN (0, 1)),
  -- The LINK, not the client's user id. onboarding/routes.js:255-265 established that the link
  -- carries the proof; keeping that here means an archived link stops matching immediately.
  coach_client_id INTEGER REFERENCES coach_clients(id) ON DELETE SET NULL,
  -- Denormalised from the link so the client's own guard is single-table `WHERE client_user_id = ?`.
  -- Also the reason a client keeps reading their plan after the coach archives them.
  client_user_id  INTEGER REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  source_plan_id  INTEGER REFERENCES workout_plans(id) ON DELETE SET NULL,
  source_revision INTEGER CHECK (source_revision IS NULL OR source_revision > 0),
  name TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (length(trim(name)) BETWEEN 1 AND 120),
  description TEXT CHECK (description IS NULL OR length(description) <= 2000),
  -- Same vocabulary as onboarding_profiles.primary_goal, verbatim, so a suggestion query can join
  -- the two without a translation layer between two spellings of the same idea.
  goal TEXT CHECK (goal IS NULL OR goal IN (
    'strength', 'muscle', 'fat-loss', 'endurance', 'mobility', 'health', 'sport'
  )),
  status TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'draft' CHECK (status IN ('draft', 'active', 'archived')),
  -- The schedule is a RULE, not a table of dates: a 7-day week or a 14-day A/B block, anchored at
  -- starts_on. Materialising occurrences would need a job and would drift the moment starts_on moved.
  cycle_days INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 7 CHECK (cycle_days BETWEEN 1 AND 56),
  starts_on TEXT CHECK (starts_on IS NULL OR starts_on GLOB '[0-9][0-9][0-9][0-9]-[0-9][0-9]-[0-9][0-9]'),
  ends_on   TEXT CHECK (ends_on   IS NULL OR ends_on   GLOB '[0-9][0-9][0-9][0-9]-[0-9][0-9]-[0-9][0-9]'),
  -- Bumped by the app inside the same transaction as any structural edit. Logs snapshot it, so a
  -- rewritten plan never re-labels the sessions that ran against the old one.
  revision INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 1 CHECK (revision > 0),
  -- ICS subscription URLs cannot carry a cookie, so the calendar feed needs its own bearer secret.
  -- Stored as a hash and shown once, exactly like invite_codes.code_hash; regenerate to see it again.
  ics_token_hash TEXT,
  ics_token_issued_at INTEGER,
  created_at INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT (unixepoch()),
  updated_at INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT (unixepoch()),
  archived_at INTEGER,
  -- A template belongs to nobody; an assigned plan belongs to exactly one client. Overloading one
  -- row for both is what makes clone-to-client a single INSERT ... SELECT instead of a second table.
  CHECK ((is_template = 1 AND client_user_id IS NULL AND coach_client_id IS NULL)
      OR (is_template = 0 AND client_user_id IS NOT NULL)),
  -- No link means self-coaching: the client must be the owner. This is the constraint that stops a
  -- coach assigning a plan to a stranger by putting a raw user id in the body.
  CHECK (coach_client_id IS NOT NULL OR client_user_id IS NULL OR client_user_id = owner_user_id),
  CHECK (ends_on IS NULL OR starts_on IS NULL OR ends_on >= starts_on),
  CHECK (status <> 'archived' OR archived_at IS NOT NULL)
);

-- The coach's library and template picker.
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS workout_plans_owner_idx  ON workout_plans (owner_user_id, is_template, status);
-- The client's own plans and the Home "today" card.
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS workout_plans_client_idx ON workout_plans (client_user_id, status, id);
-- The coach reading one client, joined through the link so archiving ends it.
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS workout_plans_link_idx   ON workout_plans (coach_client_id, status);
-- Provenance analytics: how many plans came from this template, and how did they do.
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS workout_plans_source_idx ON workout_plans (source_plan_id);
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS workout_plans_ics_unique
  ON workout_plans (ics_token_hash) WHERE ics_token_hash IS NOT NULL;

-- 008 form, WHEN-guarded so it cannot recurse through its own UPDATE and cannot clobber an
-- updated_at the caller set deliberately.
CREATE TRIGGER IF NOT EXISTS trg_workout_plans_touch
AFTER UPDATE ON workout_plans FOR EACH ROW
WHEN NEW.updated_at = OLD.updated_at
BEGIN
  UPDATE workout_plans SET updated_at = unixepoch() WHERE id = NEW.id;
END;

tables.name: workout_plan_days
tables.purpose: One session slot in the cycle. `day_index` is a position in the cycle (0..cycle_days-1), never a date. `slot` allows a genuine two-a-day without weakening the uniqueness that keeps the calendar deterministic. A rest day is an explicit row so 'recover today' and 'nothing scheduled' are different messages and adherence does not punish a prescribed rest.
tables.ddl:
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS workout_plan_days (
  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  plan_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES workout_plans(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  -- Position in the cycle, 0-based. The calendar maps it to a date through the plan's starts_on;
  -- the row itself never knows a date. (day_index < plan.cycle_days is enforced in zod and in the
  -- day-create transaction: SQLite cannot express a CHECK against a parent row.)
  day_index INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (day_index BETWEEN 0 AND 55),
  -- Two-a-days are real. Without this, UNIQUE(plan_id, day_index) would forbid them.
  slot INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 CHECK (slot BETWEEN 0 AND 3),
  name TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (length(trim(name)) BETWEEN 1 AND 80),
  notes TEXT CHECK (notes IS NULL OR length(notes) <= 2000),
  -- An explicit rest row, not a gap. Adherence counts prescribed sessions; a gap is not one.
  is_rest INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 CHECK (is_rest IN (0, 1)),
  est_minutes INTEGER CHECK (est_minutes IS NULL OR est_minutes BETWEEN 5 AND 300),
  created_at INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT (unixepoch()),
  updated_at INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT (unixepoch())
);

-- UNIQUE here on purpose, unlike the `position` columns below: (day_index, slot) is a SEMANTIC
-- coordinate the calendar resolves, not a drag-reorder index. Copy-day and move-day pick a free
-- slot rather than swapping values, so there is no mid-transaction collision to dance around.
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS workout_plan_days_slot_unique
  ON workout_plan_days (plan_id, day_index, slot);

CREATE TRIGGER IF NOT EXISTS trg_workout_plan_days_touch
AFTER UPDATE ON workout_plan_days FOR EACH ROW
WHEN NEW.updated_at = OLD.updated_at
BEGIN
  UPDATE workout_plan_days SET updated_at = unixepoch() WHERE id = NEW.id;
END;

tables.name: workout_plan_groups
tables.purpose: The superset/circuit container. EVERY item belongs to a group, including a solo exercise (kind='single'), so ordering within a day is total and unambiguous and no renderer needs an 'is this grouped' branch. Exists as a real table rather than a group_key string because rounds, inter-round rest and a time cap are attributes of the GROUP and have nowhere else to live.
tables.ddl:
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS workout_plan_groups (
  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  day_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES workout_plan_days(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  kind TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'single'
       CHECK (kind IN ('single', 'superset', 'circuit', 'emom', 'amrap')),
  position INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 CHECK (position >= 0),
  -- A circuit repeats the whole GROUP; a straight set repeats the ITEM. That is why rounds is here
  -- and target_sets is on the item, and why a `group_key TEXT` on the item could not have worked.
  rounds INTEGER CHECK (rounds IS NULL OR rounds BETWEEN 1 AND 50),
  rest_seconds INTEGER CHECK (rest_seconds IS NULL OR rest_seconds BETWEEN 0 AND 3600),
  cap_seconds  INTEGER CHECK (cap_seconds  IS NULL OR cap_seconds  BETWEEN 10 AND 7200),
  label TEXT CHECK (label IS NULL OR length(trim(label)) BETWEEN 1 AND 40),
  created_at INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT (unixepoch()),
  CHECK (kind <> 'single' OR (rounds IS NULL AND cap_seconds IS NULL))
);

-- Deliberately NOT unique. A drag-reorder rewrites every position in one transaction, and SQLite
-- checks UNIQUE per statement, so a unique (day_id, position) would abort halfway through a legal
-- reorder. `id` is the tie-break that keeps the order total when two positions collide.
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS workout_plan_groups_day_idx ON workout_plan_groups (day_id, position, id);

tables.name: workout_plan_items
tables.purpose: The prescription: which exercise, how many sets, reps OR time OR distance, load, %1RM, RPE, tempo, rest. Carries a trigger-enforced denormalised day_id so that 'all items of a day' is one seek and an item can never be re-parented into another plan's day. The weight columns store canonical kilograms plus the unit and number the coach actually typed, with a CHECK that the two describe the same load.
tables.ddl:
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS workout_plan_items (
  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  group_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES workout_plan_groups(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  -- Denormalised from the group, trigger-enforced. Renders a whole day without a three-table join
  -- and makes cross-plan re-parenting impossible rather than merely discouraged.
  day_id   INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES workout_plan_days(id)   ON DELETE CASCADE,
  -- RESTRICT, not CASCADE: an exercise that appears in a plan cannot be hard-deleted out from under
  -- it. Soft delete (deleted_at) remains the normal path and is unaffected.
  exercise_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES exercises(id) ON DELETE RESTRICT,
  position INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 CHECK (position >= 0),

  target_metric TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'reps' CHECK (target_metric IN ('reps', 'time', 'distance')),
  target_sets INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 3 CHECK (target_sets BETWEEN 1 AND 50),
  -- A RANGE, because "8-12" is how coaches actually write it. A single target_reps would force
  -- min = max and lose the coach's intent.
  target_reps_min INTEGER CHECK (target_reps_min IS NULL OR target_reps_min BETWEEN 1 AND 1000),
  target_reps_max INTEGER CHECK (target_reps_max IS NULL OR target_reps_max BETWEEN 1 AND 1000),
  target_seconds    INTEGER CHECK (target_seconds    IS NULL OR target_seconds    BETWEEN 1 AND 7200),
  -- Metres. Never miles, never a unit column: distance has the same double-conversion hazard as load.
  target_distance_m INTEGER CHECK (target_distance_m IS NULL OR target_distance_m BETWEEN 1 AND 200000),

  target_weight_kg REAL CHECK (target_weight_kg IS NULL OR (target_weight_kg >= 0 AND target_weight_kg <= 1000)),
  -- What the coach TYPED, in the unit they typed it in. Not a duplicate of target_weight_kg: it is a
  -- separate historical fact, it makes the imperial round-trip exact instead of 225 -> 224.99 lb,
  -- and it is what a future "we shipped a conversion bug" audit re-derives from.
  target_weight_entry_unit  TEXT CHECK (target_weight_entry_unit IS NULL OR target_weight_entry_unit IN ('kg', 'lb')),
  target_weight_entry_value REAL CHECK (target_weight_entry_value IS NULL OR (target_weight_entry_value >= 0 AND target_weight_entry_value <= 2500)),
  target_percent_1rm REAL CHECK (target_percent_1rm IS NULL OR target_percent_1rm BETWEEN 1 AND 200),
  -- RPE moves in half points. RIR is deliberately absent: RIR = 10 - RPE, and two columns for one
  -- fact is two chances to disagree.
  target_rpe REAL CHECK (target_rpe IS NULL OR target_rpe IN
    (1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, 3.5, 4, 4.5, 5, 5.5, 6, 6.5, 7, 7.5, 8, 8.5, 9, 9.5, 10)),
  rest_seconds INTEGER CHECK (rest_seconds IS NULL OR rest_seconds BETWEEN 0 AND 3600),
  -- Four-digit tempo notation, e.g. '3010' or '30X1'.
  tempo TEXT CHECK (tempo IS NULL OR tempo GLOB '[0-9X][0-9X][0-9X][0-9X]'),
  notes TEXT CHECK (notes IS NULL OR length(notes) <= 1000),
  created_at INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT (unixepoch()),
  updated_at INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT (unixepoch()),

  CHECK (target_reps_max IS NULL OR target_reps_min IS NULL OR target_reps_max >= target_reps_min),
  CHECK (target_metric <> 'reps'     OR target_reps_min   IS NOT NULL),
  CHECK (target_metric <> 'time'     OR target_seconds    IS NOT NULL),
  CHECK (target_metric <> 'distance' OR target_distance_m IS NOT NULL),
  -- THE double-conversion guard. A 225 lb prescription stored as 225 kg fails at write time instead
  -- of shipping a 2.2x error to a client's phone.
  CHECK (target_weight_kg IS NULL OR target_weight_entry_value IS NULL
      OR (target_weight_entry_unit = 'kg' AND abs(target_weight_kg - target_weight_entry_value) < 0.02)
      OR (target_weight_entry_unit = 'lb' AND abs(target_weight_kg - target_weight_entry_value * 0.45359237) < 0.02))
);

CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS workout_plan_items_group_idx    ON workout_plan_items (group_id, position, id);
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS workout_plan_items_day_idx      ON workout_plan_items (day_id, position, id);
-- Serves both "which plans use this exercise" (a coach editing their library) and the EXISTS clause
-- that grants a client read access to a non-global exercise they have been prescribed.
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS workout_plan_items_exercise_idx ON workout_plan_items (exercise_id);

CREATE TRIGGER IF NOT EXISTS trg_workout_plan_items_parent
BEFORE INSERT ON workout_plan_items FOR EACH ROW
WHEN NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM workout_plan_groups g WHERE g.id = NEW.group_id AND g.day_id = NEW.day_id)
BEGIN
  SELECT RAISE(ABORT, 'workout_plan_items.day_id must match the parent group day');
END;

CREATE TRIGGER IF NOT EXISTS trg_workout_plan_items_reparent
BEFORE UPDATE OF group_id, day_id ON workout_plan_items FOR EACH ROW
WHEN NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM workout_plan_groups g WHERE g.id = NEW.group_id AND g.day_id = NEW.day_id)
BEGIN
  SELECT RAISE(ABORT, 'workout_plan_items.day_id must match the parent group day');
END;

CREATE TRIGGER IF NOT EXISTS trg_workout_plan_items_touch
AFTER UPDATE ON workout_plan_items FOR EACH ROW
WHEN NEW.updated_at = OLD.updated_at
BEGIN
  UPDATE workout_plan_items SET updated_at = unixepoch() WHERE id = NEW.id;
END;

tables.name: workout_plan_item_sets
tables.purpose: Optional per-set refinement for ramping and pyramid work ('5 @ 80, 3 @ 90, 1 @ 100'), which a uniform 3x5 item cannot express. If an item has rows here they win; if it has none, startWorkoutTx expands target_sets uniformly. The branch therefore lives in exactly one place — the session-start transaction — and never in a renderer.
tables.ddl:
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS workout_plan_item_sets (
  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  item_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES workout_plan_items(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  set_index INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (set_index BETWEEN 1 AND 50),
  -- Prescribed warmups exist and must be excluded from volume and PRs just like logged ones.
  is_warmup INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 CHECK (is_warmup IN (0, 1)),
  target_reps       INTEGER CHECK (target_reps       IS NULL OR target_reps       BETWEEN 0 AND 1000),
  target_seconds    INTEGER CHECK (target_seconds    IS NULL OR target_seconds    BETWEEN 1 AND 7200),
  target_distance_m INTEGER CHECK (target_distance_m IS NULL OR target_distance_m BETWEEN 1 AND 200000),
  target_weight_kg REAL CHECK (target_weight_kg IS NULL OR (target_weight_kg >= 0 AND target_weight_kg <= 1000)),
  target_weight_entry_unit  TEXT CHECK (target_weight_entry_unit IS NULL OR target_weight_entry_unit IN ('kg', 'lb')),
  target_weight_entry_value REAL CHECK (target_weight_entry_value IS NULL OR (target_weight_entry_value >= 0 AND target_weight_entry_value <= 2500)),
  target_percent_1rm REAL CHECK (target_percent_1rm IS NULL OR target_percent_1rm BETWEEN 1 AND 200),
  target_rpe REAL CHECK (target_rpe IS NULL OR target_rpe IN
    (1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, 3.5, 4, 4.5, 5, 5.5, 6, 6.5, 7, 7.5, 8, 8.5, 9, 9.5, 10)),
  rest_seconds INTEGER CHECK (rest_seconds IS NULL OR rest_seconds BETWEEN 0 AND 3600),
  CHECK (target_weight_kg IS NULL OR target_weight_entry_value IS NULL
      OR (target_weight_entry_unit = 'kg' AND abs(target_weight_kg - target_weight_entry_value) < 0.02)
      OR (target_weight_entry_unit = 'lb' AND abs(target_weight_kg - target_weight_entry_value * 0.45359237) < 0.02))
);

-- UNIQUE is safe here because set_index is semantic and the editor replaces the whole ladder
-- delete-then-insert inside one transaction (the onboarding_equipment precedent), never incrementally.
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS workout_plan_item_sets_unique ON workout_plan_item_sets (item_id, set_index);

tables.name: workout_plan_day_exceptions
tables.purpose: The sparse escape hatch from the cycle rule: 'skip this Tuesday' or 'move it to Wednesday'. One row only when a human intervenes, so a year of a plan running normally costs zero rows. This is what makes a rule-based calendar survive contact with real life without materialising every occurrence.
tables.ddl:
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS workout_plan_day_exceptions (
  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  plan_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES workout_plans(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  day_id  INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES workout_plan_days(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  -- The date the CYCLE would have produced. The calendar generator emits occurrences and left-joins
  -- this table, so an exception is a diff against the rule, not a replacement for it.
  occurrence_date TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (occurrence_date GLOB '[0-9][0-9][0-9][0-9]-[0-9][0-9]-[0-9][0-9]'),
  action TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (action IN ('skip', 'move')),
  moved_to_date TEXT CHECK (moved_to_date IS NULL OR moved_to_date GLOB '[0-9][0-9][0-9][0-9]-[0-9][0-9]-[0-9][0-9]'),
  reason TEXT CHECK (reason IS NULL OR length(reason) <= 200),
  created_by INTEGER REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE SET NULL,
  created_at INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT (unixepoch()),
  CHECK (action <> 'move' OR moved_to_date IS NOT NULL),
  CHECK (action <> 'skip' OR moved_to_date IS NULL)
);

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS workout_plan_day_exceptions_unique
  ON workout_plan_day_exceptions (day_id, occurrence_date);
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS workout_plan_day_exceptions_plan_idx
  ON workout_plan_day_exceptions (plan_id, occurrence_date);

tables.name: workout_logs
tables.purpose: One training session. Snapshots the plan's identity (revision, plan name, day name) so history renders after the plan is rewritten or deleted, snapshots bodyweight and the user's local date so analytics never depend on a profile that changes, and carries session rollups written ONLY by the transactions that can invalidate them. Two partial unique indexes do work that would otherwise be racy application logic: one live session per client, one log per prescribed occurrence.
tables.ddl:
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS workout_logs (
  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  client_user_id  INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  -- Provenance of WHO prescribed it, and the coach's read path. SET NULL, not CASCADE: deleting a
  -- coaching relationship must never delete the client's training history.
  coach_client_id INTEGER REFERENCES coach_clients(id) ON DELETE SET NULL,
  plan_id     INTEGER REFERENCES workout_plans(id)     ON DELETE SET NULL,
  plan_day_id INTEGER REFERENCES workout_plan_days(id) ON DELETE SET NULL,
  -- Which revision of the plan this session ran against. "These 40 sessions used revision 3" is an
  -- analytics question that a mutable plan cannot answer without this.
  plan_revision INTEGER CHECK (plan_revision IS NULL OR plan_revision > 0),
  -- Name snapshots, once per session (not per set). The session must still say what it was even
  -- after the plan is deleted and the FK above has gone to NULL.
  plan_name_snapshot TEXT CHECK (plan_name_snapshot IS NULL OR length(plan_name_snapshot) <= 120),
  day_name_snapshot  TEXT CHECK (day_name_snapshot  IS NULL OR length(day_name_snapshot)  <= 80),
  occurrence_date TEXT CHECK (occurrence_date IS NULL OR occurrence_date GLOB '[0-9][0-9][0-9][0-9]-[0-9][0-9]-[0-9][0-9]'),
  title TEXT CHECK (title IS NULL OR length(trim(title)) BETWEEN 1 AND 120),

  status TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'in_progress' CHECK (status IN ('in_progress', 'completed', 'abandoned')),
  started_at   INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT (unixepoch()),
  completed_at INTEGER,
  -- THE analytic unit. Epoch seconds are UTC; a 01:00 session in UTC+2 is the previous UTC day, so
  -- grouping by date(started_at,'unixepoch') puts it in the wrong week. Computed SERVER-side in JS
  -- from started_at and the profile's IANA timezone (SQLite has no tz database), never sent by the
  -- client, and never recomputed: the workout happened on that Tuesday forever, even if the user
  -- later moves to Australia.
  local_date TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (local_date GLOB '[0-9][0-9][0-9][0-9]-[0-9][0-9]-[0-9][0-9]'),
  tz_name TEXT CHECK (tz_name IS NULL OR length(tz_name) BETWEEN 3 AND 64),
  tz_offset_minutes INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 CHECK (tz_offset_minutes BETWEEN -840 AND 840),

  -- Snapshot, not a join to onboarding_profiles: bodyweight changes, and bodyweight-relative volume
  -- for a 2026 session must use the 2026 number.
  bodyweight_kg REAL CHECK (bodyweight_kg IS NULL OR bodyweight_kg BETWEEN 25 AND 400),
  -- NOT completed_at - started_at. A session left open on a locked phone has a real duration the
  -- player tracks and a wall-clock span that is a lie; both are facts, so both are stored.
  duration_seconds INTEGER CHECK (duration_seconds IS NULL OR duration_seconds BETWEEN 0 AND 86400),
  perceived_effort INTEGER CHECK (perceived_effort IS NULL OR perceived_effort BETWEEN 1 AND 10),
  notes TEXT CHECK (notes IS NULL OR length(notes) <= 2000),

  -- Rollups. The ONLY stored aggregate in the schema, and it is safe for one reason: it is
  -- recomputed by the same IMMEDIATE transaction as every write that could invalidate it
  -- (completeWorkoutTx, voidSetTx, appendSetTx). A rollup drifts when the mutation path and the
  -- recompute path are different transactions; here there is no such path.
  total_sets         INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 CHECK (total_sets >= 0),
  total_working_sets INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 CHECK (total_working_sets >= 0),
  total_reps         INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 CHECK (total_reps >= 0),
  total_volume_kg    REAL    NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 CHECK (total_volume_kg >= 0),
  total_work_seconds INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 CHECK (total_work_seconds >= 0),
  -- Makes a stale rollup visible instead of merely wrong. A rollup_at older than the newest set in
  -- the session is a bug the smoke test can assert on.
  rollup_at INTEGER,

  created_at INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT (unixepoch()),
  updated_at INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT (unixepoch()),

  CHECK (status <> 'completed' OR completed_at IS NOT NULL),
  CHECK (completed_at IS NULL OR completed_at >= started_at)
);

-- The client's history feed, streaks and calendar. local_date leads because the user's day, not the
-- UTC instant, is what every one of those groups by.
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS workout_logs_client_date_idx ON workout_logs (client_user_id, local_date, id);
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS workout_logs_link_idx        ON workout_logs (coach_client_id, local_date);
-- Adherence: which prescribed occurrences were actually trained.
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS workout_logs_plan_idx        ON workout_logs (plan_id, occurrence_date);
-- One live session per client, enforced by the database. Two phones cannot start two workouts and
-- then both write PRs; the second INSERT simply fails.
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS workout_logs_one_active
  ON workout_logs (client_user_id) WHERE status = 'in_progress';
-- One log per prescribed occurrence. A double-tapped "Start workout" is deduped here rather than by
-- a SELECT-then-INSERT in the route, which would be a race.
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS workout_logs_occurrence_unique
  ON workout_logs (client_user_id, plan_day_id, occurrence_date)
  WHERE plan_day_id IS NOT NULL AND status <> 'abandoned';

CREATE TRIGGER IF NOT EXISTS trg_workout_logs_touch
AFTER UPDATE ON workout_logs FOR EACH ROW
WHEN NEW.updated_at = OLD.updated_at
BEGIN
  UPDATE workout_logs SET updated_at = unixepoch() WHERE id = NEW.id;
END;

-- A finished session cannot be re-dated into a different week, re-owned, or reopened. Rollup columns
-- and notes stay writable so a correction can recompute them.
CREATE TRIGGER IF NOT EXISTS trg_workout_logs_frozen
BEFORE UPDATE ON workout_logs FOR EACH ROW
WHEN OLD.status = 'completed'
 AND (NEW.client_user_id IS NOT OLD.client_user_id
   OR NEW.local_date     IS NOT OLD.local_date
   OR NEW.started_at     IS NOT OLD.started_at
   OR NEW.completed_at   IS NOT OLD.completed_at
   OR NEW.status         IS NOT OLD.status)
BEGIN
  SELECT RAISE(ABORT, 'a completed session cannot be re-dated, re-owned or reopened');
END;

tables.name: workout_log_exercises
tables.purpose: The per-exercise grouping inside a session. Exists so the exercise's display name is snapshotted once per session instead of once per set, so a per-exercise note and superset grouping have a home, and so the guided player's 'previous performance' lookup has a natural unit. Its user_id is trigger-checked against the parent log.
tables.ddl:
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS workout_log_exercises (
  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  log_id  INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES workout_logs(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  -- Denormalised owner, trigger-enforced against the log. Makes every ownership guard single-table.
  user_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  exercise_id  INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES exercises(id) ON DELETE RESTRICT,
  plan_item_id INTEGER REFERENCES workout_plan_items(id) ON DELETE SET NULL,
  -- The exercise's name in the CLIENT's language at the time. This is the safety net for the
  -- visibility problem: a coach's private exercise, a renamed exercise, or an exercise an admin
  -- hard-deletes must still render in a two-year-old log. It is a SNAPSHOT, not a replacement for
  -- exercise_id — the FK is what the progress graph and the muscle map still join on.
  exercise_name_snapshot TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (length(trim(exercise_name_snapshot)) BETWEEN 1 AND 200),
  exercise_lang_snapshot TEXT CHECK (exercise_lang_snapshot IS NULL OR exercise_lang_snapshot GLOB '[a-z][a-z]'),
  group_kind TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'single'
             CHECK (group_kind IN ('single', 'superset', 'circuit', 'emom', 'amrap')),
  group_ordinal INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 CHECK (group_ordinal >= 0),
  position INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 CHECK (position >= 0),
  target_metric TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'reps' CHECK (target_metric IN ('reps', 'time', 'distance')),
  notes TEXT CHECK (notes IS NULL OR length(notes) <= 1000),
  created_at INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT (unixepoch())
);

CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS workout_log_exercises_log_idx  ON workout_log_exercises (log_id, group_ordinal, position, id);
-- "The last time this user trained this exercise" — the player's PREVIOUS column resolves the prior
-- log_exercise here, then reads its whole set list, instead of one query per set row.
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS workout_log_exercises_hist_idx ON workout_log_exercises (user_id, exercise_id, id);

CREATE TRIGGER IF NOT EXISTS trg_workout_log_exercises_parent
BEFORE INSERT ON workout_log_exercises FOR EACH ROW
WHEN NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM workout_logs l WHERE l.id = NEW.log_id AND l.client_user_id = NEW.user_id)
BEGIN
  SELECT RAISE(ABORT, 'workout_log_exercises.user_id must be the owning session client');
END;

tables.name: workout_log_sets
tables.purpose: The atom of history and the only table analytics ever scans. Carries trigger-enforced user_id/exercise_id/local_date denormalisation so every PR, graph and ownership query is a single covering index seek with no joins. weight_kg is canonical kilograms; entry_unit/entry_value record what the human typed and a CHECK refuses a double conversion. volume_kg is a STORED generated column (a definition, cannot drift). e1rm_kg is app-written and frozen (a model, must not retro-change) with its formula code alongside, and is NULL outside Epley's reliable window rather than wrong inside it. A completed set is immutable at trigger level: the only edit is a void.
tables.ddl:
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS workout_log_sets (
  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  log_exercise_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES workout_log_exercises(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  -- log_id / user_id / exercise_id are denormalised from the parent and enforced by
  -- trg_workout_log_sets_parent. Two reasons, both load-bearing:
  --   (1) ANTI-IDOR: the guard inside every UPDATE becomes `WHERE id = ? AND user_id = ?` — one
  --       table, no join, impossible to get subtly wrong.
  --   (2) ANALYTICS: every progress and PR query is (user_id, exercise_id, ...). Without this each
  --       one is a three-table join over the largest table in the database.
  -- Enforced denormalisation is not drift: the trigger makes disagreement impossible.
  log_id      INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES workout_logs(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  user_id     INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  exercise_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES exercises(id) ON DELETE RESTRICT,
  plan_item_set_id INTEGER REFERENCES workout_plan_item_sets(id) ON DELETE SET NULL,

  -- The idempotency key. Minted ONCE by the player per set row and reused on every retry, so a
  -- replayed insert collides on the UNIQUE index below instead of creating a phantom set.
  client_set_uid TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (length(client_set_uid) BETWEEN 8 AND 64),
  set_index INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (set_index BETWEEN 1 AND 100),
  -- Warmups are excluded from volume, from PRs and from every partial index below. Forgetting this
  -- is the single most common way a fitness app reports a fake PR.
  is_warmup INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 CHECK (is_warmup IN (0, 1)),
  set_kind TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'straight'
           CHECK (set_kind IN ('straight', 'warmup', 'drop', 'amrap', 'failure', 'backoff')),

  -- The PRESCRIPTION, frozen onto the row at session start. This is why plans can stay mutable
  -- documents: "did the client hit the target?" is answerable forever from the log alone, even after
  -- the coach rewrote the plan the next morning. Same pattern as an order line's price snapshot.
  target_reps       INTEGER CHECK (target_reps       IS NULL OR target_reps       BETWEEN 0 AND 1000),
  target_seconds    INTEGER CHECK (target_seconds    IS NULL OR target_seconds    BETWEEN 1 AND 7200),
  target_distance_m INTEGER CHECK (target_distance_m IS NULL OR target_distance_m BETWEEN 1 AND 200000),
  target_weight_kg  REAL    CHECK (target_weight_kg  IS NULL OR (target_weight_kg >= 0 AND target_weight_kg <= 1000)),
  target_rpe REAL CHECK (target_rpe IS NULL OR target_rpe IN
    (1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, 3.5, 4, 4.5, 5, 5.5, 6, 6.5, 7, 7.5, 8, 8.5, 9, 9.5, 10)),
  target_rest_seconds INTEGER CHECK (target_rest_seconds IS NULL OR target_rest_seconds BETWEEN 0 AND 3600),

  -- What actually happened. Kilograms, always. The bounds are history integrity, not politeness: one
  -- 999999 kg set poisons every chart and every PR for that exercise, permanently.
  weight_kg REAL CHECK (weight_kg IS NULL OR (weight_kg >= 0 AND weight_kg <= 1000)),
  entry_unit TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'kg' CHECK (entry_unit IN ('kg', 'lb')),
  entry_value REAL CHECK (entry_value IS NULL OR (entry_value >= 0 AND entry_value <= 2500)),
  reps       INTEGER CHECK (reps       IS NULL OR reps       BETWEEN 0 AND 1000),
  seconds    INTEGER CHECK (seconds    IS NULL OR seconds    BETWEEN 0 AND 7200),
  distance_m INTEGER CHECK (distance_m IS NULL OR distance_m BETWEEN 0 AND 200000),
  rpe REAL CHECK (rpe IS NULL OR rpe IN
    (1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, 3.5, 4, 4.5, 5, 5.5, 6, 6.5, 7, 7.5, 8, 8.5, 9, 9.5, 10)),
  -- Actual rest, reported by the player. Distinct from completed_at deltas, which include racking,
  -- talking and phone-checking. Density analytics needs the real number.
  rest_taken_seconds INTEGER CHECK (rest_taken_seconds IS NULL OR rest_taken_seconds BETWEEN 0 AND 3600),

  -- GENERATED, because tonnage is a DEFINITION (weight x reps) with no competing formula. SQLite
  -- computes it, so it cannot drift and cannot be forged. STORED so a year-long volume scan reads it
  -- rather than evaluating an expression per row.
  volume_kg REAL GENERATED ALWAYS AS (
    CASE WHEN weight_kg IS NOT NULL AND reps IS NOT NULL THEN weight_kg * reps END
  ) STORED,
  -- NOT generated, on purpose. A 1RM estimate is a MODEL, not a definition: there are five formulas.
  -- A generated column would silently re-shape every historical chart the day the formula changed.
  -- Written by completeSetTx, frozen by the trigger below, and tagged with the formula that produced
  -- it so old points keep their old model and new points can use a new one.
  e1rm_kg REAL CHECK (e1rm_kg IS NULL OR (e1rm_kg > 0 AND e1rm_kg <= 2000)),
  e1rm_formula TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'epley' CHECK (e1rm_formula IN ('epley', 'brzycki', 'lombardi')),

  -- Denormalised from the log so the progress graph is a covering index scan with no join at all.
  local_date TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (local_date GLOB '[0-9][0-9][0-9][0-9]-[0-9][0-9]-[0-9][0-9]'),
  completed_at INTEGER,
  -- Corrections are appends. `voided_at` is the tombstone every analytics query filters out, and
  -- `corrects_set_id` links the replacement to what it replaced. Nothing in the log path deletes.
  voided_at INTEGER,
  voided_reason TEXT CHECK (voided_reason IS NULL OR length(voided_reason) <= 200),
  corrects_set_id INTEGER REFERENCES workout_log_sets(id) ON DELETE SET NULL,
  created_at INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT (unixepoch()),

  -- THE double-conversion guard: the number the user typed and the canonical kilograms must describe
  -- the same load. 225 lb entered and 225 stored as kg is a write failure, not a silent 2.2x error.
  CHECK (entry_value IS NULL OR weight_kg IS NULL
      OR (entry_unit = 'kg' AND abs(weight_kg - entry_value) < 0.02)
      OR (entry_unit = 'lb' AND abs(weight_kg - entry_value * 0.45359237) < 0.02)),
  CHECK (is_warmup = 0 OR set_kind = 'warmup'),
  CHECK (voided_at IS NULL OR voided_reason IS NOT NULL),
  -- Epley is unreliable past ~12 reps and undefined without load. NULL is honest; a number here
  -- would put a fake 1RM on the chart from a 30-rep bodyweight set.
  CHECK (e1rm_kg IS NULL OR (weight_kg > 0 AND reps BETWEEN 1 AND 12)),
  -- The arithmetic itself, checked by the database, and VERSIONED BY THE FORMULA COLUMN: a future
  -- 'brzycki' row is permitted unconditionally while every historical 'epley' row stays verified.
  -- Note reps = 1 returns the weight itself; naive Epley would inflate every single by 3.3%.
  CHECK (e1rm_kg IS NULL OR e1rm_formula <> 'epley'
      OR abs(e1rm_kg - (CASE WHEN reps = 1 THEN weight_kg ELSE weight_kg * (1.0 + reps / 30.0) END)) < 0.01)
);

-- Idempotency backstop. A replayed set write cannot create a second row.
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS workout_log_sets_uid_unique
  ON workout_log_sets (log_id, client_set_uid);

-- The player's own grid.
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS workout_log_sets_grid_idx
  ON workout_log_sets (log_exercise_id, set_index, id);

-- The session rollup recompute.
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS workout_log_sets_rollup_idx
  ON workout_log_sets (log_id, voided_at, is_warmup);

-- THE analytics index. Covering: the months-of-data progress graph and the player's PREVIOUS column
-- both read entirely from the index and never touch the table. Partial, so voided sets and warmups
-- are not merely filtered — they are not in the index at all.
-- Measured: 61 us for a full per-day GROUP BY over 72k rows, 20 us for previous-performance.
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS workout_log_sets_progress_idx
  ON workout_log_sets (user_id, exercise_id, local_date, set_index, weight_kg, reps, e1rm_kg, volume_kg)
  WHERE voided_at IS NULL AND is_warmup = 0 AND completed_at IS NOT NULL;

-- Rep-max PR: "heaviest ever at exactly 5 reps" is one seek to the head of the DESC run.
-- Measured: 15 us over 72k rows.
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS workout_log_sets_repmax_idx
  ON workout_log_sets (user_id, exercise_id, reps, weight_kg DESC)
  WHERE voided_at IS NULL AND is_warmup = 0 AND completed_at IS NOT NULL;

-- e1RM PR. The predicate is `e1rm_kg IS NOT NULL` rather than a reps range ON PURPOSE: with a reps
-- range here the PR query must repeat it, and the planner then prefers repmax_idx and adds a TEMP
-- B-TREE sort (verified). Because e1rm_kg is already NULL outside the reliable window, the query
-- mentions no reps term at all and this index wins cleanly. Measured: 17 us over 72k rows.
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS workout_log_sets_e1rm_idx
  ON workout_log_sets (user_id, exercise_id, e1rm_kg DESC)
  WHERE voided_at IS NULL AND is_warmup = 0 AND completed_at IS NOT NULL
    AND e1rm_kg IS NOT NULL;

-- The denormalisation is a guarantee, not a convention.
CREATE TRIGGER IF NOT EXISTS trg_workout_log_sets_parent
BEFORE INSERT ON workout_log_sets FOR EACH ROW
WHEN NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM workout_log_exercises x
   WHERE x.id = NEW.log_exercise_id
     AND x.log_id = NEW.log_id
     AND x.user_id = NEW.user_id
     AND x.exercise_id = NEW.exercise_id
)
BEGIN
  SELECT RAISE(ABORT, 'workout_log_sets: log_id/user_id/exercise_id must match the parent log exercise');
END;

-- The single most important line in this schema. Once a set is checked, its MEASUREMENTS are frozen
-- by the database: no route, no migration script and no console session can rewrite what happened.
-- Un-checking is included deliberately — the undo button calls voidSetTx, which leaves a tombstone
-- and invalidates the PR it earned, rather than erasing the evidence that it was ever awarded.
-- `voided_at`, `voided_reason` and `rest_taken_seconds` stay writable; nothing else does.
CREATE TRIGGER IF NOT EXISTS trg_workout_log_sets_frozen
BEFORE UPDATE ON workout_log_sets FOR EACH ROW
WHEN OLD.completed_at IS NOT NULL
 AND (NEW.weight_kg   IS NOT OLD.weight_kg
   OR NEW.reps        IS NOT OLD.reps
   OR NEW.seconds     IS NOT OLD.seconds
   OR NEW.distance_m  IS NOT OLD.distance_m
   OR NEW.entry_unit  IS NOT OLD.entry_unit
   OR NEW.entry_value IS NOT OLD.entry_value
   OR NEW.e1rm_kg     IS NOT OLD.e1rm_kg
   OR NEW.e1rm_formula IS NOT OLD.e1rm_formula
   OR NEW.is_warmup   IS NOT OLD.is_warmup
   OR NEW.exercise_id IS NOT OLD.exercise_id
   OR NEW.user_id     IS NOT OLD.user_id
   OR NEW.log_id      IS NOT OLD.log_id
   OR NEW.local_date  IS NOT OLD.local_date
   OR NEW.completed_at IS NOT OLD.completed_at)
BEGIN
  SELECT RAISE(ABORT, 'a completed set is immutable: void it and log a correction instead');
END;

tables.name: workout_set_records
tables.purpose: PR EVENTS, not current bests. An append-only fact table: 'at this moment, this set established a new best of kind K, beating this previous value'. There is deliberately NO current-bests cache table anywhere — the current best is one 17 microsecond index seek. What is NOT derivable is that a badge was shown and a reward may have been granted, which is exactly what this stores. A row is never rewritten; a void only sets invalidated_at.
tables.ddl:
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS workout_set_records (
  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id     INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  exercise_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES exercises(id) ON DELETE RESTRICT,
  set_id INTEGER REFERENCES workout_log_sets(id) ON DELETE SET NULL,
  log_id INTEGER REFERENCES workout_logs(id) ON DELETE SET NULL,
  -- THREE kinds, and the choice is the whole argument about what a PR is:
  --   'e1rm'           the PRIMARY badge. The only measure that is monotone in BOTH weight and reps,
  --                    so it is comparable across rep schemes and cannot be gamed by dropping reps.
  --   'rep_max'        the SECONDARY badge, bucketed by rep count, because lifters do not trust
  --                    formulas and want "100 kg for 5, for the first time".
  --   'session_volume' best single-session tonnage for one exercise. Written by completeWorkoutTx,
  --                    not per set, and the one that matters to a hypertrophy-goal client.
  -- Rejected: 'heaviest ever, any reps' (1x100 would beat 10x95) and 'reps_at_weight' (redundant
  -- with rep_max in practice and a fourth thing to invalidate).
  kind TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (kind IN ('e1rm', 'rep_max', 'session_volume')),
  -- reps 1..12 exact, 13+ collapses to 13, 0 = not applicable. NOT NULL with a 0 sentinel rather
  -- than nullable, because SQLite treats NULLs as distinct in a UNIQUE index — a nullable column
  -- here would silently let a replay insert a second e1rm record for the same set.
  rep_bucket INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 CHECK (rep_bucket BETWEEN 0 AND 13),
  value REAL NOT NULL CHECK (value > 0),
  -- The value that was beaten, captured at the moment of beating. Not drift-prone (both operands
  -- were immutable when it was written) and it renders "+2.5 kg on your 5RM" with no second query.
  previous_value REAL CHECK (previous_value IS NULL OR previous_value > 0),
  previous_set_id INTEGER REFERENCES workout_log_sets(id) ON DELETE SET NULL,
  formula TEXT CHECK (formula IS NULL OR formula IN ('epley', 'brzycki', 'lombardi')),
  local_date TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (local_date GLOB '[0-9][0-9][0-9][0-9]-[0-9][0-9]-[0-9][0-9]'),
  achieved_at INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT (unixepoch()),
  -- Set when the source set is voided. The row survives: a coin ledger keyed on this id must still
  -- find its anchor, and "we awarded this and later withdrew it" is itself history.
  invalidated_at INTEGER,
  invalidated_reason TEXT CHECK (invalidated_reason IS NULL OR length(invalidated_reason) <= 200),
  created_at INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT (unixepoch()),
  CHECK (kind <> 'rep_max' OR rep_bucket > 0),
  CHECK (kind <> 'e1rm' OR (rep_bucket = 0 AND formula IS NOT NULL)),
  CHECK (kind <> 'session_volume' OR (rep_bucket = 0 AND set_id IS NULL AND log_id IS NOT NULL)),
  -- A "record" that is not better than what it replaced is a bug, and the database says so.
  CHECK (previous_value IS NULL OR value > previous_value),
  CHECK (invalidated_at IS NULL OR invalidated_reason IS NOT NULL)
);

-- THE reward-idempotency guarantee. Even if completeSetTx were replayed past every other guard, a
-- second PR event for the same (set, kind, rep_bucket) cannot exist. A future coin ledger keys its
-- own idempotency on ('pr', workout_set_records.id), which is why no reward column is invented here.
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS workout_set_records_set_unique
  ON workout_set_records (set_id, kind, rep_bucket) WHERE set_id IS NOT NULL;
-- The same guarantee for session-volume records, which have no set_id.
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS workout_set_records_session_unique
  ON workout_set_records (log_id, exercise_id) WHERE kind = 'session_volume';
-- The records screen: my live bests for one exercise.
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS workout_set_records_current_idx
  ON workout_set_records (user_id, exercise_id, kind, rep_bucket, value DESC)
  WHERE invalidated_at IS NULL;
-- The profile feed: my recent PRs across everything.
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS workout_set_records_feed_idx
  ON workout_set_records (user_id, achieved_at DESC)
  WHERE invalidated_at IS NULL;

-- The audit_log lesson applied to records. A BEFORE DELETE trigger is deliberately absent — it would
-- abort the ON DELETE CASCADE from users and make account deletion impossible.
CREATE TRIGGER IF NOT EXISTS trg_workout_set_records_immutable
BEFORE UPDATE ON workout_set_records FOR EACH ROW
WHEN NEW.user_id        IS NOT OLD.user_id
  OR NEW.exercise_id    IS NOT OLD.exercise_id
  OR NEW.set_id         IS NOT OLD.set_id
  OR NEW.kind           IS NOT OLD.kind
  OR NEW.rep_bucket     IS NOT OLD.rep_bucket
  OR NEW.value          IS NOT OLD.value
  OR NEW.previous_value IS NOT OLD.previous_value
  OR NEW.formula        IS NOT OLD.formula
  OR NEW.local_date     IS NOT OLD.local_date
  OR NEW.achieved_at    IS NOT OLD.achieved_at
BEGIN
  SELECT RAISE(ABORT, 'a personal record is a historical fact: only invalidation may change it');
END;

tables.name: body_area_muscle_map
tables.purpose: The missing bridge that makes T2.5.4 implementable at all. onboarding_limitations.body_area is joint-centric ('knee', 'shoulder') and muscle_groups is muscle-centric ('quads', 'lats'); nothing in the schema joins them, so the avoid-list currently cannot filter a single exercise. A junction with a relation code, seeded from the existing slugs.

tables.name: onboarding_profiles (ALTER)
tables.purpose: The one column the existing profile is missing. Without an IANA timezone the server cannot compute the user's local date, and every 'today' card, streak and weekly-volume bucket silently uses UTC days — which puts a 01:00 session in Budapest into the previous day, and in the previous WEEK once a month. Nullable with no default, which is all ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN permits; the app treats NULL as 'UTC'.
tables.ddl:
-- Nullable and without a default, because SQLite forbids a non-constant DEFAULT on ADD COLUMN and a
-- constant 'UTC' would be indistinguishable from a user who genuinely chose UTC. The client may send
-- its detected IANA zone as a HINT on any profile PATCH; workout_logs.local_date is then computed
-- server-side with Intl.DateTimeFormat and never taken from the request.
ALTER TABLE onboarding_profiles ADD COLUMN timezone TEXT
  CHECK (timezone IS NULL OR length(timezone) BETWEEN 3 AND 64);

keyDecisions.decision: There is NO current-bests cache table. The current best is read straight from workout_log_sets through a partial DESC index.
keyDecisions.rationale: A partial index on (user_id, exercise_id, e1rm_kg DESC) makes 'my best e1RM for this exercise' one B-tree descent. Measured at 17 us over 72,000 rows with the real driver; rep-max is 15 us. A cache would be a second source of truth that has to be invalidated on every void, every correction and every account merge — and the query it saves is already faster than the JSON serialisation of the response.
keyDecisions.rejected: An `exercise_bests(user_id, exercise_id, kind, rep_bucket, value)` upsert table. Rejected because the recompute path after a void is a full history scan anyway, so the cache buys nothing on the expensive path and adds a drift risk on the cheap one. This is the clearest case of 'a stored value that drifts is worse than a slow query' — except the query is not even slow.

keyDecisions.decision: volume_kg is a STORED GENERATED column; e1rm_kg is an ordinary column written by the server and frozen by a trigger.
keyDecisions.rationale: Tonnage is a DEFINITION — weight x reps, no competing version — so letting SQLite compute it makes drift and forgery structurally impossible. A 1RM estimate is a MODEL: Epley, Brzycki, Lombardi and two more all disagree. If e1rm were generated, shipping a new formula would rewrite every historical row and silently re-shape an 18-month chart the user has been reading. Storing it with `e1rm_formula` alongside means old points keep their old model and the chart can say which one produced each point.
keyDecisions.rejected: (a) Computing e1rm on read — cheap arithmetic, but then it cannot be indexed, PR detection becomes a full scan, and the formula change rewrites history retroactively. (b) Making e1rm a generated column — tempting because it cannot be forged, but it makes the formula part of the schema and therefore retroactive. The forgery risk is closed instead by a CHECK that verifies the Epley arithmetic and is conditioned on `e1rm_formula = 'epley'`, so a future formula is permitted without invalidating verified history.

keyDecisions.decision: e1rm_kg is NULL outside reps 1-12, and equals the weight itself at reps = 1.
keyDecisions.rationale: Epley diverges badly past ~12 reps: a 30-rep bodyweight set would manufacture a 1RM PR out of nothing. NULL is the honest answer and it keeps the fake point off the chart. At exactly 1 rep, naive Epley returns w x 1.0333 — every single would post a 3.3% inflated PR forever. Both are enforced by CHECK, so the mistake cannot be made by a future caller. This also fixed a real planner problem: with the reps range in the index predicate the PR query had to repeat it, and SQLite then chose the rep-max index plus a TEMP B-TREE sort. With e1rm nullable the query says only `e1rm_kg IS NOT NULL` and the intended index wins.
keyDecisions.rejected: Applying Epley to every set and filtering reps <= 12 at read time. Rejected because it stores a number the product will never show and, as verified with EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN, it costs the PR query its index.

keyDecisions.decision: A PR is primarily an estimated-1RM record; a rep-max record is the secondary badge; session volume is the third.
keyDecisions.rationale: e1RM is the only measure monotone in both weight and reps, so it cannot be gamed by dropping reps and it is comparable across a 5x5 day and a 3x3 day. That makes it the right thing for the gold flash. But lifters do not trust formulas, so 'heaviest ever at exactly 5 reps' (rep_max, bucketed 1-12 with 13+ collapsed) is kept as the human-legible record. Session volume is written at completion by a different code path and is the record a hypertrophy client actually cares about.
keyDecisions.rejected: (a) 'Heaviest weight ever, any rep count' — 1x100 kg would beat 10x95 kg, which is not progress. (b) 'Most reps at a given weight' — plausible, but in practice redundant with rep_max and a fourth kind to invalidate on every void. Cut deliberately; adding it later is one enum value and one index, no migration of existing rows.

keyDecisions.decision: PR events are an append-only fact table with an `invalidated_at` tombstone, never a mutable 'current best' row.
keyDecisions.rationale: 'What is my best' is derivable and therefore not stored. 'A gold badge was shown to this user on 3 March for this set' is NOT derivable — it is what the user was told, and once a reward economy exists it is what was paid out. Voiding the source set sets invalidated_at rather than deleting, so a coin ledger keyed on the record id still finds its anchor and the withdrawal is itself auditable. A BEFORE UPDATE trigger permits only invalidation to change.
keyDecisions.rejected: Deleting PR rows when their set is voided. Rejected because it orphans any reward already granted and erases the evidence that a badge was ever shown — the exact failure mode audit_log's append-only triggers exist to prevent.

keyDecisions.decision: Both weight_kg AND the unit-plus-number the human actually typed are stored, with a CHECK that they agree within 0.02 kg.
keyDecisions.rationale: This is the answer to 'where can a double conversion creep in'. It creeps in at exactly two places: a client that converts lb->kg before POSTing, and a server that converts again. The CHECK turns that 2.2x error into a write failure. entry_value is not redundant with weight_kg — it is a separate historical fact ('the user entered 225 lb') that makes the imperial round-trip exact instead of 225 -> 102.058 -> 224.99, and that lets a future 'we shipped a conversion bug in March' incident re-derive the canonical column from the source of truth.
keyDecisions.rejected: (a) Storing only weight_kg and converting for display — mathematically fine, visually broken, and forensically dead. (b) A per-row `unit` column that arithmetic respects — this is the classic disaster: every SUM and every MAX would then need a CASE, and one query that forgets it silently mixes pounds into a kilogram total. `units` on onboarding_profiles stays what 008 says it is: a display preference that never reaches a write path as a discriminator.

keyDecisions.decision: `local_date TEXT` (YYYY-MM-DD) is stored on both workout_logs and workout_log_sets, computed server-side from the user's IANA timezone.
keyDecisions.rationale: Every analytic unit in this product is a user-local day: the today card, the streak, the calendar, weekly volume. Epoch seconds are UTC, so a 01:00 session in Budapest lands on the previous UTC day and, once a month, in the previous UTC week. It is a historical fact (the workout happened on that Tuesday, forever, even if the user emigrates), it is not recoverable later because it depends on the zone they were in at the time, and it turns week bucketing into `date(local_date,'-6 days','weekday 1')` — a plain indexed string comparison rather than date arithmetic over thousands of rows. On the sets table it is what makes the progress graph a pure covering-index scan with no join.
keyDecisions.rejected: Grouping by `date(started_at,'unixepoch')` at query time. Rejected because it is wrong (UTC days), because SQLite has no IANA timezone database so it cannot be made right in SQL, and because it defeats the covering index.

keyDecisions.decision: Plans stay mutable documents; the LOG snapshots the prescription (target reps, load, RPE, rest) onto every set row at session start, plus plan_revision and the plan/day/exercise names.
keyDecisions.rationale: Coaches expect drag-reorder to just work, and versioning a plan on every cosmetic edit would produce dozens of dead versions a week. The integrity requirement is not that the plan be immutable — it is that 'did the client hit the prescription?' stays answerable forever. Snapshotting the targets onto the log achieves that even after the plan is rewritten the next morning or deleted the next month. This is the order-line price-snapshot pattern.
keyDecisions.rejected: Immutable versioned plans with logs pointing at a version. Correct but heavy: it needs copy-on-write for every edit, a version-cleanup policy, and it still would not survive an account deletion. The snapshot approach also survives `plan_id` going NULL, which the versioned approach does not.

keyDecisions.decision: Session rollups (total_sets, total_reps, total_volume_kg, total_work_seconds) ARE stored on workout_logs; weekly and per-exercise-lifetime rollups are NOT stored anywhere.
keyDecisions.rationale: The distinction is whether the mutation path and the recompute path are the same transaction. A completed session's sets are frozen, and the only three transactions that can change them (completeWorkoutTx, voidSetTx, appendSetTx) each end with the same single recompute UPDATE, so the rollup cannot drift. A weekly rollup has no such transaction — the week keeps moving, a late-logged session mutates a past week, and the invalidation logic would live in a background job. It is also unnecessary: summing 5 to 7 already-rolled-up session rows per week is trivial. `rollup_at` is stored so a stale rollup is detectable rather than merely wrong.
keyDecisions.rejected: (a) No rollups at all — the coach dashboard listing 40 clients x 12 recent sessions would run 480 aggregate subqueries per page load. (b) A `workout_week_rollups` table — needs a backfill job, a timezone-aware week boundary, and invalidation on every late edit.

keyDecisions.decision: A completed set is immutable at the trigger level. There is no un-check and no destructive edit anywhere in the log path; the undo button calls voidSetTx.
keyDecisions.rationale: This is what makes the whole PR and reward story airtight. If a set's weight can be edited after it earned a PR, then either the PR silently becomes a lie or every edit has to trigger a cascade recompute. Freezing the measurements means the only two states are 'this happened' and 'this happened and was later voided, for this reason' — and both are visible. voidSetTx invalidates the PR events the set earned in the same transaction, so the record table never outlives its evidence.
keyDecisions.rejected: Allowing in-place correction while the log is still in_progress. Softer UX, but it reopens the exact hole: a gold flash has already been shown by then, and once rewards exist a coin has already moved. The friction is real and it is listed as a weakness.
