keyDecisions.decision: Ownership is anchored on coach_clients.id (the LINK), and user_id/client_user_id are denormalised onto every child row and enforced by BEFORE INSERT triggers.
keyDecisions.rationale: The link id is the repo's canonical cross-user proof (onboarding/routes.js:255-265) and it gives archiving its documented property: access ends on the next read, not at the next token refresh. The denormalisation is what lets every guard live inside a single-table UPDATE — `WHERE id = ? AND user_id = ?` — which is the hard rule about guards in the UPDATE rather than in a preceding SELECT. Trigger enforcement is what makes it a guarantee rather than a convention: a set whose user_id disagrees with its log cannot be inserted.
keyDecisions.rejected: Keying the API on /clients/:userId/... and joining up the tree for each ownership check. Rejected because it breaks the archive-ends-access property and because a four-level join in every UPDATE's WHERE clause is where anti-IDOR bugs live.

keyDecisions.decision: A client's read access to a coach's non-global exercise is DERIVED from plan membership and log history, not granted by a table.
keyDecisions.rationale: The existing VISIBLE predicate makes a coach's private exercise invisible to their own client, so a plan built from the coach's custom library would 404 for the client. A derived predicate is automatically correct: access exists exactly while the exercise is prescribed or appears in the client's own history, with nothing to keep in sync. The new predicate is a second build-time constant next to VISIBLE (three `?`, each bound to req.user.id) and is used ONLY on plan, log and exercise-detail reads — never on the general library browse, where a client must still not see the coach's library.
keyDecisions.rejected: (a) An `exercise_grants` table — a second thing to sync, and everyone forgets to revoke it when the plan item is removed. (b) Extending VISIBLE globally with an EXISTS over coach_clients — grants blanket access to the coach's entire private library including exercises the client was never given. (c) Snapshotting the exercise into the plan item and dropping the FK — kills media, muscle map and translations. The name snapshot on workout_log_exercises is kept as a rendering safety net only, alongside the FK, never instead of it.

keyDecisions.decision: Every plan item belongs to a group, including a solo exercise (kind='single'). Groups own rounds, inter-round rest and the time cap.
keyDecisions.rationale: Ordering within a day becomes total and unambiguous — groups order in the day, items order in the group — with no COALESCE and no 'is this grouped' branch in any renderer. A circuit repeats the GROUP while a straight set repeats the ITEM, so `rounds` genuinely belongs to the group and a `group_key TEXT` on the item would have had nowhere to put it.
keyDecisions.rejected: A nullable `group_key` string on the item. Rejected because ordering between grouped and ungrouped items becomes ambiguous, and because rounds/cap/inter-round rest would have to be duplicated onto every member where two members can disagree.

keyDecisions.decision: Ordering columns (`position`) carry NON-unique indexes with an `id` tie-break; semantic coordinates (`day_index, slot`, `set_index`) carry UNIQUE indexes.
keyDecisions.rationale: SQLite checks UNIQUE per statement, not deferred to commit. A drag-reorder that rewrites positions 1..N inside one transaction WILL collide mid-way against a unique (parent, position), so a unique ordering index would abort a perfectly legal reorder. The tie-break on id keeps the order total even if two positions coincide, and a duplicate position is cosmetically harmless. Where the coordinate is semantic and the calendar must resolve it deterministically, UNIQUE is correct — and those are replaced whole (delete-then-insert) rather than incrementally, following the onboarding_equipment precedent.
keyDecisions.rejected: Unique ordering indexes with a negative-offset shuffle to avoid mid-transaction collisions. Rejected as a trick that every future contributor has to rediscover.

keyDecisions.decision: Idempotency uses the domain's own natural key (`client_set_uid`) rather than a generic idempotency_keys table.
keyDecisions.rationale: A generic table needs TTL sweeping, stored response bodies, and a decision about what counts as 'the same request'. The set row already has an identity the player controls; a UNIQUE on (log_id, client_set_uid) makes a replay structurally impossible and needs no maintenance. The same shape covers session start (partial unique on the occurrence) and PR grants (unique on set+kind+bucket) — three natural keys instead of one generic mechanism.
keyDecisions.rejected: An `idempotency_keys(key, route, response_json, expires_at)` table. Worth building when a route has no natural key — a payment, for instance. Not worth it here, and building it now would mean building the sweeper now too.

keyDecisions.decision: No workout_plan_translations table is created, but `workout_plans.origin` reserves the case that will need one.
keyDecisions.rationale: A coach's plan name is the coach's own prose, like onboarding_profiles.notes, and machine-translating it would be worse than showing the original. Only a product-shipped starter library (origin='system') would ever need per-language names, and 005_drop_legacy_text established that dead schema is not harmless. So the discriminator ships now and the table ships with the templates, following the taxonomy_translations shape verbatim.
keyDecisions.rejected: (a) Creating an empty workout_plan_translations table now — dead schema. (b) `name_hu` style per-language columns — the exact mistake 004 and 007 were written to undo.

designs.idempotency:
A replayed "set checked" request cannot double-count, and it is blocked four independent times.

LAYER 1 — THE SET IS AN UPDATE, NOT AN INSERT. startWorkoutTx materialises the whole set grid when the session begins, so checking a set is `UPDATE workout_log_sets SET completed_at = ?, weight_kg = ?, reps = ?, e1rm_kg = ?, ... WHERE id = ? AND user_id = ? AND completed_at IS NULL`. The guard is inside the UPDATE, never in a preceding SELECT. A replay matches zero rows because `completed_at IS NULL` is already false, so `info.changes === 0`, and the named transaction branches on that BEFORE it writes anything else.

LAYER 2 — THE PRE-WRITE READ INSIDE AN IMMEDIATE TRANSACTION. `completeSetTx` (a NAMED worker export, because writeTx cannot inspect an intermediate result) runs, in this exact order:

  1. SELECT s.completed_at, s.exercise_id, s.reps, l.status
       FROM workout_log_sets s JOIN workout_logs l ON l.id = s.log_id
      WHERE s.id = ? AND s.user_id = ?;
     -- miss  -> throw NotFound  (route maps to 404, never 403)
     -- log not 'in_progress' -> throw LogClosed
  2. if (row.completed_at !== null) {
       const records = SELECT id, kind, rep_bucket, value, previous_value
                         FROM workout_set_records
                        WHERE set_id = ? AND invalidated_at IS NULL;
       return { applied: false, replayed: true, set: row, records };   // ZERO writes
     }
  3. -- prior bests, read BEFORE the write so they cannot include this set:
     SELECT e1rm_kg FROM workout_log_sets
      WHERE user_id = ? AND exercise_id = ? AND voided_at IS NULL AND is_warmup = 0
        AND completed_at IS NOT NULL AND e1rm_kg IS NOT NULL
      ORDER BY e1rm_kg DESC LIMIT 1;                       -- 17 us, workout_log_sets_e1rm_idx
     SELECT weight_kg FROM workout_log_sets
      WHERE user_id = ? AND exercise_id = ? AND reps = ? AND voided_at IS NULL AND is_warmup = 0
        AND completed_at IS NOT NULL
      ORDER BY weight_kg DESC LIMIT 1;                     -- 15 us, workout_log_sets_repmax_idx
  4. -- FIRST WRITE. From here the body may only complete or throw (ADR-0005: better-sqlite3
     -- commits on return, so a `return { code: 'VALIDATION' }` after a write commits it silently).
     UPDATE workout_log_sets SET ... WHERE id = ? AND user_id = ? AND completed_at IS NULL;
  5. if (e1rm > best)      INSERT INTO workout_set_records (..., kind='e1rm', rep_bucket=0, ...);
     if (weight > bestAt)  INSERT INTO workout_set_records (..., kind='rep_max', rep_bucket=?, ...);
  6. return { applied: true, records };

Step 2 is the replay branch and it is the ONLY place an "already done" result is produced — before any write, which is what ADR-0005 requires. It is race-free for one specific reason: `tx.immediate(...)` takes SQLite's single write lock on the FIRST statement, so no concurrent request can interleave between the read in step 1 and the write in step 4. In a DEFERRED transaction this exact code would be a TOCTOU. That is not a style preference; it is the whole reason the pattern is safe.

LAYER 3 — THE UNIQUE INDEX ON THE PR EVENT.
  CREATE UNIQUE INDEX workout_set_records_set_unique
    ON workout_set_records (set_id, kind, rep_bucket) WHERE set_id IS NOT NULL;
Even if layers 1 and 2 were both defeated, a second PR event for the same (set, kind, rep_bucket) raises SQLITE_CONSTRAINT_UNIQUE and rolls the whole transaction back. `rep_bucket` is NOT NULL with a 0 sentinel precisely for this: SQLite treats NULLs as distinct in a UNIQUE index, so a nullable rep_bucket would let two 'e1rm' rows coexist for one set and the backstop would silently not exist.

LAYER 4 — THE REWARD ANCHOR. No reward column is invented here. `workout_set_records.id` is a stable, unique, effectively append-only integer, so a future coin ledger writes its own row with a unique key of ('pr', workout_set_records.id) inside the same transaction that mints the record. Because layer 3 guarantees at most one record per (set, kind, bucket), at most one coin can ever be granted per PR — and because a void sets `invalidated_at` instead of deleting, the withdrawal has something to point at.

FREE-FORM (unplanned) SETS take the same shape with the natural key doing the work directly: the player mints `client_set_uid` once per row and reuses it on every retry, and `UNIQUE (log_id, client_set_uid)` means a replayed INSERT collides. The tx reads that key first (still before any write) and returns `{ deduped: true, set: existing }`.

SESSION START is idempotent by the same principle at a different grain:
  CREATE UNIQUE INDEX workout_logs_occurrence_unique
    ON workout_logs (client_user_id, plan_day_id, occurrence_date)
    WHERE plan_day_id IS NOT NULL AND status <> 'abandoned';
  CREATE UNIQUE INDEX workout_logs_one_active
    ON workout_logs (client_user_id) WHERE status = 'in_progress';
A double-tapped "Start workout" and a second phone both fail at the database rather than producing two set grids that each later claim the same PR.

Per the existing house rule, `changes === 0` maps to a status code per endpoint: here a replay is `200 { applied: false, replayed: true }`, not an error — the same reasoning as onboarding/routes.js:243, "a double-tapped submit button is the client's most ordinary mistake and must not read as a failure". An ownership miss is 404.
designs.ownership:
EVERY predicate below is expressed on a single table because user_id / client_user_id is denormalised onto every child row and enforced by a BEFORE INSERT trigger. A miss is always 404, never 403 — a 403 confirms the id is real, which is enough to enumerate another coach's library (exercises/routes.js:22-25). Role gates (requireCoach) still return 403; that distinction is unchanged.

THE CLIENT reading or writing their own data:
  workout_plans           WHERE id = ? AND client_user_id = ?
  workout_plan_days       WHERE id = ? AND plan_id IN (SELECT id FROM workout_plans WHERE client_user_id = ?)
  workout_plan_groups     WHERE id = ? AND day_id IN (SELECT d.id FROM workout_plan_days d JOIN workout_plans p ON p.id = d.plan_id WHERE p.client_user_id = ?)
  workout_plan_items      WHERE id = ? AND day_id IN (same subquery)
  workout_logs            WHERE id = ? AND client_user_id = ?
  workout_log_exercises   WHERE id = ? AND user_id = ?
  workout_log_sets        WHERE id = ? AND user_id = ?
  workout_set_records     WHERE id = ? AND user_id = ?
Note the deliberate absence of any coach_clients status filter on the client's own path: a client keeps full read and write access to their plans and history after a coach archives them. They own their training history; the coach owned only the relationship.

THE COACH reading or writing a client's data — always through the LINK id from the URL, never a client user id:
  workout_plans           WHERE p.id = ? AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM coach_clients cc
                                                       WHERE cc.id = p.coach_client_id
                                                         AND cc.coach_id = ?
                                                         AND cc.status = 'active')
  workout_logs            same shape on l.coach_client_id
  child rows (days, groups, items, log exercises, log sets, records) resolve to their plan or log
                          first and apply the clause above to THAT row, never to themselves.
The plan/log-listing endpoints are keyed /clients/:linkId/plans and /clients/:linkId/logs, and the link is resolved exactly as onboarding/routes.js:259-265 already does:
  SELECT client_id FROM coach_clients WHERE id = ? AND coach_id = ? AND status = 'active'

HOW AN ARCHIVED LINK ENDS ACCESS IMMEDIATELY:
`/clients/:id/archive` (coaching/routes.js:166-170) sets status='archived' and archived_at in one guarded UPDATE. Because every coach-side predicate above requires `cc.status = 'active'` and joins the link row live on every request, the very next read matches zero rows and returns 404 — with the SAME access token, no refresh, no revocation list, no cache to bust. There is no grant copied into the JWT and no denormalised coach_id on any plan or log row that could go stale. That is the entire reason `workout_plans.coach_client_id` and `workout_logs.coach_client_id` point at the link and not at a user.

WHY status = 'active' AND NOT status <> 'archived':
The repo is inconsistent here — the roster listing uses `<> 'archived'` (coaching/routes.js:119) while the cross-user onboarding read uses `= 'active'` (onboarding/routes.js:261). This design picks `= 'active'` for every plan and log read, deliberately and everywhere. It is the stricter of the two and it is already the established rule for reading another user's DATA rather than listing relationship metadata: an 'invited' link is a pending relationship, and a coach must not be able to read a client's training history before that client has accepted.

WHAT ARCHIVING DOES NOT DO:
It does not cascade. `coach_client_id` is ON DELETE SET NULL on both plans and logs, so even hard-deleting the link leaves the client's plans and history intact and merely orphaned from the coach. Deleting a coaching relationship must never delete a client's training history.

FOREIGN-ID VALIDATION (anti-IDOR on the write path):
A `coach_client_id` or `plan_id` arriving in a request body is validated with an explicit ownership SELECT before use, the pattern already established for team_id at coaching/routes.js:197-203. In addition the CHECK constraint `coach_client_id IS NOT NULL OR client_user_id IS NULL OR client_user_id = owner_user_id` makes it structurally impossible to assign a plan to an arbitrary user id without a link that the SELECT has already proven belongs to the caller.

EXERCISE VISIBILITY inside a plan or log (a client may see a coach's private exercise only where it was actually prescribed or actually performed) — a second build-time constant beside VISIBLE, used ONLY on plan/log/detail reads and NEVER on the general library browse; each `?` is bound to req.user.id, three times, matching how VISIBLE binds today:
  (e.deleted_at IS NULL AND (
     e.status = 'global'
     OR e.owner_id = ?
     OR EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM workout_log_sets s
                 WHERE s.exercise_id = e.id AND s.user_id = ?)
     OR EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM workout_plan_items i
                  JOIN workout_plan_days d ON d.id = i.day_id
                  JOIN workout_plans     p ON p.id = d.plan_id
                 WHERE i.exercise_id = e.id AND p.client_user_id = ?)
  ))
Served by workout_plan_items_exercise_idx and the (user_id, exercise_id) prefix of workout_log_sets_progress_idx.

NAMED WORKER TRANSACTIONS this design requires (each is a two-file change: an export in src/db/worker.js doing getDb().transaction(...).immediate(...), plus a facade line `export const x = (args) => pool.run(args, { name: 'x' })` in src/db/index.js; arguments and returns cross a structured-clone boundary so they must be plain JSON-able data). These are the first named transactions in the repo — today every write goes through the generic writeTx, which cannot branch:
  startWorkoutTx     — ownership-check, expand items (and item_sets) into the log set grid, snapshot targets and names. One tx: a half-built grid is garbage.
  completeSetTx      — the idempotent set check plus PR detection. Detailed above.
  voidSetTx          — set voided_at/voided_reason, invalidate the PR events the set earned, and recompute the session rollup if the log is already completed. One tx, because a voided set whose PR survives is exactly the drift this design exists to prevent.
  completeWorkoutTx  — close the session, compute rollups, detect session_volume PRs.
  clonePlanTx        — template -> client instantiation of plan + days + groups + items + item_sets, recording source_plan_id and source_revision.
Plan reordering and day/week copying need no named transaction: every UPDATE carries its own ownership guard in the WHERE clause and the steps are independent, so writeTx is sufficient and correct.
weaknesses: REP-MAX PRs ARE NOISY FOR BEGINNERS. Bucketing by exact rep count means a novice who has never done a set of 7 gets a 'PR' the first time they do one, at any weight. That is technically true and emotionally worthless, and it will devalue the badge in the first month of use. The e1RM record does not have this problem, which is why it is the primary badge — but the schema does nothing to suppress the rep_max noise. A fix (only fire rep_max when the weight also exceeds the best at every higher rep count) is a query change, not a schema change, so nothing here blocks it; it is simply not designed in.

SESSION ROLLUPS ARE A CODE DISCIPLINE, NOT A DATABASE GUARANTEE. They cannot drift only as long as every transaction that touches a completed session's sets ends with the recompute UPDATE. That is three transactions today and there is nothing stopping a fourth being written next year without it. `rollup_at` makes the staleness detectable but does not prevent it. An AFTER INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE trigger set on workout_log_sets would make it structural, at the cost of firing on all 25 sets of every session; I chose the cheaper option and this is where that choice can bite.

THE TIMEZONE STORY HAS A GAP AT BOTH ENDS. A user with no onboarding profile, or a NULL timezone, gets UTC days — and because local_date is deliberately never recomputed, a user who trains for two months before fixing a wrong timezone has two months of permanently mis-dated sessions and possibly mis-bucketed weeks. The alternative (recompute on tz change) would rewrite history, which this design forbids everywhere else. There is no good answer; the schema picks 'wrong but stable' over 'corrected but retroactive' and that will surprise someone.

THE 'ONE LIVE SESSION' PARTIAL UNIQUE IS BLUNT. It kills the two-phones bug at the database, which is worth a lot, but it also blocks the legitimate case of a client who starts a morning session, forgets to close it, and wants to start an evening one. They must abandon the first, and the route has to offer that clearly or it reads as a bug. It also means a crashed client with a stale in_progress log is locked out until something cleans it up; nothing in this design does that cleanup.

ASSISTED AND WEIGHTED BODYWEIGHT MOVEMENTS ARE NOT MODELLED. weight_kg is external load and is constrained >= 0, so an assisted pull-up with 30 kg of counterweight stores 0 and reports zero volume, and a weighted dip stores only the added plate. bodyweight_kg is snapshotted on the log so a bodyweight-inclusive volume CAN be computed later without storing a second derived number, but there is no assistance column and no per-exercise 'uses bodyweight' flag, so that computation currently has no input telling it which exercises to apply it to. This is a real hole for a large class of exercises.

FREEZING e1rm AT reps 1-12 BAKES A POLICY INTO DATA. If the reliability window is later widened to 15, every historical 13-15 rep set keeps a NULL e1rm forever, because backfilling it would be exactly the retroactive rewrite the design forbids. The chart would show a visible discontinuity at the deploy date. I think that is the right trade — it is the same argument as the formula versioning — but it is a one-way door and it should be walked through knowingly.

NO IN-SESSION UNCHECK IS REAL UX FRICTION. Tapping the wrong row is common, and the answer here is a void that leaves a visible tombstone with a reason. Users will find a strikethrough row confusing, and the UI has to decide whether to hide voided rows (losing the transparency the design paid for) or show them (looking broken). I would not soften the trigger, but I would expect this to be the most-argued decision in review.

workout_plan_item_sets IS THE PIECE MOST LIKELY TO BE CUT. It doubles the authoring surface — another CRUD, another reorder, another ownership predicate — for ramping and pyramid sets that the roadmap never explicitly asked for. It earns its place only if the product is a real coaching tool rather than a template filler. If it is cut, startWorkoutTx loses a branch and nothing else in the schema changes.

THE RECORDS SCREEN IS NOT DESIGNED FOR. 'My best e1RM for this ONE exercise' is 17 microseconds. 'My bests across all 200 exercises I have ever trained' is 200 seeks or one large GROUP BY over the whole history, and neither is served by a purpose-built index. The workout_set_records table helps (it is small and has a feed index) but it holds EVENTS, so reading current bests from it means a per-group MAX with an invalidated_at filter. If that screen becomes a main navigation destination, this is the first thing that will need work — and it is the one place where the 'no cache table' decision might have to be revisited.

TWO VISIBILITY PREDICATES IS TWO THINGS TO KEEP STRAIGHT. VISIBLE (library browse) and the derived history/plan predicate must never be swapped. Using the derived one on the library browse leaks nothing today but would let a client's search results shift as plans change; using VISIBLE on a plan read 404s the coach's own prescription. The repo's habit of writing the predicate once as a named constant helps, but a name is not a type and there is no test that would catch the swap.

NON-UNIQUE `position` COLUMNS PERMIT DUPLICATES. Ordering is total only because of the `id` tie-break, which means a bug in the reorder transaction produces a subtly wrong order rather than a loud constraint failure. I traded loudness for the ability to reorder in one transaction; a deferred-unique database would not force this choice, but SQLite is not one.

THE QUERY PLANS WERE VERIFIED WITHOUT ANALYZE, AND THE APP NEVER RUNS IT. All four hot queries chose the intended index on a 72,000-row synthetic table both with and without stats, but planner choices without stats depend on data shape, and the e1RM index already had to be reshaped once because the planner preferred the rep-max index and added a TEMP B-TREE. A different real-world distribution could re-open that. There is no ANALYZE in the boot path and no INDEXED BY hint anywhere, so nothing would catch a regression except someone noticing the app got slow.

ON DELETE RESTRICT ON exercise_id IS CORRECT AND ANNOYING. Once anyone has logged an exercise, an admin can no longer hard-delete it — only soft-delete. That is the right answer for history integrity, but it means the moderation queue's 'reject and remove' action will start failing on exactly the exercises that matter most, and the admin UI has to explain why.

PLAN NAMES ARE NOT SEARCHABLE. A coach with 200 templates gets a LIKE scan or nothing. Adding FTS5 later is possible — the tables are rowid tables, so the 004 trap does not apply — but it is not designed in, and the surrogate-id-plus-UNIQUE shape that would be needed for a translations table is not there either.

fatalFlaws.flaw: IDOR via session materialisation: `workout_logs.plan_id` / `plan_day_id` are client-supplied FKs with NO ownership predicate anywhere in the design. `startWorkoutSession` reads the plan once and copies the entire prescription into set rows the attacker OWNS — laundering another user's data into rows that every read predicate (`user_id = me`) happily returns. This is exfiltration through a write endpoint, and the 404-not-403 rule never gets a chance to fire.
fatalFlaws.scenario: Client A (role 'user', no coach) posts `POST /api/v1/sessions {plan_day_id: 8123, client_uid: '01J...'}` where day 8123 belongs to coach B's plan for client C. Nothing in the schema stops it: `workout_plan_days` has no owner column, `workout_logs.plan_day_id` is a bare FK, and the design's only stated plan-read predicate (`WHERE p.client_id = ? AND p.status <> 'draft'`) is described for the plan READ endpoint, not for materialisation. The tx expands C's day into A's own `workout_log_entries` + `workout_log_sets`: `exercise_name_snapshot`, `target_weight_kg`, `target_reps`, `target_rpe`, `target_rest_seconds`, tempo and the coach's per-item `notes` are all now rows with `user_id = A`. A then GETs their own session and reads coach B's entire proprietary programming for client C. Burp: iterate `plan_day_id` 1..50000, 201 each time, diff the responses. Bonus: per the design's own rule, materialisation also mints `workout_exercise_grants` rows for B's private exercises, so A now permanently sees B's private library too.
fatalFlaws.fix: `plan_day_id` must never be dereferenced without proving the plan is the caller's. Resolve it in ONE statement inside the named tx: `INSERT INTO workout_logs (...) SELECT ... FROM workout_plan_days d JOIN workout_plans p ON p.id = d.plan_id WHERE d.id = :dayId AND p.client_id = :me AND p.deleted_at IS NULL AND p.status IN ('active','paused')` and treat `changes = 0` as 404. Every subsequent materialisation INSERT...SELECT must carry the same join, not just the day id. Add the freestyle case as `plan_day_id IS NULL` explicitly rather than as an unvalidated fallthrough.

fatalFlaws.flaw: `workout_exercise_grants` is a self-service capability table. Nothing — no CHECK, no trigger, no FK to `coach_clients`, no requirement that `granted_by` owns the exercise or differs from `user_id` — prevents a user from minting a grant for themselves against ANY exercise id. The design says grants are written "when the exercise enters the client's plan or log", and both of those are client-driven inserts.
fatalFlaws.scenario: Client A creates their own plan (the design explicitly allows `owner_id` = the client for a self-made plan), then posts `POST /plans/:mine/days/:mine/items {exercise_id: 1337, prescription_kind:'reps', target_reps_min: 5}` where 1337 is coach B's `status='private'` exercise. `workout_plan_items.exercise_id` is a plain FK — it only requires the row to EXIST, not to be visible. Per the design's own rule the route now writes `INSERT INTO workout_exercise_grants (user_id, exercise_id, granted_by) VALUES (A, 1337, A)`. `GET /exercises/1337` — which must now consult the grant table, otherwise grants do nothing — returns B's private exercise: name, description, the full `instructions` JSON, media. Loop `exercise_id` 1..2000 and A has dumped every coach's private library. The same works via a freestyle log entry with no plan at all. Worse, an FK violation on a nonexistent id vs. a 201 on a real one is also a clean existence oracle for the id space.
fatalFlaws.fix: A grant is a coach→client capability and must be unwritable by the grantee. Add to the DDL: `CHECK (granted_by IS NOT NULL AND granted_by <> user_id)`, and a BEFORE INSERT trigger that RAISE(ABORT)s unless `EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM exercises x WHERE x.id = NEW.exercise_id AND x.owner_id = NEW.granted_by)` AND `EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM coach_clients cc WHERE cc.coach_id = NEW.granted_by AND cc.client_id = NEW.user_id AND cc.status = 'active')`. Separately: any route that accepts a client-supplied `exercise_id` (plan item, log entry, substitution) must resolve it through the VISIBLE predicate + grant table in the same statement and 404 on a miss, so an invisible id is indistinguishable from a nonexistent one.

fatalFlaws.flaw: Coach→coach IDOR via `source_plan_id`. `clonePlan` takes a source plan id from the client, and the design's ownership section specifies a predicate for plan WRITES (`WHERE id = ? AND owner_id = ?`) but never for the clone SOURCE — which is a READ. `idx_workout_plans_source` even indexes the resulting provenance, so the theft is self-documenting.
fatalFlaws.scenario: Coach A posts `POST /plans/clone {source_plan_id: 412}` where 412 is coach B's private template. The clone reads B's `workout_plan_days` + `workout_plan_items` + `workout_plan_item_sets` and writes copies owned by A. A now reads their own clone: every day, every exercise, every set/rep/RPE/tempo/rest prescription and every coaching note in B's flagship 12-week programme. `source_plan_id` = 412 is left on A's row as a receipt. Burp-iterate `source_plan_id` 1..N; each 201 is another coach's entire product. The `is_template` flag does not gate this — the design's only stated template rule is `CHECK (is_template = 0 OR client_id IS NULL)`, which is about assignment, not visibility.
fatalFlaws.fix: The source must be scoped in the same SELECT that reads it: `... FROM workout_plans p WHERE p.id = :src AND p.deleted_at IS NULL AND (p.owner_id = :me OR (p.is_template = 1 AND p.owner_id IS NULL))` — i.e. mine, or a product-shipped stock template. `changes = 0` / no row → 404. Same predicate on every child SELECT in the clone, not just the root, so a forged `day_id` in a copy-day request cannot reach across.

fatalFlaws.flaw: Coach reaches an UNLINKED client via `workout_plans.client_id`. The assignment is an INSERT, and an INSERT ... VALUES has no WHERE clause. The design's coach-write guard (`EXISTS ... coach_clients ... status='active'`) is written only for the UPDATE path; nothing constrains `client_id` at creation time to be a user this coach actually coaches.
fatalFlaws.scenario: Coach A posts `POST /plans {title:'Program', client_id: 4242, status:'active'}` where 4242 is a user A has never been linked to. The row is legal: `is_template = 0`, `client_id` non-NULL, `owner_id = A`. Victim 4242's home card, week strip and 'today' card — which the design says read `WHERE p.client_id = ? AND p.status <> 'draft'` — now render a plan authored by a stranger, including a 2000-char `description` and 1000-char per-item `notes` (phishing/harassment surface delivered inside the trusted app chrome). The victim trains it; `workout_logs.plan_id` points at A's plan. If any coach-side query is scoped by 'plans I own' rather than by the link (and `idx_workout_logs_plan_day` is built precisely for `WHERE plan_day_id = ? AND status = ?`), A then reads the victim's completed sessions: weights, reps, RPE, bodyweight-derived volume — for a person who never consented to being coached by A.
fatalFlaws.fix: Make the link the source of the client id, never the body. Take `link_id` instead of `client_id` and resolve it in the insert: `INSERT INTO workout_plans (owner_id, client_id, ...) SELECT :me, cc.client_id, ... FROM coach_clients cc WHERE cc.id = :linkId AND cc.coach_id = :me AND cc.status = 'active'` — `changes = 0` → 404. This matches `onboarding/routes.js:255-265` exactly. Add a BEFORE INSERT trigger as a backstop: abort when `client_id IS NOT NULL AND client_id <> owner_id AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM coach_clients WHERE coach_id = NEW.owner_id AND client_id = NEW.client_id AND status = 'active')`.

fatalFlaws.flaw: THE ownership predicate that is not expressible in a single WHERE clause: `workout_plan_days`, `workout_plan_items` and `workout_plan_item_sets` have no owner column and are 1, 2 and 3 FK hops from `workout_plans.owner_id` — and INSERT ... VALUES admits no WHERE. The design solves this for UPDATE (correlated EXISTS) and conspicuously uses BEFORE INSERT parent triggers on the `workout_log_*` tree while omitting them from the `workout_plan_*` tree. So the authoring side's INSERT path is protected by route discipline only, which is exactly the SELECT-then-INSERT race the hard rules forbid.
fatalFlaws.scenario: Coach A posts `POST /plans/1/days/9001/items {exercise_id: 55, target_reps_min: 5, notes: '<attacker text>'}`. Day 9001 belongs to coach B's plan for client C. A naive route validates plan 1 (A's own, passes), then inserts with `day_id = 9001` — the FK is satisfied because the day exists. The item lands in C's plan and materialises into C's next session. Deeper: `POST /plan-items/:itemId/sets {item_id: <B's item>, set_number: 1, target_weight_kg: 400}` — `workout_plan_item_sets` is three joins from an owner and its only constraint is `UNIQUE (item_id, set_number)`, so A prescribes a 400 kg set to another coach's client. The write is silent, the victim coach sees an item they never wrote, and the client trains it.
fatalFlaws.fix: Every insert into the plan tree must be `INSERT ... SELECT ... WHERE EXISTS(<walk to workout_plans.owner_id = :me AND deleted_at IS NULL>)` with `changes = 0` → 404, so the check and the write are one statement. Belt-and-braces: give each of the three tables a BEFORE INSERT trigger mirroring `trg_workout_log_sets_parent` — e.g. on `workout_plan_item_sets`, abort when `NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM workout_plan_items i JOIN workout_plan_days d ON d.id = i.day_id WHERE i.id = NEW.item_id)` is insufficient; it must assert the full chain resolves to a single plan. Cheapest structural fix: denormalise `plan_id` onto `workout_plan_items` and `workout_plan_item_sets` with a parent-consistency trigger, so every write has a one-hop predicate.

fatalFlaws.flaw: PR detection reads `exercise_records` — a cache the design itself flags as possibly stale via `needs_recompute` — and the hot write path never checks that flag. The repair is on the READ path only. Result: silently missing PRs and a record book displaying a number no set in the database supports.
fatalFlaws.scenario: Day 1: client logs 100 kg × 5 → `est_1rm_kg` = 116.7 → PR row created, `exercise_records.best_est_1rm_kg = 116.7`. Day 2: client fixes a typo and edits that set to 60 kg × 5 → per the design the edit sets `needs_recompute = 1` and leaves `best_est_1rm_kg` at 116.7 (the design never says the edit lowers it). Day 3: client genuinely lifts 90 kg × 5 → `est_1rm_kg` = 105 → layer 4's `WHERE ... s.est_1rm_kg > r.best_est_1rm_kg` is `105 > 116.7` = false → NO PR row, no badge, no coin, even though 105 beats every surviving set. The client's 'my records' screen keeps showing 116.7 until they happen to open it and trigger the repair — and the repair never retroactively creates the Day-3 PR event, so the badge and the (Phase 7) reward are lost forever. Nothing detects this; no constraint fires.
fatalFlaws.fix: `logSetOp` must not proceed against a stale cache. Either (a) make layer 1's SELECT also read `r.needs_recompute` and, when it is 1, run the recompute inline BEFORE the first write (ADR-0005-safe: it is all pre-write), or (b) make the edit path repair synchronously rather than flagging — an edit is rare and can afford the MAX() scan. Additionally, `needs_recompute` must be set on the DELETE/void path too, not just the lower-the-value path, and the recompute must be able to run without a read request ever arriving (a boot-time sweep over `idx_exercise_records_stale`).

fatalFlaws.flaw: Archived access does NOT end immediately: `calendar_feed_tokens` is a durable, non-expiring bearer capability that the design's own four-step archive story never enumerates. It has `revoked_at` but no `expires_at`, no link to `coach_clients`, and `plan_id NULL` means 'every plan this user can see' — a scope evaluated at fetch time against a capability minted under a relationship that no longer exists.
fatalFlaws.scenario: Coach A mints an ICS feed token while linked to client C, and subscribes to it in Google Calendar (webcal://…/feed/<token>). The relationship ends; C's link is archived (`status='archived'`). The design's archive transaction flips the status and runs `DELETE FROM workout_exercise_grants WHERE user_id = ? AND granted_by = ?`. `calendar_feed_tokens` is untouched. Google's servers keep polling that URL every few hours, from Google IPs, forever, and keep receiving C's full training schedule — exercise names, prescribed loads, session times — for a client who fired their coach. There is no expiry to run out and nobody thinks to revoke a calendar subscription. Secondary: the fetch path writes `last_used_at` on an unauthenticated request, so an attacker brute-forcing the token space drives one DB write per attempt against a single-writer SQLite database, and the normal per-user rate limiters cannot key on anything (no session).
fatalFlaws.fix: (1) Add `expires_at INTEGER NOT NULL` with a bounded default (e.g. 90 days) and refuse an expired token. (2) Add `link_id INTEGER REFERENCES coach_clients(id) ON DELETE CASCADE` for any token whose subject is not the token owner, and make the feed query re-assert `cc.status = 'active'` on every fetch — the token authenticates, the link authorises. (3) Add `DELETE FROM calendar_feed_tokens WHERE link_id = :link` to the archive transaction, alongside the grants delete. (4) Do not write `last_used_at` per fetch; coarsen it (`WHERE last_used_at < unixepoch() - 3600`) or drop it. (5) Constrain `token_hash` (`GLOB` a 64-char hex) and require ≥256 bits of entropy. Note the archive route currently holds only the LINK id, so the grants DELETE also needs `user_id = (SELECT client_id FROM coach_clients WHERE id = ?)` and the whole thing must move from `db.run` into one transaction.

fatalFlaws.flaw: `syncOfflineQueue` is structurally unimplementable as specified: it promises ONE IMMEDIATE transaction, per-op `{accepted|replayed}` results, AND `throw NotFound` for a bad op. Under better-sqlite3's commit-on-return law (ADR-0005) you can have any two of those, never all three. Either one bad op discards the whole workout, or the tx returns error results after writes and commits them while telling the client they failed.
fatalFlaws.scenario: Client trains a 45-minute session in a basement with no signal: 6 exercises, 24 set-check ops, one 'add ad-hoc set' op, one 'finish'. On reconnect the batch flushes. Op #14 references an `entry_id` whose creating op was dropped by the client's own queue-pruning bug (or duplicates a `set_number`, hitting `UNIQUE (entry_id, set_number)`, or arrives after the 'finish' op so layer 1's `l.status = 'active'` fails). Path A — the design's stated `throw`: the IMMEDIATE transaction rolls back and all 24 checked sets, the ad-hoc set and the finish are gone. The client, having flushed, prunes its queue on the 500 or keeps retrying the same poisoned batch forever. The user's entire workout is deleted. Path B — collect per-op results and return them: ops 1-13 have already written, so the return COMMITS them, and the response says op 14 failed — but the log's rollups were computed mid-batch and `finishWorkoutSession` never ran, leaving an 'active' session that `idx_workout_logs_one_active` now blocks the next workout on.
fatalFlaws.fix: Split it. Validate the ENTIRE batch before the first write (resolve every uid to a row id, check every parent, check every `set_number` collision) and return a 400 with the offending op index if anything fails — that is pure pre-write validation and is ADR-0005-legal. Then apply the validated batch in one IMMEDIATE tx where every remaining op is either a guarded UPDATE (`changes = 0` = replayed, not an error) or an `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`, so no op can throw and the return is unconditionally a success shape. Ops that fail validation are reported per-op and left in the client's queue; they must never be able to take their neighbours down.

seriousFlaws.flaw: The submitted `workout_plan_days` DDL references a table that does not exist — `plan_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES workout_plan_days_parent_guard_placeholder_removed_plan(id) ON DELETE CASCADE`. SQLite resolves FK targets lazily, so `CREATE TABLE` succeeds and the migration commits and bumps `user_version` — the failure is invisible until the first write.
seriousFlaws.scenario: `npm run migrate` reports success. The first `INSERT INTO workout_plan_days` throws `SQLITE_ERROR: no such table: main.workout_plan_days_parent_guard_placeholder_removed_plan`, which `errorHandler` (backend/src/lib/http.js) turns into a generic 500 with no clue. Because the version bumped, the file is never re-applied — the only recovery is a new migration, and `ALTER TABLE` cannot change an FK, and the 12-step table rebuild is unavailable inside a migration transaction (`PRAGMA foreign_keys = OFF` is a no-op there). The entire authoring tree is dead and unfixable in place.
seriousFlaws.fix: `REFERENCES workout_plans(id) ON DELETE CASCADE`. Then add a boot-time `PRAGMA foreign_key_check` (or a smoke assertion) so a dangling FK target can never again survive a green migration.

seriousFlaws.flaw: Migration number 009 is already taken. `backend/src/db/migrations/009_language_roster.sql` exists in the repo — the current `user_version` is 9, not 8. `migrate()` in backend/src/db/worker.js skips any file whose version is `<= current`, so a file named `009_workouts.sql` is silently never applied, on every database, with no error.
seriousFlaws.scenario: Existing DB at user_version 9: both 009 files are `<= 9` → both skipped → no workout tables, `migrate()` returns `{applied: [], version: 9}`. Fresh DB: `readdir().sort()` yields `009_language_roster.sql` before `009_workouts.sql`; the first applies and bumps to 9; the second is then `9 <= 9` → skipped. Either way the entire workout schema never exists and the boot log says migrations succeeded. The first `/api/v1/sessions` call 500s with 'no such table: workout_logs'.
seriousFlaws.fix: Name the file `010_workouts.sql` and bump to 10. Independently, harden `migrate()`: reject a `files` array containing duplicate version numbers at load time rather than silently skipping — a collision is always a mistake and it currently fails closed and quiet.

seriousFlaws.flaw: Warm-up sets are excluded from PR evaluation but INCLUDED in the entry rollups the progress graph reads. `top_weight_kg` and `top_est_1rm_kg` are computed as bare `MAX(...) WHERE entry_id = :e AND status = 'done'` with no `set_kind <> 'warmup'` filter, while layer 4's PR insert has `AND s.set_kind <> 'warmup'`. The design's own DDL comment says warmup is 'load-bearing, not cosmetic'.
seriousFlaws.scenario: Client does a warm-up single at 100 kg × 1 (`set_kind='warmup'`, Epley = 103.3), then three working sets at 80 kg × 8 (Epley = 101.3). `workout_log_entries.top_est_1rm_kg` = 103.3; `exercise_records.best_est_1rm_kg` = 101.3. The progress graph (which the design says reads the entry columns directly, 'no GROUP BY on the read path') plots 103.3. The records screen says 101.3. No PR badge fires. Two contradicting 'best' numbers for the same session, both server-computed, both wrong relative to each other — and next session's graph point moves purely as a function of how the client tagged their warm-up.
seriousFlaws.fix: Add `AND set_kind <> 'warmup'` to the `top_weight_kg`, `top_est_1rm_kg` and `top_duration_seconds` subqueries. Decide deliberately whether `total_volume_kg` and `total_reps` include warm-ups (volume arguably should; the record book must not) and write the decision into the column comments, because these five columns are read by three different screens.

seriousFlaws.flaw: `workout_log_entries.performed_at` is `INTEGER NOT NULL` with NO default — so it MUST be supplied by the INSERT, which makes it client-settable in any naive materialisation that passes the payload through. It is the sort key of `idx_workout_log_entries_history`, i.e. the column that resolves the frozen `prev_entry_id` and orders the record book. The design's comment says 'Server clock, copied from workout_logs.started_at' but no constraint enforces it, and `workout_logs.started_at` is itself only `DEFAULT (unixepoch())` — a default a route overrides for free.
seriousFlaws.scenario: Client posts a freestyle session with `performed_at: 4102444800` (year 2100) on one entry. That entry is now permanently the first row off `idx_workout_log_entries_history` for that (user, exercise). Every future session's `prev_entry_id` resolves to it — and because the design freezes the pointer at materialisation, every future workout for the rest of the account's life shows a fabricated 'previous performance' with no repair path (the design admits no recompute job exists). The same column poisons the 'records over time' ordering. Negative values work equally well in the other direction.
seriousFlaws.fix: `performed_at INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT (unixepoch())` and never accept it from a payload; better, populate it in the materialisation SELECT as `(SELECT started_at FROM workout_logs WHERE id = :log)` so it cannot diverge from its parent. Add `CHECK (performed_at BETWEEN 1600000000 AND 4000000000)` as a sanity backstop, and the same bound on `client_started_at` / `client_completed_at`, which are currently unbounded in both directions. Adopt the repo's explicit column allow-list pattern (`onboarding/routes.js:83-91`) for every one of these tables rather than spreading req.body.

seriousFlaws.flaw: `last_client_seq` is a client-supplied monotonic counter with only `CHECK (last_client_seq >= 0)` — no upper bound — and the guard is `:seq > last_client_seq`. A single op with a huge value permanently bricks that set row, and the failure is reported to the user as SUCCESS (`replayed: true`).
seriousFlaws.scenario: One op arrives with `seq: 9007199254740991` (a JS MAX_SAFE_INTEGER from a buggy client that used `Date.now()*1000`, or a deliberate Burp send). It passes the CHECK and wins. Every subsequent legitimate write to that set — correcting the weight, fixing the reps, un-skipping it — has `seq` in the hundreds, fails `> last_client_seq`, changes zero rows, and returns `{replayed: 1}`. The player renders a checkmark. The set is frozen at whatever the poisoned op wrote, forever, with no server-side detection and no reset path in the schema. The design's weakness list covers the reinstall/counter-reset case but not the ceiling case, which is a single request.
seriousFlaws.fix: Bound it: `CHECK (last_client_seq BETWEEN 0 AND 1000000)` and define seq as a small per-session ordinal, not a timestamp. Return the server's current `last_client_seq` on every response (including the replayed one) so the client can fast-forward instead of silently losing writes. Make the response distinguish 'your write was applied' from 'your write was older than what I have' — `replayed` currently conflates a harmless double-tap with data loss, and only one of those should be invisible to the user.

seriousFlaws.flaw: Plan size is unbounded because the calendar-slot UNIQUE index is partial. `idx_workout_plan_days_slot` is `UNIQUE (plan_id, week_index, weekday) WHERE weekday IS NOT NULL` — so free-floating days (`weekday NULL`) have no cap at all, and neither do items-per-day or the total materialisation size. Materialisation runs in ONE IMMEDIATE transaction holding SQLite's single write lock.
seriousFlaws.scenario: An authenticated coach scripts 20,000 `weekday: null` days into one plan, then 2,000 items into a single day (`workout_plan_items` has no per-day count constraint), each with `target_sets: 20`. A client starts that day: `startWorkoutSession` expands it into 2,000 entries and 40,000 set rows inside one `tx.immediate()`. For the tens of seconds that runs, every other writer in the process — every set check, every login, every audit_log insert — waits on the write lock, hits `busy_timeout = 5000`, and gets SQLITE_BUSY, which `errorHandler` renders as a generic 500. One request from one authenticated coach account takes the write path down for every user on the instance. The design's own note says 'Keep named transactions short'; nothing enforces it.
seriousFlaws.fix: Cap it in the schema and at the route. Add a per-plan day counter or a BEFORE INSERT trigger asserting `(SELECT COUNT(*) FROM workout_plan_days WHERE plan_id = NEW.plan_id) < 400`, and the same shape for items-per-day (`< 40`). Reject a materialisation whose projected set count exceeds a hard ceiling (e.g. 300) BEFORE the first write, so the refusal is a 400 rather than a rollback. Bound `week_index` against the plan's own `week_count` rather than the free-standing 0..51.

seriousFlaws.flaw: `idx_workout_logs_one_active` (UNIQUE on user_id WHERE status='active') is not covered by the exactly-once adoption path. The design's `ON CONFLICT (user_id, client_uid) DO NOTHING` names only ONE of the two unique indexes on `workout_logs`, so a violation of the other one is raised, not suppressed — and there is no typed error mapping in this codebase (backend/src/lib/http.js:62-63).
seriousFlaws.scenario: Client forgets to tap Finish on Monday. Tuesday they start a workout: the INSERT carries a fresh `client_uid`, so the named conflict target does not match, and `idx_workout_logs_one_active` raises SQLITE_CONSTRAINT_UNIQUE. `errorHandler` returns `{error:'internal server error', code:'INTERNAL'}` 500 — the user cannot train and is told the server is broken. Now compound it with the offline batch: that INSERT is inside `syncOfflineQueue`'s single IMMEDIATE transaction, so the throw discards the entire reconnect batch (see the fatal finding on syncOfflineQueue). A second device starting a session concurrently produces the same 500.
seriousFlaws.fix: Either drop the one-active index and let 'resume' pick `ORDER BY started_at DESC LIMIT 1 WHERE status='active'`, or keep it and make session creation a pre-write check inside the named tx that returns a typed `{code:'SESSION_ACTIVE', logId}` BEFORE any write, which the route maps to 409 with a resume/discard choice. Whichever you pick, the stale-session sweeper the design names must actually exist, and `errorHandler` needs a SQLITE_CONSTRAINT_UNIQUE branch so a constraint can never again reach a user as 'internal server error'.

seriousFlaws.flaw: The design claims the partial UNIQUE index on `(log_set_id, kind)` satisfies T2.10.3 for rewards — 'one constraint, both requirements'. It stops a REPLAY double-award. It does not stop RE-CREATION: sets are cheap, so each cycle produces a genuinely new `log_set_id` and the index never fires. `workout_prs.reward_state` has no 'revoked' value and there is no clawback.
seriousFlaws.scenario: Client adds an ad-hoc set to a freestyle session, checks it at 200 kg × 1 → PR (`kind='est-1rm'`), `reward_state='pending'` → the Phase 7 worker grants coins. Client edits that set down to 20 kg × 1 → the PR is `revoked_at`-stamped, `needs_recompute=1`, the coins stay (nothing in the schema takes them back). Recompute drops `best_est_1rm_kg` to 20. Client adds another set, checks it at 200 kg × 1 → new `log_set_id`, new PR row, new coins. The loop is bounded only by the write rate limiter (60/15min), which is thousands of coins a day per account, from a single exercise, using only legitimate endpoints.
seriousFlaws.fix: Do not tie the reward to a PR row. Add `reward_state` value 'revoked' plus a `workout_pr_rewards` ledger keyed on `(user_id, exercise_id, kind, value_bucket)` so a reward is granted once per genuinely new record LEVEL, not once per PR event. Gate reward eligibility on the PR surviving a settling window (e.g. `achieved_at < unixepoch() - 3600 AND revoked_at IS NULL`) so an edit inside the window costs nothing. Cap ad-hoc set creation per session.

seriousFlaws.flaw: `exercise_records.exercise_id` is NOT NULL, but `workout_log_entries.exercise_id` is nullable (`ON DELETE SET NULL`). The two are joined in the hot path. An orphaned entry makes every subsequent set check throw — after first inserting a bogus PR.
seriousFlaws.scenario: An exercise row is hard-deleted (an admin purge, or a coach user row deleted, which CASCADEs `exercises.owner_id`). Any client with a live entry for it now has `entry.exercise_id = NULL`. Next set check: layer 4's `LEFT JOIN exercise_records r ON r.exercise_id = e.exercise_id` never matches (NULL = NULL is never true), so `r.best_est_1rm_kg IS NULL` is true and a 'first ever PR' row is inserted with `exercise_id NULL` — a spurious gold badge and a pending coin. Layer 5 then does `INSERT INTO exercise_records (user_id, exercise_id, ...) VALUES (:me, NULL, ...)` → NOT NULL violation → the whole tx throws → 500. The rollback discards the bogus PR too, but also the set check itself: the client can never mark that set done, and every retry 500s identically with no explanation.
seriousFlaws.fix: Skip records and PRs entirely when `exercise_id IS NULL` — add `AND e.exercise_id IS NOT NULL` to the layer 4 SELECT and make layer 5 conditional on the same. Since `exercise_records` is a per-(user, exercise) cache, an orphaned entry legitimately has no record row; the entry rollups and `exercise_name_snapshot` are enough to render it. Also add `AND e.exercise_id IS NOT NULL` to `idx_workout_log_entries_history`'s partial WHERE so an orphan can never become someone's 'previous performance'.

seriousFlaws.flaw: The parent-consistency triggers are sold as an authorization control but are neither: they are BEFORE INSERT only (no UPDATE coverage) and they assert internal consistency with the parent, never that `user_id` equals the authenticated caller. The design states they mean 'the denormalisation cannot be used to forge a claim' — that is only half true.
seriousFlaws.scenario: (a) UPDATE bypass: any route that touches `workout_log_sets.entry_id` or `log_id` — a 'move this set to another exercise' or 'reorder entries' feature, or a careless PATCH allow-list — runs with no trigger at all, so the denormalised `user_id` can be left pointing at the old parent while `entry_id` points at a new one. Every ownership check downstream (`WHERE user_id = ?`) then reads a row that belongs to someone else's session. (b) Forward-consistency: a route that derives the insert's `log_id`/`user_id` FROM the supplied `entry_id` (the obvious way to satisfy the trigger — `SELECT log_id, user_id FROM workout_log_entries WHERE id = ?`) satisfies it perfectly while writing a set into the VICTIM's entry, because nothing compares the result to `req.user.id`. (c) When the trigger does fire it RAISE(ABORT)s into a generic 500, not the 404 the anti-IDOR rule requires.
seriousFlaws.fix: Mirror both triggers as BEFORE UPDATE OF entry_id, log_id, user_id. Make the INSERT itself carry the caller: `INSERT INTO workout_log_sets (entry_id, log_id, user_id, ...) SELECT e.id, e.log_id, e.user_id, ... FROM workout_log_entries e JOIN workout_logs l ON l.id = e.log_id WHERE e.id = :entryId AND e.user_id = :me AND l.status = 'active'` — zero rows inserted → 404. The trigger then stays what it should be: a data-integrity backstop, not the control.

seriousFlaws.flaw: Mass-assignment surface is large and mostly undefended. The design's only structural defence is the two generated columns; every other server-authoritative column is a plain writable column protected by nothing but route discipline, and the design never states an allow-list despite the repo having an explicit precedent for one (`onboarding/routes.js:83-91`, `exercises/routes.js:408-419`).
seriousFlaws.scenario: A `PATCH /sessions/:id` that spreads req.body lets a client set, in one request: `status:'finished'`, `finished_at`, `duration_seconds: 0`, `total_volume_kg: 999999`, `pr_count: 50`, `total_sets`, `exercise_count`, `plan_version`, `started_at` (reordering their own record book), `user_id` (there is no trigger on workout_logs at all). On `workout_log_sets`: `completed_at` (only constrained to be non-NULL when status='done'), `status:'done'` without ever supplying weight or reps, and every `target_*` snapshot column — so a client fabricates 'my coach prescribed 200 kg' in the very log the coach reads for a dispute, and the design's central claim that the snapshot is authoritative history of the prescription is false for any set the client created offline. On `workout_plans`: `owner_id`, `client_id`, `is_template`, `source_plan_id`, `version`.
seriousFlaws.fix: Write the allow-list into the design, per table, the way the repo already does. Client-writable is exactly: `workout_log_sets` → weight_kg, reps, duration_seconds, distance_m, rpe, rest_taken_seconds, notes, set_kind (only for client-added sets), plus the op envelope (seq, op_id, client_completed_at). Everything else on that table is server-set. `workout_logs` → title, notes, perceived_effort, local_date, client_uid only. `workout_plans` → title, title_lang, description, goal, start_date, timezone, week_count, repeats, status only. Additionally: `target_*` on a client-created set must be NULL, not client-supplied — a set the coach never prescribed has no prescription. Enforce with `CHECK (origin <> 'added' OR target_weight_kg IS NULL)` on the entry/set pair or set them server-side to NULL.

seriousFlaws.flaw: Several smaller but concrete gaps that each produce a wrong answer: (a) no uniqueness on the client's live plan; (b) the body-area map has no rows for 'other' or the 'full-body' muscle group; (c) `workout_exercise_grants` is never revoked when the exercise leaves the plan, only on link archive.
seriousFlaws.scenario: (a) `idx_workout_plans_client (client_id, status, deleted_at)` is non-unique, so a coach can leave three plans at `status='active'` for one client. The home card's 'which plan is live for me' and the 'today' card have no deterministic answer and will flip between plans depending on index order. (b) A client with a limitation of `body_area='other'` (a legal value in `onboarding_limitations`) gets zero rows from `body_area_muscle_map`, so T2.5.4 filtering silently does nothing — and the `full-body` muscle group is mapped from no body area at all, so 'avoid knee' never excludes a single full-body exercise (burpees, thrusters, cleans — precisely the knee-loading ones). (c) Coach adds private exercise X to a client's plan (grant minted), then removes the item and deletes the plan. The grant row survives; the client reads X forever, including any later edits the coach makes to its description.
seriousFlaws.fix: (a) `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ... ON workout_plans (client_id) WHERE status = 'active' AND deleted_at IS NULL AND client_id IS NOT NULL` — and make activating a plan a single guarded statement that deactivates the incumbent in the same transaction. (b) Seed `('other', full-body)` and add `full-body` to the knee/hip/lower-back/shoulder rows, or state explicitly that 'other' is advisory-only and surfaces as a warning rather than a filter. (c) Re-derive grants rather than accumulating them: on plan-item delete and plan soft-delete, `DELETE FROM workout_exercise_grants WHERE user_id = :client AND exercise_id = :ex AND NOT EXISTS (<any surviving plan item or log entry for that client>)`. Add `plan_id`/`source` to the grant so revocation is scoped rather than best-effort.

strengths: Materialising set rows as `status='pending'` at session start so the hot path is a guarded UPDATE and never an INSERT. This is the single best idea here: it eliminates the double-tap duplicate-row class structurally rather than by dedupe, and it is what makes 'the guard lives inside the UPDATE' actually expressible for the busiest write in the product. Keep this regardless of what else is discarded.

`volume_kg` and `est_1rm_kg` as VIRTUAL GENERATED columns. A generated column has no INSERT/UPDATE surface at all, so 'the client cannot submit a derived value' stops being a convention a future contributor can forget and becomes a property of the schema. Gating both expressions on `status = 'done'` so voiding a set auto-removes its contribution is a genuinely elegant touch. VIRTUAL over STORED is the right call (no bytes, still indexable).

Recompute-by-aggregate for every rollup instead of `col = col + ?`. The reasoning is exactly right — a recompute is idempotent by construction and costs ~5 row reads, an increment's correctness depends entirely on a guard that depends on a client-supplied counter. This is a real second independent layer, not a restatement of the first.

The two partial UNIQUE indexes on `workout_prs` — `(log_set_id, kind) WHERE log_set_id IS NOT NULL` and `(log_entry_id, kind) WHERE log_set_id IS NULL`. A database-level backstop for double-PR/double-award that does not depend on the transaction above it being correct, and the reasoning about SQLite treating NULLs as distinct in a UNIQUE index (hence two partials, not one) is correct and non-obvious.

The prescription SNAPSHOT onto log rows, with `plan_id`/`plan_day_id`/`plan_item_id` as nullable `ON DELETE SET NULL` breadcrumbs. Correctly identifies that a log read through a live join to a mutable plan means a coach's edit retroactively rewrites history and a plan delete becomes a history delete. The CASCADE-on-the-plan-side / SET-NULL-on-the-log-side asymmetry is deliberate and right.

Civil `TEXT` dates (`YYYY-MM-DD`, GLOB-constrained) for `scheduled_date` / `local_date` alongside an epoch `started_at`, with the explicit argument that the epoch rule governs instants and a scheduled day is not an instant. Correct, well defended, and the rejection of epoch-of-local-midnight is the right rejection. Adherence-vs-ordering being two different columns is the part most designs get wrong.

Keying every cross-user read on the `coach_clients` LINK id rather than the client's user id, and deliberately resolving the repo's own inconsistency by taking the stricter `status = 'active'` (so an 'invited' link that was never accepted grants nothing). It copies `onboarding/routes.js:255-265` exactly and it correctly explains why the URL must be `/clients/:linkId/...`.

Naming the exercise-visibility hole at all, and rejecting 'extend VISIBLE with an EXISTS over coach_clients' for the correct reason — that it would expose a coach's entire private library, drafts included, to any client who types into the search box. The grant MECHANISM is broken (see fatal #2), but the problem statement, the rejected alternative, and the reasoning against snapshotting 1652 exercises are all correct and should survive into the synthesis.

`exercise_name_snapshot` on the log entry with `exercise_id ON DELETE SET NULL`. History renders forever without needing read access to the exercise row, which is what lets the archive path re-hide a coach's library without destroying the client's training record. This is the right decomposition of 'what must survive' vs 'what must be revocable'.

`body_area_muscle_map` as a seeded junction table rather than a CHECK or a JSON list, seeded BY SLUG rather than by id. It correctly identifies that `onboarding_limitations`' joint-centric vocabulary and the exercises' muscle-group tagging were never connected, which is the actual blocker on T2.5.4 — and every slug it references does exist in the 003 seed (verified).

Recognising that this feature set is the first thing in the codebase that structurally requires named worker transactions, and specifying BOTH halves (the `worker.js` export and the `index.js` facade line) plus the six function names. The design knows `writeTx` cannot read, branch or inspect an intermediate result and does not pretend otherwise.

A prescribed rest day as a real row (`is_rest`) so adherence can distinguish 'rest was prescribed' from 'session was missed'. Small, cheap, and the kind of thing that is painful to retrofit once an adherence ring is already shipped.

An honest, specific weaknesses section that pre-identifies the `last_client_seq` reset case, the frozen-prev-pointer backfill bug, the one-active-session UX cliff, the cache-drift risk and the crudeness of the body-area map. Several of these are real and the design does not hide them — that materially raises the trustworthiness of the rest.

fatalFlaws.flaw: `workout_log_sets.log_id` is a client-supplied denormalised column with NO coherence constraint to `workout_log_items.log_id`, and STEP 5's total-recompute UPDATE is keyed on it. Cross-tenant write. The design added a BEFORE INSERT coherence trigger for `workout_log_items.client_id` and explicitly listed 'denormalised columns protected only on INSERT' as a weakness — but it never noticed that the one unprotected denormalised column is the one that names another user's row. STEP 0 of `recordSet` selects `li.id, li.exercise_id, l.status` and does NOT select `li.log_id`, so `log_id` can only be coming from the request.
fatalFlaws.scenario: Attacker is client A. A starts their own workout: gets `workout_logs.id = 500`, `workout_log_items.id = 900`. `workout_logs.id` is a plain rowid alias, so 499 is almost certainly another client's log. A posts `{ log_item_id: 900, log_id: 499, set_index: 0, weight_kg: 300, reps: 20 }`. STEP 0 passes — item 900 genuinely belongs to A and log 500 is genuinely in_progress. STEP 1 inserts `workout_log_sets(log_item_id=900, log_id=499, weight_kg=300, reps=20)`; the FK to `workout_logs(499)` is satisfied, no trigger exists, no CHECK applies. STEP 5 then runs `UPDATE workout_logs SET total_volume_kg = (SELECT SUM(...) FROM workout_log_sets WHERE log_id = 499), ... WHERE id = 499` — victim B's session row is written by A, and B's total_volume_kg now includes 6000 kg A never lifted. B's coach's dashboard, B's weekly-volume graph and B's adherence are all poisoned, permanently, and nothing in the schema can detect it because the poisoned set row is invisible in B's log (it hangs off A's log_item). Repeat across ids 1..N to corrupt every client in the instance.
fatalFlaws.fix: Never accept `log_id` from the client. Derive it inside the transaction: STEP 0 becomes `SELECT li.id, li.log_id, li.exercise_id, li.client_id, l.status FROM workout_log_items li JOIN workout_logs l ON l.id = li.log_id WHERE li.id = ? AND li.client_id = ? AND l.status = 'in_progress'`, and STEP 1/STEP 5 bind `row.log_id`. Then make it structural, since the design's own thesis is that guards belong in the schema: add `CREATE TRIGGER trg_log_set_log_match BEFORE INSERT ON workout_log_sets FOR EACH ROW WHEN (SELECT log_id FROM workout_log_items WHERE id = NEW.log_item_id) IS NOT NEW.log_id BEGIN SELECT RAISE(ABORT, ...); END;` plus the BEFORE UPDATE OF log_id, log_item_id twin. Do the same for the missing UPDATE twins on `trg_log_item_client_match` and `trg_plan_schedule_client_match`.

fatalFlaws.flaw: The PR ratchet is monotonic (`WHERE excluded.value > exercise_records.value`) but the row it derives from is MUTABLE through the very same call. `recordSet` is simultaneously the create path and the correction path — its ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE branch overwrites weight_kg/reps — yet it only ever raises `exercise_records`, never lowers it, and it never invokes `recomputeExerciseRecord`. The design treats 'replay' and 'correction' as the same operation and then applies replay-only reasoning to it.
fatalFlaws.scenario: Client logs bench set 3 as 100 kg × 5 (fat-fingered; the bar was 60). STEP 3 fires: `max_weight` 100, `max_e1rm` 116.7, `source_set_id` = 4711, `previous_value` = 92.5. STEP 4 sets `workout_log_sets.is_pr = 1`. Client immediately notices and re-checks the same set at 60 kg × 5 — same `(log_item_id, set_index)`, so STEP 1 rewrites row 4711 to 60 kg. STEP 3 runs again: `60 > 100` is FALSE, changes = 0. STEP 4's `is_pr` is deliberately excluded from the DO UPDATE list, so the badge stays. Final state: `workout_log_sets` row 4711 says 60 kg, `is_pr = 1`; `exercise_records` says max_weight = 100 kg, max_e1rm = 116.7, `source_set_id = 4711` — a record pointing at a set that contradicts it. The client's PR list, their progress graph's y-axis ceiling, and every future `target_pct_1rm` resolution (the design computes prescribed kg from `exercise_records.max_e1rm` server-side) are now derived from a lift that never happened. The coach programs 85% of a phantom 116.7 kg. Nothing detects it; `recomputeExerciseRecord` exists but no code path calls it, because the correction went through `recordSet`.
fatalFlaws.fix: Make `recordSet` detect that it OVERWROTE an existing completed set rather than created one, and branch: if STEP 1 hit the ON CONFLICT branch AND any of (weight_kg, reps, seconds, distance_m) changed, run the full `recomputeExerciseRecord` aggregate for that (user, exercise, metric) set INSIDE the same transaction instead of the monotonic upsert. To detect it without a pre-read, use `ON CONFLICT ... DO UPDATE SET ... RETURNING id, (weight_kg IS NOT excluded.weight_kg OR reps IS NOT excluded.reps) AS changed` (better-sqlite3 supports RETURNING). Also clear the stale badge in the recompute path: `UPDATE workout_log_sets SET is_pr = 0 WHERE id = ? AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM exercise_records WHERE source_set_id = ?)`. And add the missing constraint that would have made this visible: `exercise_records` should carry no value it cannot re-derive.

fatalFlaws.flaw: Out-of-order arrival is unhandled. The idempotency story is exact-duplicate-only: it proves that replaying the SAME payload is safe, and then silently assumes that is the only thing an offline queue does. There is no sequence number, no client timestamp, no `If-Match` on the set row, and no `WHERE updated_at <= ?` precondition — so for two DIFFERENT payloads addressed to the same `(log_item_id, set_index)`, the winner is whichever HTTP request the network delivered last.
fatalFlaws.scenario: Client is on a train, offline, mid-workout. At 10:04 they check set 3 = 100 kg × 5 (request A queued). At 10:05 they realise the bar was 60 and re-check set 3 = 60 kg × 5 (request B queued). At 10:08 connectivity returns and the queue flushes over HTTP/1.1 keep-alive with 6 parallel connections; A and B land on different sockets and B's `recordSet` acquires SQLite's write lock first. Final row: 100 kg × 5 — the value the client explicitly corrected away, now persisted as fact, with is_pr = 1 and a matching `exercise_records` row (see the ratchet flaw, which compounds it). The client's log shows a set they did not perform, and no retry, refresh or re-sync will ever fix it because from the server's point of view both writes succeeded and the data is 'settled'. The same mechanism corrupts any set the client edits twice while offline, which is exactly what a rest-timer-driven player encourages.
fatalFlaws.fix: Give the set row a monotonic client-side ordinal and make it a guard inside the UPDATE, not a preceding check. Add `client_seq INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0` to `workout_log_sets`, have the player stamp a per-device monotonically increasing counter on every queued mutation, and write `ON CONFLICT (log_item_id, set_index) DO UPDATE SET weight_kg = excluded.weight_kg, ..., client_seq = excluded.client_seq WHERE excluded.client_seq > workout_log_sets.client_seq`. A stale replay then matches nothing (changes = 0) and is reported as an accepted no-op, exactly like `onboarding/routes.js:237`'s `alreadyComplete`. This also fixes the exact-duplicate case more honestly than the current COALESCE trick, and it is the precondition that makes the recompute branch above decidable.

fatalFlaws.flaw: `exercise_records.value REAL NOT NULL CHECK (value > 0)` combined with six unconditional metric upserts per set-check means a bodyweight set aborts the ENTIRE `recordSet` transaction — including STEP 1, the set the client just checked. A raised CHECK reaches the route as a generic 500 (`lib/http.js:62` maps only ZodError), so the failure is both total and undiagnosable.
fatalFlaws.scenario: Client's plan day contains push-ups (`prescription_kind = 'reps'`, no target_weight_kg, exercise_type = 'strength'). They check set 1: 20 reps, `weight_kg` NULL. STEP 3 iterates the six metrics as the design specifies. `max_weight` = COALESCE(weight_kg, 0) = 0 → `CHECK (value > 0)` fails → RAISE. better-sqlite3 propagates, the `.immediate()` transaction rolls back, and STEP 1's set row goes with it. `max_e1rm` = 0 × (1 + 20/30) = 0 would fail identically. The route returns 500. The client's offline queue treats 5xx as retryable, retries forever, and the set is never recorded. Push-ups, pull-ups, dips, planks and every cardio row are unloggable — and the failure mode is 'the app is broken' with a SQLITE_CONSTRAINT_CHECK buried in the server log. Worse, the same abort takes out any set in the same request batch. This is the most common exercise class in the product and it is a hard stop, not a degradation.
fatalFlaws.fix: Two changes. (1) The worker must compute a metric list, not a fixed six: skip any metric whose value is NULL or <= 0, and never upsert `max_weight`/`max_e1rm` for a set with no external load. (2) Relax the storage constraint so the schema cannot turn a data-shape question into a rollback: `CHECK (value > 0)` should stay, but the guard belongs in JS before the statement is bound, because the design's own ground truth (worker.js has no typed error mapping) means every CHECK is a 500. Separately, decide what a bodyweight PR IS — `max_reps` for push-ups, and `max_e1rm` computed against `workout_logs.bodyweight_kg + COALESCE(weight_kg,0)` for weighted pull-ups — otherwise the snapshot column you added has no consumer.

fatalFlaws.flaw: The migration number 009 is ALREADY TAKEN. `C:/Users/Petike/Documents/Cursor/tracker/backend/src/db/migrations/009_language_roster.sql` exists on disk (23 language rows). The ground-truth brief said user_version = 8 and 'the next migration must be 009' — that was true when the brief was written and is not true now. Because `db/index.js:39-46` derives the target version from the filename and `worker.js:131` skips any file whose version <= current user_version, a second 009 is not an error — it is a SILENT no-op.
fatalFlaws.scenario: Fresh developer checkout or new deploy. `migrate()` reads the directory, filters `/^\d+_.*\.sql$/`, and `.sort()`s lexicographically: `009_language_roster.sql` sorts before `009_workout_plans.sql`. The roster file runs, `PRAGMA user_version = 9` commits. The loop reaches `009_workout_plans.sql`, evaluates `9 <= 9`, and `continue`s. `migrate()` returns `{ applied: [9], version: 9 }` — success. `server.js` binds the port. There is no error, no warning, no log line. The database now claims schema version 9 while missing all 14 workout tables. The first coach to open the plan builder gets `SQLITE_ERROR: no such table: workout_plans` as a 500. On an existing dev machine already at user_version 9 the file is skipped from the very first boot, so the developer who wrote it never sees their own schema apply and will spend the afternoon debugging the pool.
fatalFlaws.fix: Number the file `010_workout_plans.sql` and bump to 10. Then close the hole permanently, because this will recur the moment two branches add a migration: in `backend/src/db/index.js`'s `migrate()`, after building `files`, assert that the version numbers are strictly increasing and unique, and throw at boot with the colliding filenames if not. A duplicate migration number must be a startup crash, never a skip — it is the one failure this runner's design cannot otherwise detect.

fatalFlaws.flaw: Start-of-workout idempotency exists only for SCHEDULED sessions. `workout_logs_schedule_unique` is `ON workout_logs (schedule_id) WHERE schedule_id IS NOT NULL AND status <> 'abandoned'` — an ad-hoc workout has `schedule_id` NULL and is therefore excluded from the index entirely. The design explicitly argues 'a double-tapped Start workout is the client's most ordinary mistake' and then solves it for the case where the client is following a plan, i.e. the case where they are least likely to be improvising.
fatalFlaws.scenario: Client opens the app in the gym with no plan for today and taps 'Start empty workout'. The request is slow on gym wifi; they tap again. Two `startWorkout` calls, both with `schedule_id` NULL, both insert. `workout_logs` now has rows 800 and 801, both `status = 'in_progress'`, both `client_id` = them, both `performed_on` = today. Nothing collides. The client's session then holds `log_item_id`s from log 801 (the second response), but the first response's items were already rendered — so on a flaky connection the player's queued set-checks split across BOTH logs. Final state: two workouts on the same day, one with 4 sets and one with 7, `total_volume_kg` correct for neither, `workout_logs_open_idx` returning two rows so 'Resume your workout' is ambiguous forever, and the coach's adherence view showing a client who trained twice. There is no constraint that can be added retroactively to merge them.
fatalFlaws.fix: Add a second partial unique index covering the ad-hoc case: `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX workout_logs_open_unique ON workout_logs (client_id) WHERE status = 'in_progress'` — one live session per client, which is also physically true (a human cannot be in two gyms). `startWorkout` then upserts against it and returns the existing log, which is the behaviour the design already wants. If genuinely-concurrent sessions must be allowed later, replace it with a client-supplied `start_key TEXT` under `UNIQUE(client_id, start_key)`; but the single-open-session index is the honest model and it also makes the 'Resume' index deterministic.

seriousFlaws.flaw: Nothing ties `workout_plan_days.week_index` to `workout_plans.weeks`, and the materialiser must use `weeks` as the cycle stride. A day at `week_index >= weeks` collides with the next cycle's dates, and `plan_schedule_slot_unique (assignment_id, cycle_index, plan_day_id)` cannot catch it because the colliding rows have different `plan_day_id`.
seriousFlaws.scenario: Coach creates a 4-week block (`weeks = 4`, days at week_index 0..3), assigns it with `repeat_cycles = 3`, then later uses 'copy week' to add a deload at week_index 4 — legal, since `CHECK (week_index >= 0)` has no ceiling and `weeks` is never re-validated on day insert. The materialiser computes `date = starts_on + (cycle_index * weeks * 7) + (week_index * 7) + day_offset`. Cycle 0 / week 4 / Monday lands on day 28. Cycle 1 / week 0 / Monday also lands on day 28. Both rows insert cleanly. The client's Home card for that Monday returns two sessions; the calendar week shows two Push Days stacked; adherence counts two scheduled sessions where the coach authored one. The coach never sees it, because the plan builder renders weeks 0..4 correctly.
seriousFlaws.fix: Either derive the stride from the data instead of the column — `stride_weeks = (SELECT MAX(week_index) + 1 FROM workout_plan_days WHERE plan_id = ?)` computed inside `assignPlan` and stored on `plan_assignments` as `cycle_weeks INTEGER NOT NULL` so the schedule is reproducible — or add a BEFORE INSERT/UPDATE trigger on `workout_plan_days` rejecting `week_index >= (SELECT weeks FROM workout_plans WHERE id = NEW.plan_id)`. Storing `cycle_weeks` on the assignment is better: it also makes the plan editable after assignment without silently re-dating an existing schedule.
