seriousFlaws.flaw: The client-side read of `plan_schedule` is scoped by `client_id` alone — the design states this explicitly ('Client: AND client_id = ? directly'). So archiving a link does NOT remove the schedule from the client's app, which directly contradicts the design's own claim that 'the plan disappears from their app too'. The result is not a leak of much content, but it is a permanently broken screen.
seriousFlaws.scenario: Coach archives the link on 1 March. The client's Home 'today' card queries `plan_schedule WHERE client_id = ? AND scheduled_on = 20260302` — the row is still there (nothing cascades, by design, so un-archiving restores everything). The card renders 'Today: Upper A'. The client taps it; the player fetches the plan day, which DOES apply the `cc.status = 'active'` EXISTS, and gets 404. The client sees a workout they cannot open, every day, for the remaining 40 scheduled sessions, with no explanation. If they tap 'Start' the log may still be created (workout_logs is client-owned with no link check), producing a log whose `plan_day_id` they cannot read.
seriousFlaws.fix: Either scope the client's schedule read through the assignment's link the same way the plan read is scoped — `AND (ps.assignment_id IN (SELECT a.id FROM plan_assignments a WHERE a.client_link_id IS NULL OR EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM coach_clients cc WHERE cc.id = a.client_link_id AND cc.client_id = ? AND cc.status = 'active')))` — or, cheaper and more honest, make `archiveClient` set `plan_assignments.status = 'ended'` for that link in the same guarded UPDATE and have every schedule read require `a.status = 'active'`. The second keeps the hot Home query a two-column index seek plus one join and makes the state change explicit and auditable.

seriousFlaws.flaw: Every failure mode of the eight new named transactions collapses to HTTP 500, because `errorHandler` (`C:/Users/Petike/Documents/Cursor/tracker/backend/src/lib/http.js:50-68`) maps ZodError and body-parser faults and nothing else, and `worker.js:61-67`'s rethrow flattens an error into `{message, code: 'SQLITE_*'}` with no slot for an application code. The design acknowledges this in its weaknesses but understates the consequence: 500 is retryable by convention, 409 is not.
seriousFlaws.scenario: Client finishes a workout, taps Finish, then their queue flushes three set-checks that were still pending. `recordSet` STEP 0 finds `l.status = 'completed'`, throws CONFLICT. The route has no mapping, so the client receives 500 `internal_error`. Every offline-queue implementation retries 5xx with backoff and gives up on 4xx — so the queue retries these three requests indefinitely, each one taking SQLite's IMMEDIATE write lock, until the app is reinstalled. Same shape for the reorder: a stale-`rev` 409 arrives as a 500, so the coach's UI cannot distinguish 'refetch and replay the drag' from 'server is down', and will either lose the edit or retry it into a loop. Compounding this, the route contract's write tier is 60 requests / 15 min — a single 40-set workout flushed after a dropped connection, with retries, exceeds it and starts returning 429, dropping sets.
seriousFlaws.fix: Establish the convention the design assumes: define `class AppError extends Error { constructor(code, status) }` in `src/lib/errors.js`, have every named worker transaction throw it, and extend `rethrow` in `worker.js` to preserve `err.appCode`/`err.status` as enumerable fields so they survive structured clone. Add one branch to `errorHandler`: `if (err?.appCode) return sendError(res, err.status, err.appCode, ...)`. Separately, give log-write endpoints their own rate tier (the design needs something like 600/15min, matching the read tier) — an offline-first log path cannot live under the 60/15min write limiter.

seriousFlaws.flaw: 'Copy day is a plain INSERT..SELECT with no renumbering' — one of the three stated justifications for contiguous positions — is false. `trg_plan_item_group_same_day_ins` aborts any copied item whose `group_id` still points at a group on the source day, so copy-day requires cloning `workout_plan_groups` first and remapping ids. The same applies to `clonePlanToClient`, which must remap four levels (days → groups → items → item_sets).
seriousFlaws.scenario: Coach builds Monday with a superset (two items sharing group 12) and taps 'Copy day to Wednesday'. The implementer writes the INSERT..SELECT the DDL comment promises. Every grouped item raises 'a plan item may only join a group on its own day' → generic 500. The obvious fix under deadline is to add `NULL AS group_id` to the SELECT — at which point copy-day silently destroys every superset and circuit in the copied day, and the coach discovers it when the client's player renders eight separate exercises instead of four pairs. Copy-week multiplies it across seven days, and `clonePlanToClient` (the operation the ENTIRE copy-on-assign thesis rests on) does it to every client instantiation.
seriousFlaws.fix: Delete the misleading claim from the DDL comment and specify the copy transaction properly: insert the day, then `INSERT INTO workout_plan_groups (day_id, kind, label, rounds, ...) SELECT ?, kind, label, rounds, ... FROM workout_plan_groups WHERE day_id = ? ORDER BY id`, capturing the id map via `RETURNING id` (better-sqlite3 supports it and it is the only way to build the map without n round-trips), then insert items joining old→new group ids. Because the design needs this map at four levels, write ONE `clonePlanTree(sourcePlanId, target)` worker function and have copy-day, copy-week, clone-to-client and clone-from-system all call it — otherwise there will be four subtly different remappers and the group-drop bug will live in three of them.

seriousFlaws.flaw: The coach dashboard's adherence query has no usable index. The only index whose leading column is `workout_logs.schedule_id` is the PARTIAL unique index `WHERE schedule_id IS NOT NULL AND status <> 'abandoned'`, and SQLite will only use a partial index when the query's WHERE clause provably implies the index's. A LEFT JOIN's ON clause implies `schedule_id IS NOT NULL` but cannot imply `status <> 'abandoned'`, so the planner falls back to a full scan of `workout_logs` per outer row.
seriousFlaws.scenario: 200 clients, 6 months in: `workout_logs` ≈ 20,800 rows, `plan_schedule` ≈ 22,000 rows. The coach opens the dashboard, which asks 'for each of my clients, how many of the last 4 weeks' scheduled sessions were completed': `SELECT ps.client_id, COUNT(wl.id) FROM plan_schedule ps LEFT JOIN workout_logs wl ON wl.schedule_id = ps.id WHERE ps.client_id IN (...) AND ps.scheduled_on BETWEEN 20260201 AND 20260301 GROUP BY ps.client_id`. The outer side is ~3,200 rows via `plan_schedule_today_idx`; the inner side is a 20,800-row scan each time. ~66 million row visits, several seconds, on a single write-locked SQLite file with a 5-second busy_timeout — so it also starves concurrent `recordSet` calls from clients who are mid-workout. This is the first query in the design to die, and it dies on the screen the coach opens most.
seriousFlaws.fix: `CREATE INDEX workout_logs_schedule_idx ON workout_logs (schedule_id) WHERE schedule_id IS NOT NULL;` — a plain (non-unique, no status predicate) partial index the join CAN use. Keep the existing unique index for its constraint value. Also add `plan_schedule_assignment_idx ON plan_schedule (assignment_id, scheduled_on)` so the coach can range-scan one client's block without going through `client_id`. Separately, `workout_log_items_exercise_idx (exercise_id)` is dead weight — the correlated `EXISTS (... li.exercise_id = e.id AND li.client_id = ?)` is served better by the existing `workout_log_items_history_idx (client_id, exercise_id, ...)`; the plan-side EXISTS is the one that actually lacks an index, and it needs `workout_plan_items (exercise_id, day_id)` at minimum.

seriousFlaws.flaw: `total_volume_kg` is defined as `SUM(COALESCE(weight_kg,0) * COALESCE(reps,0))`, which is zero for every bodyweight movement — while `workout_logs.bodyweight_kg` is justified in its own comment as existing 'so bodyweight-exercise volume ... do not silently rewrite themselves'. The column has no consumer. Separately, the same aggregate counts `set_kind = 'warmup'` rows in `total_sets` and `total_reps`.
seriousFlaws.scenario: Client does a calisthenics session: 5×20 push-ups, 5×10 pull-ups, 3×60s plank. Every set has `weight_kg` NULL. `total_volume_kg` = 0. The Home screen shows '0 kg volume', the weekly-volume graph shows a hole, and the coach's dashboard ranks this client as inactive next to someone who did three machine sets. Meanwhile a barbell client whose plan prescribes 3 warmup sets per exercise reports 33 sets for a 24-working-set session, so 'sets per week' — the number every strength coach actually manages — is inflated by ~40% and is not comparable between two clients whose coaches prescribe warmups differently.
seriousFlaws.fix: Make the aggregate load-aware: `SUM(COALESCE(weight_kg, 0) * COALESCE(reps,0) + CASE WHEN weight_kg IS NULL AND reps IS NOT NULL THEN COALESCE((SELECT bodyweight_kg FROM workout_logs WHERE id = ?), 0) * reps ELSE 0 END)` — or, cleaner, resolve the effective load once in JS at set-check time and store `effective_load_kg REAL` on `workout_log_sets`, so the aggregate stays a plain SUM and the bodyweight snapshot has the consumer its comment promises. Then split the counters: `total_work_sets` (`set_kind IN ('work','backoff','amrap','failure')`) alongside `total_sets`, because those are two different questions and only one of them is the coaching metric.

seriousFlaws.flaw: `exercise_records.exercise_id REFERENCES exercises(id) ON DELETE CASCADE` while `workout_log_items.exercise_id` is `ON DELETE SET NULL`. The design carefully defends log history against the coach-account-deletion cascade (`exercises.owner_id ... ON DELETE CASCADE`, confirmed in `003_exercises.sql:37`) with `exercise_name_snapshot`, and then leaves the sibling table with a hard cascade — so the same event that history survives destroys every client's PRs on those exercises, unrecoverably, because the recompute needs `exercise_id` and the log items' copy is now NULL.
seriousFlaws.scenario: A coach with 40 clients has 25 custom exercises (their own barbell variations). The coach deletes their account — a feature that does not exist today but which GDPR erasure requires and which the design explicitly anticipates in the `workout_log_items` rationale. `exercises` rows cascade-delete. `workout_log_items.exercise_id` → NULL (history readable, names intact — the design's win). `exercise_records` rows → GONE. Forty clients lose their PR history on those movements permanently, and `recomputeExerciseRecord` cannot rebuild them because there is no surviving `exercise_id` to group by. The clients' 'Recent PRs' screens quietly shrink and nobody can say why.
seriousFlaws.fix: Change to `exercise_id INTEGER REFERENCES exercises(id) ON DELETE SET NULL` and make the natural key survive it — but `UNIQUE(user_id, exercise_id, metric)` with a NULL exercise_id stops being unique in SQLite, so add `exercise_name_snapshot TEXT NOT NULL` to `exercise_records` (mirroring the log items) and index `(user_id, exercise_id, metric)` for the live case plus a partial `(user_id, exercise_name_snapshot, metric) WHERE exercise_id IS NULL` for the orphaned case. Better still: stop hard-deleting exercises on user delete — change `exercises.owner_id` to `ON DELETE SET NULL` with a status transition, since a movement that 40 clients have performed is not the coach's to erase.

seriousFlaws.flaw: Kilogram storage is correct, but nothing records the unit the value was ENTERED in, and the PR guard is a bare float comparison. Imperial users generate phantom PRs from conversion rounding, and no round-trip is stable.
seriousFlaws.scenario: Client's `units = 'imperial'`. They log 225 lb × 5 on Monday; the app converts and stores 102.0582 kg; `exercise_records.max_weight` = 102.0582. On Friday they log the identical 225 lb × 5, but a frontend release in between changed the conversion to round to 2 decimals, so 102.06 is stored. STEP 3: `102.06 > 102.0582` is TRUE → changes = 1 → gold-frame badge, 'New PR', `previous_value` 102.0582, and the UI computes the delta as '+0.00 kg'. The client gets a celebration for repeating a lift. Even without a frontend change, any client whose device does the conversion in float32 vs float64, or who enters 225 vs 224.9, trips it. In the other direction, a client switching metric→imperial sees their clean 100 kg squat as 220.46 lb and can never enter it back exactly.
seriousFlaws.fix: Two things. (1) Quantise on write: snap `weight_kg` to the nearest 0.25 kg (or 0.5 lb equivalent) in the worker before binding, so the same physical lift always produces the same stored float — this alone kills the phantom PR. (2) Add `entered_unit TEXT CHECK (entered_unit IN ('kg','lb'))` and `entered_value REAL` to `workout_log_sets`, nullable, display-only. Storage stays canonical metric (008's law is right), but the log can then render exactly what the client typed instead of a lossy re-conversion. Optionally tighten the guard to `excluded.value > exercise_records.value + 0.01` so float noise can never move a record.

seriousFlaws.flaw: `exercise_records` stores `max_e1rm` as a bare REAL with no formula identifier and no version. When the formula changes, there is no way to tell a recomputed row from a stale one, `previous_value` is never recomputable at all, and rows whose `source_set_id` went NULL (the FK is ON DELETE SET NULL) can never be rebuilt.
seriousFlaws.scenario: Next year the product switches Epley to Brzycki for high-rep accuracy. A recompute job runs over `workout_log_items_history_idx`. It succeeds for records whose source sets still exist. But (a) `previous_value` on every row is an Epley number the job has no source for and does not touch, so every 'PR delta' badge mixes two formulas; (b) any record whose source set was deleted has `source_set_id` NULL and a value the job cannot re-derive — it stays Epley forever, indistinguishable from a Brzycki row; (c) if the job is interrupted at row 40,000 of 90,000 (5-second busy_timeout, one write lock), the table is now half one formula and half the other with NO column that says which, and re-running it is not idempotent for the rows already converted unless it recomputes from source — which for the NULL-source rows it cannot. Meanwhile `target_pct_1rm` prescriptions resolve against a mixed-scale column, so two clients get different real loads for the same '85%'.
seriousFlaws.fix: Add `formula TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'epley' CHECK (formula IN ('epley','brzycki','lombardi'))` to `exercise_records` now, while the table is empty. A migration then becomes: recompute where possible and stamp the new formula; leave un-recomputable rows stamped 'epley' and let the UI mark them. Drop `previous_value` in favour of deriving the delta from the second-best value at read time, or accept that it is a display cache and stamp it with the same formula column. Also reconsider `metric` as a lookup TABLE rather than a CHECK — the design's own rule says a lookup table is used 'wherever an admin must edit the set', and a metric list that will grow (max_e1rm_brzycki, max_reps_at_bodyweight) is exactly that.

seriousFlaws.flaw: ICS is broken as specified. `plan_assignments.ics_uid` is documented as 'the stable UID of every VEVENT this assignment emits' — but iCalendar UID is the per-event identity key, so a feed where 84 VEVENTs share one UID collapses to one event in Google/Apple Calendar. Separately, moving a session UPDATEs `plan_schedule` while SEQUENCE comes from `plan_assignments.rev`, and nothing links the two.
seriousFlaws.scenario: Coach assigns a 12-week block; the client subscribes to the ICS URL. Google Calendar ingests 84 VEVENTs all carrying UID `a7f3...`, treats them as 84 revisions of one event, and displays exactly one workout — the last one in the file. The client's calendar shows a single session in week 12. The coach then pushes Thursday to Friday: `UPDATE plan_schedule SET scheduled_on = ?, moved_from_on = ? WHERE id = ? AND ...` succeeds, `plan_assignments.rev` is untouched (it is a different table and a different statement), SEQUENCE stays 0, and every subscribed client keeps whatever they had cached. The 'coaches move sessions constantly' argument that justified materialising the schedule in the first place is the exact case the ICS design cannot express.
seriousFlaws.fix: Emit UID as `${plan_assignments.ics_uid}-${plan_schedule.id}` — stable per occurrence, unguessable, and it survives a move because the row id does not change. Bump SEQUENCE per occurrence, not per assignment: add `rev INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0` to `plan_schedule` and increment it inside the same guarded UPDATE that moves the date (`SET scheduled_on = ?, moved_from_on = scheduled_on, rev = rev + 1 WHERE id = ? AND ...`), so SEQUENCE is a property of the event it describes. Also note `ics_token` lives only on `coach_clients`, so self-coached users (scope='personal', no link) have no feed at all — put the token on a per-user row or on `plan_assignments` if personal plans are meant to export.

seriousFlaws.flaw: Names invite the wrong mental model in three places, and one of them is destructive. `workout_plans.owner_user_id` holds the COACH for `scope='client'` rows; and `workout_plan_items` / `workout_log_items` / `workout_plan_item_sets` / `workout_log_sets` are four tables whose names differ by one word and whose meanings are prescription-vs-performance.
seriousFlaws.scenario: Six months from now a developer adds 'archive all my plans' to the coach's settings screen. The obvious statement is `UPDATE workout_plans SET archived_at = unixepoch() WHERE owner_user_id = ? AND archived_at IS NULL` — which is exactly the shape of every other ownership write in the repo. It archives the coach's templates AND all 200 live client instances, and because the client's read filters `archived_at IS NULL`, every client's plan vanishes from their app simultaneously. The reverse error is quieter: a 'my plans' screen for a user writes `WHERE owner_user_id = ?` and returns their personal plans while silently omitting the coached plan they actually follow, because that row is owned by the coach. Separately, in a copy transaction touching all four items/sets tables, `INSERT INTO workout_plan_item_sets ... SELECT ... FROM workout_log_sets` is a one-character-class typo that type-checks, runs, and produces a plan whose prescriptions are someone's performance.
seriousFlaws.fix: Rename `owner_user_id` to `author_user_id` — it is the authoring identity, never the subject, and the name should say so; then every 'whose plan is this' question is forced to go through `client_link_id`. Rename the four leaf tables so they cannot be transposed: `plan_exercises` / `plan_exercise_sets` and `log_exercises` / `log_sets`. And since the design introduces a brand-new `_on` = civil-date vs `_at` = epoch convention that exists nowhere in migrations 001–009, it needs to be written into `docs/brain/20-Data-Model/` and enforced by a `lib/civildate.js` with `addDays()`/`toEpochRange()`, because `scheduled_on + 7` producing 20260833 is a bug the CHECK will catch only sometimes (20260833 is out of no bound the CHECK tests — `BETWEEN 19700101 AND 21001231` accepts it).

seriousFlaws.flaw: Coherence triggers are INSERT-only throughout, and the plan's `scope` can be changed after an assignment exists — so the 'copy-on-assign law, made structural' has an UPDATE-shaped hole in it.
seriousFlaws.scenario: A coach asks for 'save this client plan as a template'. The obvious implementation is `UPDATE workout_plans SET scope = 'template', client_link_id = NULL WHERE id = ? AND owner_user_id = ?`. The table-level CHECK passes (template + owner + NULL link). `trg_plan_assignment_scope_upd` fires only `BEFORE UPDATE OF plan_id ON plan_assignments`, so nothing fires. The existing `plan_assignments` row now points at a template — the exact state the two INSERT triggers were written to make impossible — and `trg_plan_assignment_link` (INSERT only) can no longer catch the mismatch either, since `plan_assignments.client_link_id` is now non-NULL while the plan's is NULL. The client keeps executing a plan the coach believes is a detached template, and the coach's next edit to that 'template' rewrites the client's live sessions: the precise failure the entire design was built to prevent.
seriousFlaws.fix: Add the UPDATE twins the design skipped: a `BEFORE UPDATE OF scope, client_link_id ON workout_plans` trigger that aborts when `EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM plan_assignments WHERE plan_id = NEW.id AND status <> 'ended')` and the new scope is not in ('client','personal') or the link changed; plus `BEFORE UPDATE OF client_link_id ON plan_assignments` mirroring `trg_plan_assignment_link`. Every BEFORE INSERT coherence trigger in this migration needs its UPDATE twin — `trg_plan_schedule_client_match` and `trg_log_item_client_match` are missing theirs too, and the design's own weaknesses section flags the symptom without connecting it to the assignment law.

strengths: THE NATURAL-KEY UPSERT IS THE RIGHT IDEMPOTENCY PRIMITIVE AND SHOULD SURVIVE SYNTHESIS INTACT. Modelling 'set checked' as an assertion about (log_item_id, set_index) rather than an event to append means the natural key IS the idempotency key: no idempotency_keys table, no TTL sweeper, no stored response bodies — which is the correct answer for a codebase that has zero idempotency infrastructure and should not grow a generic framework for one endpoint. It also composes forward: a future reward_ledger with UNIQUE(source_type, source_id) is double-award-proof precisely because the set's rowid is stable across replays. Everything I attacked above is a gap AROUND this idea, not in it.

THE GUARDED PR UPSERT IS THE CORRECT MECHANISM: `ON CONFLICT (user_id, exercise_id, metric) DO UPDATE ... WHERE excluded.value > exercise_records.value` puts the comparison inside the UPDATE with no preceding SELECT, so there is no check-then-write window, and it is a faithful generalisation of the one proven guard-in-UPDATE in the live code (`UPDATE invite_codes SET uses = uses + 1 WHERE uses < max_uses`, coaching/routes.js:268). The monotonic-only direction is the defect; the shape is right and should be kept, with a recompute branch bolted beside it.

RECOMPUTE-BY-AGGREGATE AS A GLOBAL LAW. `SET total = (SELECT SUM(...))` is idempotent by construction and `SET total = total + ?` is not — stated as a rule, applied consistently, and correctly bounded (~40 rows behind a dedicated index). This should be lifted out of this migration and written into the repo's decision records as a standing law, because it is the general answer to the replay requirement and it costs nothing at this row count.

OWNERSHIP KEYED ON THE LINK ID, NOT THE CLIENT USER ID, WITH status='active'. This is the single most important thing the design got right about security. It matches the canonical cross-user read at onboarding/routes.js:255-265 verbatim, it makes archiving take effect on the very next request with the same unexpired JWT (no claim to expire, no revocation list), and the per-table predicate table is specific enough to implement from. The resolution of the archive-semantics split — `status = 'active'` for data access, `<> 'archived'` for the management roster, with the reasoning that an 'invited' person has not consented to being prescribed to — is correct and well argued. Keep the whole ownership section.

COPY-ON-ASSIGN AND SNAPSHOT-THE-PRESCRIPTION. The history-integrity argument is right: a training log whose 'prescribed 4x8 @ 80kg' retroactively becomes '5x5 @ 100kg' is not a log. Deep-copying at assign time and again at start time is the correct default for this product, and the three-way justification (safety of late-night template edits, per-client personalisation without an overlay/merge layer, history immutability) is the strongest reasoning in the document. `exercise_name_snapshot TEXT NOT NULL` on the log item is exactly right and is the kind of detail that is impossible to retrofit once there is data.

THE TABLE-LEVEL CHECK OVER (scope, owner_user_id, client_link_id) making every incoherent combination unrepresentable, instead of an `is_template` boolean that permits `is_template = 1 AND client_link_id IS NOT NULL`. This is strictly stronger than a route-level convention, costs one constraint, and it held up under attack — I could not construct an incoherent plan row through it. Collapsing the roadmap's `is_template` into the enum was the right call and the rationale is reusable.

MATERIALISED plan_schedule RATHER THAN A RECURRENCE RULE. 'Push Thursday to Friday' is the operation coaches actually perform, and with a rule it becomes an exception table — a second data model that disagrees with the first at every edge. One row per session makes the move a single guarded UPDATE, the Home card a point lookup, the calendar week a range scan and adherence a LEFT JOIN. Bounding it with `repeat_cycles BETWEEN 1 AND 52` keeps the materialisation finite. Keep this, with the cycle-stride fix.

body_area_muscle_map IS A GENUINELY MISSING EDGE AND THE SEED IS CORRECT. I verified all 19 muscle slugs it references against the 003_exercises.sql seed — chest, front-delts, side-delts, rear-delts, biceps, triceps, forearms, abs, obliques, lats, traps, lower-back, glutes, quads, hamstrings, calves, adductors, abductors, neck all exist, so all 34 rows insert cleanly. Seeding through the SLUG via a JOIN rather than literal ids is exactly right (ids differ between a fresh and an upgraded database) and matches house style. It unblocks T2.5.4, and pairing the blunt heuristic with `client_exercise_prefs` as an explicit coach override is the honest way to ship an approximate filter.

CONTIGUOUS position + UNIQUE(day_id, position) + THE TWO-PASS PARKING. The size argument is correct — a workout day is 3-15 rows because a human has to perform it, so the O(n) rewrite that disqualifies contiguity in a backlog is free here. The decisive point is detectability: `max(position) = count(*) - 1` is a checkable invariant, and LexoRank never breaks and therefore never tells you it is wrong. Pass 1 as a provable bijection into a disjoint range is the right way to satisfy a non-deferrable UNIQUE. Separating concurrency (days.rev) from ordering (position) is also correct — a fractional rank does not prevent interleaved drags, it only hides them.

REV-GUARD-INSIDE-THE-UPDATE FOR STRUCTURAL EDITS, with the explicit choice of DETECTION over silent merge, and the honest note that over-counting is the safe direction (a false 409 costs a refetch, a missed one costs data). Correct trade, correctly reasoned, and it is the right shape for the reorder even though the error-mapping infrastructure it depends on does not exist yet.

THE WEAKNESSES SECTION IS UNUSUALLY HONEST AND OPERATIONALLY USEFUL. It self-reports the propagation gap, the schedule-repair gap, the heuristic bluntness, the eight-unproven-named-transactions risk, the bulk-op idempotency gap and the INSERT-only trigger problem. Several of my findings are that section's items followed one step further to their concrete consequence. A design that names its own soft spots this precisely is cheaper to maintain than one that does not, and the synthesis should carry these forward as open items rather than rediscover them.

fatalFlaws.flaw: MIGRATION NUMBER COLLISION — `009_language_roster.sql` ALREADY EXISTS in the repo (I listed the directory). The proposal's `009_workout_plans.sql` is silently skipped by the migration runner, not rejected.
fatalFlaws.scenario: `migrate()` (index.js:39-46) reads the dir, filters `/^\d+_.*\.sql$/` and `.sort()`s LEXICOGRAPHICALLY. `009_language_roster.sql` sorts before `009_workout_plans.sql`. Boot on a db at user_version 8: language_roster applies, `conn.pragma('user_version = 9')`. Loop reaches workout_plans, worker.js:131 evaluates `if (version (9) <= current (9)) continue;` — the ENTIRE workout schema is skipped. No throw, no log line, `applied` reports [9], the server binds the port. Every plan/log endpoint then dies with `SQLITE_ERROR: no such table: workout_plans` → generic 500 via errorHandler. On a db already at 9 (any dev machine that has booted since the language roster landed) BOTH files are skipped and the failure is identical. There is no error path anywhere that says 'a migration file was ignored'.
fatalFlaws.fix: Rename to `010_workout_plans.sql` and bump to 10. Separately, harden the runner: after the loop, assert that every file version >= the starting user_version was either applied or provably already applied, and throw on a duplicate version number in `entries` — a two-files-one-number collision must abort boot, not no-op.

fatalFlaws.flaw: `workout_log_items` IS A SELF-GRANTING ACL OVER THE PRIVATE EXERCISE LIBRARY. The new client-side visibility predicate grants read on any exercise the client has 'personally performed' — and the client is the party who writes the row that constitutes proof of performance. `exercise_id` carries nothing but `REFERENCES exercises(id)`.
fatalFlaws.scenario: Eve is an ordinary `role='user'` account with no coach and no plan. She hits the freestyle/ad-hoc logging path ('add an exercise to my workout'), which the roadmap's guided player implies and which the design's own nullable `plan_item_id` explicitly permits. She POSTs one log item per `exercise_id` from 1 to 1652, each with a made-up `exercise_name_snapshot`. Every insert satisfies the FK; the only ownership predicate on the table is `client_id = ?`, which is her own id, so it passes; `trg_log_item_client_match` also passes. She then GETs each exercise through the plan/player/history read path. The 'personally-performed-by-me' EXISTS is now true for all 1652, so she reads every coach's `status='private'` exercises, every `pending_review` submission, and every `rejected` row including the admin's `rejection_reason` — precisely what `exercises/routes.js:22-26` was written to prevent ('A 403 confirms the id is real, and that is enough to enumerate another coach's private library'). Rate limiting does not save this: the autosave tier is 240/15min, so a full sweep of the library is under two hours, and a targeted sweep of one coach's id range is one request.
fatalFlaws.fix: The performed-by-me grant must derive from an authorisation the SERVER issued, not from a row the client authored. Two options: (a) restrict the clause to `EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM workout_log_items li WHERE li.exercise_id = e.id AND li.client_id = ? AND li.plan_item_id IS NOT NULL)` — only server-snapshotted prescriptions count; or (b) add `granting_link_id INTEGER REFERENCES coach_clients(id)` written ONLY by `startWorkout` from the plan it copied, and make the EXISTS join that column. Additionally forbid ad-hoc log items whose `exercise_id` is not visible under the plain `VISIBLE` predicate at insert time — a BEFORE INSERT trigger cannot see `req.user.id`, so this one must be a bound `WHERE EXISTS` on an INSERT..SELECT, not a plain VALUES insert.

fatalFlaws.flaw: `plan_assignments.client_id` HAS NO COHERENCE CONSTRAINT — cross-tenant schedule injection, reachable from the lowest-privilege role. Every other denormalised owner column in this design got a BEFORE INSERT trigger (`trg_log_item_client_match`, `trg_plan_schedule_client_match`); the ROOT of the chain got none, and `trg_plan_schedule_client_match` validates against it, so plan_schedule faithfully inherits whatever it holds.
fatalFlaws.scenario: Write path, no coach role needed: Eve creates a `scope='personal'` plan (owner_user_id = Eve, client_link_id NULL). She POSTs an assignment `{plan_id: P, client_link_id: null, client_id: <victim's user id>}`. `trg_plan_assignment_scope_ins` passes ('personal' is in the allowed set). `trg_plan_assignment_link` evaluates `(SELECT client_link_id FROM workout_plans WHERE id=P) IS NOT NEW.client_link_id` → `NULL IS NOT NULL` → FALSE → no abort. plan_schedule rows are materialised with the victim's client_id and pass their own trigger. The victim's Home 'today' card is `WHERE client_id = ? AND scheduled_on = ?` — and the design states this is DELIBERATELY the only predicate available, 'since a personal plan has no link'. The victim now sees Eve's session, Eve's day names and Eve's free-text item notes on their home screen, taps Start, and gets a workout_logs row bound to Eve's plan. Read path, with a coach account: Mallory (legitimately coaching Bob) creates a `scope='client'` plan on link L_bob, then assigns with `client_id = Carol` (a stranger). Scope trigger ✓; link trigger compares the plan's client_link_id to L_bob ✓. Adherence is specified as 'a LEFT JOIN to workout_logs' from plan_schedule, and Mallory's read predicate on her own assignment is `client_link_id = ? AND EXISTS(cc.coach_id = ?)` — which passes — so she reads Carol's workout_logs totals, duration and notes. The design's ownership section never states where `client_id` comes from, so a route has nothing to copy.
fatalFlaws.fix: Two BEFORE INSERT/UPDATE triggers on plan_assignments. (1) When client_link_id IS NOT NULL: `WHEN (SELECT client_id FROM coach_clients WHERE id = NEW.client_link_id AND status='active') IS NOT NEW.client_id → RAISE(ABORT)`. (2) When client_link_id IS NULL (personal): `WHEN (SELECT owner_user_id FROM workout_plans WHERE id = NEW.plan_id) IS NOT NEW.client_id → RAISE(ABORT)` — a personal plan may only ever be assigned to its own author. Mirror both onto UPDATE OF client_id, client_link_id, plan_id.

fatalFlaws.flaw: NO CONSTRAINT TIES `workout_plans.owner_user_id` TO `coach_clients.coach_id` FOR `client_link_id` — a coach can inject a permanent, unremovable plan into a stranger's client's app. The design claims incoherent owner combinations are 'physically unrepresentable', but the table CHECK only tests NULL-ness, and an INSERT has no WHERE clause to hide an ownership guard in.
fatalFlaws.scenario: Link ids are `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY` (sequential); Mallory reads her own roster to learn the live range. She POSTs `{scope:'client', client_link_id: 4711, name:'Week 1 — deload', ...}` where 4711 is coach Bob's link to client Carol. The table CHECK passes (scope='client', owner_user_id NOT NULL, client_link_id NOT NULL). No trigger checks that 4711 is hers — the design wrote three BEFORE triggers for plan_assignments and zero for this. She creates days and items in the same flow and publishes. The design's CLIENT read predicate is `p.scope='client' AND p.published_at IS NOT NULL AND EXISTS (cc.id = p.client_link_id AND cc.client_id = ? AND cc.status='active')` — Carol matches, so Carol's app renders Mallory's plan, indistinguishable from Bob's. Worse, it is PERMANENT: the coach WRITE/archive predicate contains `EXISTS (cc.coach_id = ?)`, which Mallory now fails, so neither she nor Bob (owner_user_id ≠ Bob) can edit or archive it. Only an admin with raw SQL can remove it. The only thing standing between this and production is a route-layer SELECT the design never specifies — exactly the 'guard in a preceding SELECT' the hard rules forbid.
fatalFlaws.fix: BEFORE INSERT and BEFORE UPDATE OF owner_user_id, client_link_id, scope on workout_plans: `WHEN NEW.client_link_id IS NOT NULL AND (SELECT coach_id FROM coach_clients WHERE id = NEW.client_link_id AND status='active') IS NOT NEW.owner_user_id → SELECT RAISE(ABORT, 'plan owner must be the coach on the link')`. This is the one guard that cannot live in a WHERE clause, which is exactly why it must be a trigger.

fatalFlaws.flaw: `workout_log_sets.log_id` IS AN UNTRIGGERED DENORMALISED FK, AND BOTH STEP 1 AND STEP 5 OF `recordSet` BIND IT — cross-tenant total corruption and set leakage. The sibling table got `trg_log_item_client_match`; this one got nothing, and STEP 0's ownership check validates the ITEM, never that log_id is that item's log.
fatalFlaws.scenario: Eve POSTs a set-check with `log_item_id` = one of her own items and `log_id` = the victim's log id (the design's STEP 1 SQL lists both as separate bound parameters, and STEP 5 binds the log id three more times plus a `WHERE id = ?`). STEP 0 runs `SELECT li.id, li.exercise_id, l.status FROM workout_log_items li JOIN workout_logs l ON l.id = li.log_id WHERE li.id = ? AND li.client_id = ? AND l.status='in_progress'` — this resolves the log via `li.log_id`, so it validates EVE's log and passes. STEP 1 inserts a row whose log_item_id points into Eve's log and whose log_id points into the victim's. STEP 5 then runs `UPDATE workout_logs SET total_sets = (SELECT COUNT(*) ... WHERE log_id = ?), total_volume_kg = (...) WHERE id = ?` against the VICTIM's log, whose totals now aggregate Eve's row. The victim's coach reads it through `WHERE l.client_id = (SELECT client_id FROM coach_clients WHERE id=? AND coach_id=? AND status='active')` — the coach's log query descends from the log, not the item — so Eve's weight/reps/rpe/notes land on a stranger's coach's screen, and the victim's volume history is permanently wrong with no audit row.
fatalFlaws.fix: Either drop the column and aggregate through `JOIN workout_log_items` (the log has ~40 sets; the join is free), or add `CREATE TRIGGER trg_log_set_log_match BEFORE INSERT ON workout_log_sets WHEN (SELECT log_id FROM workout_log_items WHERE id = NEW.log_item_id) IS NOT NEW.log_id → RAISE(ABORT)` plus an UPDATE OF log_id, log_item_id twin. Also specify that `recordSet` DERIVES log_id from STEP 0's row and never accepts it from the request.

fatalFlaws.flaw: THE `recordSet` UPSERT IS SIMULTANEOUSLY THE REPLAY PATH AND THE EDIT PATH, AND THE PR HALF IS ONLY CORRECT FOR REPLAY. A downward correction leaves a phantom record that no set in the database supports — and the design feeds that record straight back into prescribed loads via `target_pct_1rm`.
fatalFlaws.scenario: Client fat-fingers set 1 as 100 kg × 5 (meant 10 kg). STEP 3 inserts `exercise_records(metric='max_e1rm', value=116.7, weight_kg=100, reps=5, source_set_id=S)`, changes=1, STEP 4 sets `S.is_pr=1`. She notices and corrects the set to 10 kg × 5 — same (log_item_id, set_index), so it is the same call. STEP 1's DO UPDATE rewrites weight_kg=10, but `is_pr` is DELIBERATELY excluded from the DO UPDATE list ('a replay must neither clear a badge already earned nor grant one it did not') and STEP 3's guard `excluded.value (11.7) > exercise_records.value (116.7)` is FALSE, so nothing moves. Final state: workout_log_sets says 10 kg with a gold PR badge; exercise_records says 116.7 kg e1RM 'from 100 kg × 5' with source_set_id pointing at a row that records 10 kg. `recomputeExerciseRecord` exists but the design never fires it from recordSet and no trigger does. The design cannot distinguish replay from correction at this layer — both are 'same natural key, possibly different values' — and it chose the semantics that are right for one and wrong for the other. Consequence beyond cosmetics: the design resolves `workout_plan_items.target_pct_1rm` to concrete kg on the SERVER from `exercise_records.max_e1rm` at read time, so the client is now prescribed 85% of a lift they never made. Same failure on delete: STEP 1 has no delete path at all, and `source_set_id ON DELETE SET NULL` leaves the inflated value behind.
fatalFlaws.fix: Make recordSet detect the mutation: capture the pre-image in STEP 0 (`SELECT weight_kg, reps, seconds, distance_m, is_pr FROM workout_log_sets WHERE log_item_id=? AND set_index=?`, before any write — ADR-0005 compliant). If any performed value CHANGED (not merely re-asserted), run the full `recomputeExerciseRecord` aggregate for that (user, exercise, metric) inside the SAME transaction and set `is_pr` from the result, rather than the one-way guarded upsert. Keep the guarded upsert only for the true first-write case where the pre-image is absent. A replay (pre-image identical) short-circuits before STEP 3 entirely.

seriousFlaws.flaw: STEP 3's 'once per metric' for all six metrics, combined with `value REAL NOT NULL CHECK (value > 0)`, makes bodyweight sets and failed sets un-checkable — a 500, not a validation error.
seriousFlaws.scenario: Client checks off a pull-up: `weight_kg` NULL, `reps` 8. `max_volume_set` computes `COALESCE(weight_kg,0) * reps = 0` → `CHECK (value > 0)` aborts → worker.js:61-67 rethrows `SQLITE_CONSTRAINT_CHECK` → lib/http.js:62-63 has no typed mapping → generic 500, and the whole `.immediate()` rolls back, so the set is never recorded at all. `max_weight`/`max_duration`/`max_distance` on the same set would each be a NOT NULL violation. Same abort for a genuinely failed set logged as `reps = 0`, which `CHECK (reps BETWEEN 0 AND 500)` explicitly permits. Bodyweight is the largest exercise category in the 1652-row dataset, so this is most of the product.
seriousFlaws.fix: State the applicability rule explicitly in the design: a metric is attempted only when its source value is non-NULL AND > 0, computed in the worker before the loop. Keep `CHECK (value > 0)` as the backstop it is meant to be. Optionally relax to `value >= 0` for max_reps so a logged failure is representable.

seriousFlaws.flaw: Schedule materialisation is unbounded on the day axis — one POST from any authenticated user holds SQLite's single write lock long enough to 500 the whole process.
seriousFlaws.scenario: `weeks BETWEEN 1 AND 52` bounds a label, not row count; nothing bounds `COUNT(*) FROM workout_plan_days WHERE plan_id = ?`, and `day_index` is left unbounded with a justification that confuses it with `workout_plan_items.position` (only the latter has a +1000000 parking range — the design's own weakness #11 admits days have no two-pass scheme). Eve creates a personal plan, bulk-inserts 400 day rows, then assigns with `repeat_cycles = 52`: ~20,800 plan_schedule inserts in one IMMEDIATE transaction. Every other writer in the process — every set-check, every token rotation — waits past `busy_timeout = 5000` and gets SQLITE_BUSY → 500. The write limiter is 60/15min, so she can repeat it 60 times. The design's claim that materialisation 'is bounded by repeat_cycles BETWEEN 1 AND 52' is only half the multiplication.
seriousFlaws.fix: `CHECK (day_index BETWEEN 0 AND 6)` and `CHECK (week_index BETWEEN 0 AND 51)` on workout_plan_days (the slot model already implies a 7-day week), plus a hard cap in `assignPlan`: refuse when `(SELECT COUNT(*) FROM workout_plan_days WHERE plan_id=?) * repeat_cycles > 400`, and chunk the materialisation across several short transactions with `plan_schedule_slot_unique` making each chunk re-runnable.

seriousFlaws.flaw: `coach_clients.ics_token` is a plaintext bearer credential in a repo that hashes every other one, and un-archiving silently resurrects a revoked feed URL.
seriousFlaws.scenario: `invite_codes.code_hash` is SHA-256 with the stated reason 'a database leak must not hand an attacker a working way into a team' (006:65-66) and `refresh_tokens.token_hash TEXT PRIMARY KEY` (001:47-48) is hashed too. `ics_token TEXT` is stored raw and resolved with `WHERE ics_token = ? AND status='active'`. What it unlocks is an unauthenticated GET returning the client's full dated training schedule — a where-and-when pattern for a named person — and the URL is by nature pasted into third-party calendar services, proxy logs and Referer headers. Second bug: coaching/routes.js:275's `ON CONFLICT(coach_id, client_id) DO UPDATE SET status='active', archived_at=NULL` un-archives the SAME row, so a coach who archived a client (killing the feed) and later re-links them silently reactivates the identical token — a URL handed out and believed revoked starts serving next week's sessions again, with no re-issue and no notification.
seriousFlaws.fix: Store `ics_token_hash` (SHA-256, partial-unique) and hand the plaintext to the coach exactly once at generation, exactly as invite codes do. Clear it on archive (`SET ics_token_hash = NULL` in the archive UPDATE) so un-archiving cannot resurrect it. Rate-limit the feed route and mount it above `requireAuth` but with its own limiter.

seriousFlaws.flaw: ARCHIVING A LINK DOES NOT STOP THE CLIENT EXECUTING THE ARCHIVED COACH'S PLAN — every predicate the design offers for the archived case is on the PLAN, and the execution path never reads the plan.
seriousFlaws.scenario: Coach archives the link at T. The plan correctly vanishes from the client's plan list (the EXISTS with `status='active'` fails). But `plan_schedule`'s client-side predicate is `client_id = ?` ALONE — the design states this is deliberate because a personal plan has no link to check — `plan_assignments.status` is still 'active', and the design says approvingly that 'nothing is deleted'. So at T+1 the client's Home 'today' card still surfaces the session, `startWorkout` still succeeds (its guard is schedule_id + client_id), and `workout_log_items` are still snapshotted out of the ex-coach's `workout_plan_items`. Combined with the self-granting-ACL finding, this means a client can mint PERMANENT read grants on the ex-coach's private exercises AFTER the relationship ended. The design's claim that 'the coach's private exercises stop resolving for that client at the same instant' is false in the only direction that matters.
seriousFlaws.fix: Add the link check to the execution path, not just the read path: `plan_schedule` client reads join `plan_assignments` and require `client_link_id IS NULL OR EXISTS (coach_clients ... status='active')`. Make the archive UPDATE a named transaction that also sets `plan_assignments.status='ended', ended_at=unixepoch()` for that link, so the schedule stops being live rather than merely unreadable at one level.

seriousFlaws.flaw: The log snapshot tables silently drop the CHECK bounds their source columns carry.
seriousFlaws.scenario: `workout_plan_items.target_weight_kg REAL CHECK (... BETWEEN 0 AND 1000)`; the snapshot is a bare `target_weight_kg REAL`. Same for `target_reps_min`, `target_reps_max`, `target_seconds`, `target_distance_m` on workout_log_items and `target_seconds`, `target_distance_m`, `target_weight_kg` on workout_log_sets — only `target_rpe` and `target_sets` kept a CHECK, while every PERFORMED column on the same rows is bounded. For an ad-hoc log item the targets come from the request, not from a plan item, so the backstop is load-bearing. Client posts `target_weight_kg: 1e308`; it stores; the coach's session view renders it and any weekly-target SUM becomes Infinity, which then serialises as `null` through JSON and blanks the coach's dashboard.
seriousFlaws.fix: Copy the CHECKs verbatim from workout_plan_items / workout_plan_item_sets onto both snapshot tables. A snapshot of a bounded value is still a bounded value.

seriousFlaws.flaw: `exercise_records.exercise_id ON DELETE CASCADE` destroys PRs the logs still evidence — the exact hazard the design solved correctly one table over.
seriousFlaws.scenario: `exercises.owner_id REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE` means deleting a coach's account hard-deletes their custom exercises. The design saw this and gave `workout_log_items` both `ON DELETE SET NULL` and `exercise_name_snapshot NOT NULL`. It gave `exercise_records` plain CASCADE and no snapshot. So when a coach deletes their account, their client's log still reads 'Trap-bar deadlift 200 kg × 3' while the PR row is gone, `recomputeExerciseRecord` cannot rebuild it (the exercise id no longer exists), and the client's 'recent PRs' list silently shortens.
seriousFlaws.fix: `ON DELETE SET NULL` on `exercise_records.exercise_id` plus an `exercise_name_snapshot` column and a partial unique index that survives NULL, OR make the unique key `(user_id, exercise_id, metric)` tolerate a tombstone. Simplest consistent answer: mirror workout_log_items exactly.

seriousFlaws.flaw: `workout_plan_items.exercise_id ON DELETE CASCADE` punches holes in LIVE client plans and permanently breaks the contiguity invariant the whole ordering design rests on.
seriousFlaws.scenario: Same trigger: coach (or admin) deletes a coach account, cascading into `exercises`, cascading into `workout_plan_items` — including items inside plans already assigned to and being executed by clients. The day survives with positions 0,1,3,4. The design's stated integrity check `max(position) = count(*) - 1` now fails on plans nobody edited, and nothing runs it. Worse, 'copy day is a plain INSERT..SELECT with no renumbering' — so the hole is faithfully replicated into every future clone and every re-assignment, forever. The client's player, walking a linear list, shows a superset whose partner exercise has evaporated with no explanation.
seriousFlaws.fix: `ON DELETE RESTRICT` is wrong (it would block account deletion). Use `ON DELETE SET NULL` on `workout_plan_items.exercise_id` plus a NOT NULL `exercise_name_snapshot` on the plan item too, so a deleted exercise degrades to a named placeholder the coach must resolve, and add a renumber pass to copyPlanDays so contiguity is restored on every copy rather than assumed.

seriousFlaws.flaw: The superset CONTIGUITY invariant is enforced on only one of the two write paths that can break it, and group-side moves are unguarded entirely.
seriousFlaws.scenario: The design's own ownership section shows the single-item write shape: `UPDATE workout_plan_items SET ..., group_id = ? WHERE id = ? AND day_id = ? AND EXISTS(...)`. That path never checks adjacency — only `savePlanDayOrder` does. A coach sets group_id=G on the items at positions 0 and 4 through the item-edit endpoint; `trg_plan_item_group_same_day_upd` checks only that G belongs to the same DAY, so it commits. The player, which the design says walks one linear list and renders a group as one card, now shows a 'superset' containing three unrelated exercises. Separately, `UPDATE workout_plan_groups SET day_id = ?` has no trigger at all — moving a group to another day orphans every member while the item-side trigger never fires, producing exactly the cross-session superset the item trigger exists to prevent.
seriousFlaws.fix: Either forbid group_id on the single-item edit path entirely (grouping changes only through savePlanDayOrder), or add an AFTER INSERT/UPDATE trigger asserting `(SELECT MAX(position) - MIN(position) FROM workout_plan_items WHERE group_id = NEW.group_id) = (SELECT COUNT(*) - 1 FROM workout_plan_items WHERE group_id = NEW.group_id)`. Add a BEFORE UPDATE OF day_id trigger on workout_plan_groups that aborts when the group has members.

seriousFlaws.flaw: `workout_logs_schedule_unique` makes a second session against the same scheduled slot permanently unloggable.
seriousFlaws.scenario: The partial index is `WHERE schedule_id IS NOT NULL AND status <> 'abandoned'`, so a COMPLETED log keeps occupying the slot. Client completes Monday morning's session; the coach asks for a second lighter session that evening against the same slot. `startWorkout` hits the conflict and — per the design, 'returns the existing log instead of a twin' — hands back the COMPLETED log. `recordSet` STEP 0 requires `l.status = 'in_progress'`, so every set-check throws CONFLICT → 409. There is no route to un-complete and no route to create a second log. The client's only recourse is an unscheduled log, which then does not count toward adherence for that session. Secondary: as an ON CONFLICT target the partial predicate must be repeated verbatim in the upsert, and a self-referential `status <> 'abandoned'` in a conflict target is considerably more delicate than 'a double-tapped Start hits the conflict' implies.
seriousFlaws.fix: Narrow the index to `WHERE schedule_id IS NOT NULL AND status = 'in_progress'` — that is the invariant actually needed (one LIVE log per slot). Let completed logs stack against a slot and let adherence pick MIN(started_at) or SUM the volume, whichever the product wants.

seriousFlaws.flaw: The YYYYMMDD CHECKs admit impossible dates, so a date-builder off-by-one produces a session visible in one calendar view and invisible in another.
seriousFlaws.scenario: `CHECK (scheduled_on BETWEEN 19700101 AND 21001231)` accepts 20260833 and 20260230. The design admits `lib/date.js` does not exist and that 'a careless scheduled_on + 7 produces 20260833'. That value passes every constraint and sorts between 20260831 and 20260901: the week-of-Aug-31 range scan (20260831..20260906) returns it and renders 'day 33 of August'; the week-of-Sep-1 scan (20260901..20260907) does not, so the session the client was told about on Monday is gone on Tuesday. ICS emits a VEVENT with an invalid DTSTART, which most calendar clients drop silently.
seriousFlaws.fix: Tighten every civil-date CHECK: `AND (col / 100) % 100 BETWEEN 1 AND 12 AND col % 100 BETWEEN 1 AND 31`. It will not catch Feb 30 but it catches every arithmetic-carry bug, which is the whole realistic failure class.

seriousFlaws.flaw: `is_pr` is never cleared, so the badge means 'was once a PR' while two other sources of truth say otherwise.
seriousFlaws.scenario: Set A at 100×5 → record value 116.7, source_set_id=A, A.is_pr=1. Set B at 110×5 → record 128.3, source_set_id=B, B.is_pr=1. A.is_pr stays 1 forever, because STEP 4 only ever sets and never clears. The design also says the player asks `exercise_records_source_idx` 'which records does this set hold?' to label the badge — for A that now returns zero rows while `A.is_pr = 1`. Two mechanisms for one badge, disagreeing on every superseded PR, and the history list shows a gold frame on every set that was ever a best, which is most of a beginner's log.
seriousFlaws.fix: Either drop the `is_pr` column and derive the badge purely from `exercise_records.source_set_id` (one source of truth, and the index for it already exists), or rename it `was_pr_at_time` and document that the player must not use it for the live badge.

seriousFlaws.flaw: `trg_plan_translation_system_only` guards INSERT only, leaving the admin translation surface pointable at private coach content.
seriousFlaws.scenario: `UPDATE workout_plan_translations SET plan_id = <a coach's private template id> WHERE id = ?` fires no trigger and violates no constraint. The row now carries admin-authored `name`/`description` attached to a coach's private plan, which is exactly the 'admin surface onto private content' the INSERT trigger was written to prevent. The same file writes UPDATE twins for both group-day triggers and for both assignment-scope triggers, so the omission is inconsistent within the migration itself.
seriousFlaws.fix: Add `CREATE TRIGGER trg_plan_translation_system_only_upd BEFORE UPDATE OF plan_id ON workout_plan_translations ... WHEN (SELECT scope FROM workout_plans WHERE id = NEW.plan_id) IS NOT 'system'` — and use the null-safe `IS NOT` form the rest of the migration uses, since `<>` is FALSE against a NULL subquery.

seriousFlaws.flaw: `set_index` is unbounded on both the plan and the log side, letting a client turn STEP 5's 'bounded to ~40 rows' aggregate into a shared-write-lock tax.
seriousFlaws.scenario: `workout_log_sets.set_index INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (set_index >= 0)` with UNIQUE(log_item_id, set_index) and nothing tying it to `target_sets`. A client scripts 10,000 set-checks at set_index 0..9999 against one log item (autosave tier, 240/15min — a day's work, or trivially faster if the set-check route lands on the write tier by accident). Every subsequent set-check in that log then runs three COUNT/SUM aggregates over 10,000 rows INSIDE the IMMEDIATE transaction, holding the single write lock, degrading every other user's writes. The design's stated bound of ~40 rows is an assumption, not a constraint.
seriousFlaws.fix: `CHECK (set_index BETWEEN 0 AND 49)` on both workout_log_sets and workout_plan_item_sets, and reject a set_index >= the item's target_sets + a small slack in zod. Same for a per-log item count cap.

seriousFlaws.flaw: MASS-ASSIGNMENT SURFACE IS LARGE AND THE DESIGN NAMES NO ALLOW-LIST, in a repo whose two existing precedents both do.
seriousFlaws.scenario: `onboarding/routes.js:83-91` keeps a twelve-column WRITABLE list with the comment 'Spreading the request body into an UPDATE is how status or completed_at ends up client-controlled', and `exercises/routes.js:408-419` uses a put() pick-list. This design specifies zero. The columns a naive route must never accept: workout_plans.{owner_user_id, scope, client_link_id, source_plan_id, published_at, rev, archived_at}; plan_assignments.{client_id, client_link_id, assigned_by, ics_uid, rev, status}; plan_schedule.{client_id, assignment_id}; workout_logs.{client_id, total_volume_kg, total_sets, total_reps, status, completed_at, duration_seconds, bodyweight_kg, schedule_id, plan_id, plan_day_id}; workout_log_items.{client_id, performed_on, exercise_name_snapshot, every target_*}; workout_log_sets.{is_pr, completed_at, log_id}; all of exercise_records. Concretely: `published_at` client-settable lets a coach's half-built week appear in the client's app; `bodyweight_kg` client-settable corrupts every relative-strength graph and is described as a server 'snapshot' with nothing enforcing that; client-settable `target_weight_kg` on a log item lets a client rewrite what the coach appears to have prescribed, which is the exact history-integrity property the whole snapshot design exists to protect.
seriousFlaws.fix: Publish the WRITABLE allow-list per table alongside the DDL, in the onboarding/routes.js:83-91 shape, and state for each server-owned column where its value is derived from. Treat this as part of the schema deliverable, not the route deliverable.

seriousFlaws.flaw: Eight named worker transactions rest on a typed-error convention that the worker boundary demonstrably does not carry.
seriousFlaws.scenario: The design maps STEP 0 misses to 404 and 'already completed' to 409 by throwing typed errors out of `.immediate()`. But worker.js's only error path is `rethrow()`, which builds a plain `new Error(...)` and sets a single `.code` — and its own comment states the reason: 'the structured clone that carries an error out of a worker keeps almost none of it'. Structured clone of an Error preserves name/message/stack/cause and DROPS arbitrary own properties, so `err.appCode = 'NOT_FOUND'` set inside the worker does not survive. The route sees an Error with a message string and falls through lib/http.js:62-63 to a generic 500. Result: a client requesting a set-check on a log id that is not theirs gets 500 instead of 404, and the errorHandler logs it as an 'unhandled route error' — filling the log with attacker-generated noise, which errorHandler explicitly tries to avoid elsewhere.
seriousFlaws.fix: Do not throw across the boundary for expected outcomes. Return a discriminated result object `{ ok: false, reason: 'NOT_FOUND' | 'CONFLICT' }` — but ONLY from before the first write (ADR-0005), which the design's STEP 0 already satisfies. For genuine post-write failures, throw and let it be a 500. Prove the convention with the first named tx before writing the other seven.

strengths: THE GUARDED PR UPSERT IS THE RIGHT PRIMITIVE AND SHOULD BE KEPT VERBATIM. `ON CONFLICT (user_id, exercise_id, metric) DO UPDATE SET ... WHERE excluded.value > exercise_records.value` puts the comparison inside the UPDATE with no preceding SELECT, so `changes === 1` is a genuine new best and a replay is provably a no-op. This is the single best idea in the proposal and it matches the proven `UPDATE invite_codes SET uses = uses + 1 WHERE uses < max_uses` shape at coaching/routes.js:268.

MODELLING 'SET CHECKED' AS AN ASSERTION RATHER THAN AN EVENT, so `UNIQUE(log_item_id, set_index)` IS the idempotency key. This eliminates the idempotency_keys table, the TTL sweeper and the stored-response-body machinery that the roadmap's T2.10.3 would otherwise demand. The reasoning that a stable set `id` across replays makes a future `reward_ledger UNIQUE(source_type, source_id)` double-award-proof is correct and worth carrying into Phase 7.

RECOMPUTE-BY-AGGREGATE FOR ALL DERIVED COUNTERS, never increment. `SET total = (SELECT SUM(...))` is idempotent by construction and the design applies it as a general law, with `rev` as the single explicitly-reasoned exception ('a false 409 costs a refetch, a missed one costs data'). Keep this rule verbatim in the ADR.

LINK-ID-AS-THE-KEY FOR EVERY COACH-FACING ROUTE, following onboarding/routes.js:255-265 exactly. The reasoning — a user id stays valid forever while a link's status does not, so keying on the user id would break immediate revocation — is correct and is the property the whole coaching surface depends on. 404-not-403 on ownership misses with 403 reserved for role gates matches the existing codebase precisely.

COPY-ON-ASSIGN AND SNAPSHOT-THE-LOG ARE THE CORRECT ARCHITECTURAL CALLS, and the history-integrity argument for them is the right argument. `exercise_name_snapshot TEXT NOT NULL` paired with `exercise_id ... ON DELETE SET NULL` is exactly the right defence against `exercises.owner_id REFERENCES users ON DELETE CASCADE` — the design spotted a real cascade hazard the brief did not mention and solved it correctly for logs.

COLLAPSING `is_template` INTO A `scope` ENUM WITH A TABLE-LEVEL CHECK. The argument that a separate boolean permits `is_template = 1 AND client_link_id IS NOT NULL` — a state every read would then have to defend against — is sound, and the four-way scope (template/client/personal/system) covers self-coached users and product-shipped starters that the roadmap implies but never names.

`body_area_muscle_map` IS A GENUINE MISSING EDGE, AND THE SEED IS CORRECT. I verified every slug in the seed against 003_exercises.sql:135-155 — all 19 referenced slugs exist. Seeding through `JOIN muscle_groups g ON v.slug = g.slug` rather than literal ids, with the stated reason that ids differ between a fresh and an upgraded database, is exactly right and is the kind of thing that silently corrupts a migration when done the other way.

IT AVOIDED THE BRIEF'S `role='client'` TRAP ENTIRELY. Every predicate in the design derives client identity from `coach_clients`, never from a role value that does not exist in the CHECK. Several other candidate designs will not have.

CIVIL DATES SEPARATED FROM INSTANTS AS A TYPE DISTINCTION. 'Monday's workout is a day in the client's own calendar and must not shift when they fly to Tokyo' is the correct reason, and keeping `*_at` as epoch seconds while dates are YYYYMMDD INTEGERs honours the repo's no-ISO-strings rule. The CHECK is too loose but the decision is right.

THE TWO-PASS POSITION PARKING IS A REAL SOLUTION TO A REAL PROBLEM. UNIQUE(day_id, position) makes duplicate slots unstorable, an arbitrary permutation genuinely does collide mid-transaction, SQLite genuinely has no DEFERRABLE unique, and `position + 1000000` is a provably collision-free bijection into a disjoint range. The choice of contiguous integers over LexoRank is correctly justified by scale (3-15 items) and by detectability ('LexoRank never breaks and therefore never tells you it is wrong').

IT RESOLVED THE ARCHIVE-SEMANTICS SPLIT DELIBERATELY AND CORRECTLY. Choosing `status = 'active'` for all data access while leaving the roster on `status <> 'archived'`, with the reasoning that an 'invited' link is a person who has not consented to being prescribed to, is the right call and the right reason.

IT NAMED THE PRIVATE-EXERCISE VISIBILITY PROBLEM INSTEAD OF STAYING SILENT ON IT. The observation that `exercises/routes.js:26`'s VISIBLE predicate makes a coach's own custom library 404 for their own client is correct and is the sharpest thing in the analysis. The prescribed-through-an-active-link half of the proposed fix is sound; only the performed-by-me half is exploitable.

THE 008-FORM WHEN-GUARDED TOUCH TRIGGER ON EVERY NEW TABLE, with the correct reasoning that the 001-form is non-recursive only because `PRAGMA recursive_triggers` is never set in worker.js and would infinite-loop six tables if it were. Picking the safer of two live precedents over the more numerous one, and saying why, is the right kind of consistency.

THE WEAKNESSES SECTION IS HONEST AND SPECIFIC. It self-reports the template-propagation tax, the plan_schedule repair gap, the day-reorder asymmetry, the missing `max(position) = count(*) - 1` checker, the denormalised-column under-defence, and the unproven typed-error convention — several of which I would otherwise have led with. A design that names its own soft spots is cheaper to harden than one that does not.

fatalFlaws.flaw: The workout_plans CHECK that the design says makes cross-tenant assignment "structurally impossible" provides ZERO protection, and nothing ties client_user_id to the link's actual client. Verified: INSERT INTO workout_plans(owner_user_id, coach_client_id, client_user_id) VALUES (7, 42, 999) is ACCEPTED. The CHECK `coach_client_id IS NOT NULL OR client_user_id IS NULL OR client_user_id = owner_user_id` short-circuits on the first disjunct the moment any coach_client_id is present — it never checks that coach_clients.client_id = client_user_id.
fatalFlaws.scenario: Coach A has a legitimate link L_A (coach_id=A, client_id=X). Via Burp, A POSTs {coach_client_id: L_A, client_user_id: Y} where Y is any user id. The route's ownership SELECT passes (L_A really is A's link). The CHECK passes. Row is written. Now: (1) victim Y's own plan list is `WHERE client_user_id = ?` — Y sees coach A's plan appear in their app unbidden; (2) Y taps it and trains, and startWorkoutTx copies coach_client_id = L_A onto the workout_log; (3) coach A's log read is `EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM coach_clients cc WHERE cc.id = l.coach_client_id AND cc.coach_id = ? AND cc.status='active')` — which now matches. Coach A reads Y's full training history, bodyweight_kg snapshots, perceived_effort and session notes for a user they have no relationship with. The design's own text tells the reviewer the CHECK covers this, which is exactly how the route-layer check gets skipped.
fatalFlaws.fix: Delete the misleading CHECK claim. Add a BEFORE INSERT/UPDATE OF coach_client_id, client_user_id trigger on workout_plans: `WHEN NEW.coach_client_id IS NOT NULL AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM coach_clients cc WHERE cc.id = NEW.coach_client_id AND cc.client_id = NEW.client_user_id) BEGIN SELECT RAISE(ABORT,'plan client must be the link client'); END;`. Same trigger on workout_logs. Better still: never accept client_user_id from the body at all — derive it in the named tx as `(SELECT client_id FROM coach_clients WHERE id = ? AND coach_id = ? AND status='active')`.

fatalFlaws.flaw: The item→day denormalisation is enforced only from the CHILD side. Moving a GROUP to another day silently desynchronises every one of its items' day_id, and the design's own claim that "an item can never be re-parented into another plan's day" and "the trigger makes disagreement impossible" is false. Verified empirically.
fatalFlaws.scenario: Coach drags a superset from Monday to Wednesday. The app runs the obvious `UPDATE workout_plan_groups SET day_id = <wed> WHERE id = ?`. trg_workout_plan_items_reparent is `BEFORE UPDATE OF group_id, day_id ON workout_plan_items` — it never fires, because no row of workout_plan_items was updated. Result verified: group.day_id = 2 (Wed), item.day_id = 1 (Mon). Now workout_plan_items_day_idx — which the design says is how "a whole day renders without a three-table join" — returns the superset on Monday, while workout_plan_groups_day_idx returns it on Wednesday. The calendar view and the ICS export show a phantom Monday session; Wednesday shows an empty group. Worse: the client opens Monday, startWorkoutTx expands the stale day_id items, and the wrong prescription is snapshotted onto workout_log_sets — where trg_workout_log_sets_frozen makes it permanent and uncorrectable.
fatalFlaws.fix: Either add the missing guard — a BEFORE UPDATE OF day_id ON workout_plan_groups trigger that RAISE(ABORT)s when the group has items, forcing the move to go through a named tx that updates both tables — or (cleaner) an AFTER UPDATE OF day_id ON workout_plan_groups trigger that cascades `UPDATE workout_plan_items SET day_id = NEW.day_id WHERE group_id = NEW.id`. Note recursive_triggers is OFF, so the cascading UPDATE will not re-fire trg_workout_plan_items_reparent. Same class of gap exists on workout_log_exercises (INSERT-only parent trigger).

fatalFlaws.flaw: Coach account deletion becomes permanently impossible, and the FK action cannot be changed by any later migration. exercises.owner_id is ON DELETE CASCADE to users; workout_log_sets.exercise_id / workout_log_exercises.exercise_id / workout_set_records.exercise_id are ON DELETE RESTRICT. Verified: SQLITE_CONSTRAINT_TRIGGER, "FOREIGN KEY constraint failed".
fatalFlaws.scenario: Coach C creates private exercise "Petike Row". Client X (a different user) is prescribed it and logs 40 sets. Coach C requests account deletion (GDPR Art. 17, or just closes their account). `DELETE FROM users WHERE id = C` cascades to exercises, which RESTRICTs against client X's workout_log_sets. The entire delete aborts. Per the repo's own error handling (worker.js:61-67 wraps it, lib/http.js:62-63 has no typed mapping) the operator sees a generic 500 with no actionable message. Tested and confirmed — note that self-deletion (a user who logged their OWN private exercise) succeeds, so this fails only in the cross-user case, i.e. only in production, only for real coaches, and never in a single-user smoke test. The trap: you cannot fix this in migration 011. Changing an FK action requires the 12-step table rebuild; `PRAGMA foreign_keys = OFF` is a documented no-op inside a transaction (and migrations are one transaction per file), and `DROP TABLE exercises` with foreign_keys ON performs an implicit DELETE FROM that fires every cascade on the way out. This is a one-way door.
fatalFlaws.fix: Do not use ON DELETE RESTRICT on exercise_id. Use ON DELETE SET NULL and make exercise_id nullable on all three tables — exercise_name_snapshot on workout_log_exercises already exists precisely so history renders without the FK, so a NULLed exercise_id degrades to "named but unlinkable", which is the intended behaviour. Block hard-deletion of a referenced exercise in the admin route (an explicit EXISTS check returning 409), not in the FK, so the policy stays changeable.

fatalFlaws.flaw: The replay branch keys on STATE (completed_at IS NULL), not on request identity, so "the same request twice" and "a different request against the same set" are indistinguishable. client_set_uid — the design's stated idempotency key — does not participate in the planned-set path at all, because startWorkoutTx creates those rows server-side and therefore invents the uid itself.
fatalFlaws.scenario: The train, exactly. User is on set 3 of bench. They tap check with 100 kg (they meant 10 kg on the dumbbell, fat-fingered the pad), see it wrong, and immediately correct it to 10 kg in the player. Connection is already down, so BOTH writes sit in the offline queue. Four minutes later they replay. Write #1 (100 kg) hits completeSetTx: completed_at IS NULL, so it applies — UPDATE succeeds, e1rm = 100 × (1 + 5/30) = 116.7 kg, no prior best exists, a gold e1rm PR row is minted in workout_set_records, and per Layer 4 a coin is paid against ('pr', record.id). Write #2 (10 kg) arrives: step 2 sees completed_at IS NOT NULL and returns 200 {applied:false, replayed:true} with ZERO writes and no payload comparison. The player has no reason to treat 200 + replayed:true as a failure — the design explicitly frames it as the success case ("a double-tapped submit must not read as a failure"). The client keeps showing 10 kg. The server holds 100 kg, a fake 116.7 kg lifetime PR, and a paid coin. trg_workout_log_sets_frozen now makes the row immutable — the only remedy is a void, which the user has no reason to perform because their screen already shows the right number. Out-of-order arrival makes it worse: if the corrected write happens to land first, the 100 kg write is the one that gets swallowed and the data is right by luck.
fatalFlaws.fix: Make the idempotency key request identity, not row state. Have the client mint client_set_uid per SET-CHECK ATTEMPT (not per set row) and carry it in the body; add `last_write_uid TEXT` to workout_log_sets. completeSetTx then branches three ways at step 2: uid matches last_write_uid → true replay, return {applied:false, replayed:true}; completed_at IS NOT NULL and uid differs → return 409 CONFLICT with the stored row so the client can show "this set was already recorded as 100 kg — void it?"; otherwise apply. Do not let a differing payload return 200.

fatalFlaws.flaw: The formula-versioning decision — the design's proudest claim — breaks the PR detector it is supposed to protect. workout_log_sets_e1rm_idx is (user_id, exercise_id, e1rm_kg DESC) with NO e1rm_formula column, and the PR query is `ORDER BY e1rm_kg DESC LIMIT 1`. It therefore compares an Epley number against a Brzycki number as if they were the same quantity. Additionally the arithmetic CHECK is conditioned on `e1rm_formula <> 'epley'`, so every non-Epley row is written with no verification at all, and e1rm_formula is in the freeze trigger's column list, so a bug in the new formula is permanently uncorrectable.
fatalFlaws.scenario: Answering Q4 directly. Year 1: user's best is 5×100 kg → Epley 116.67, stored, badged. Year 2 the product ships Brzycki for new rows. User trains 5×102.5 kg — genuine, honest progress on the same rep scheme. Brzycki gives 102.5/(1.0278−0.0278×5) = 115.32, which is LESS than the stored 116.67, so `ORDER BY e1rm_kg DESC LIMIT 1` says no PR. No badge, no coin. Verified numerically: the lifter has to reach 103.7 kg × 5 just to MATCH their old badge, and every user in the product silently stops earning e1RM PRs on the deploy date until they out-lift the formula gap. Which stored values are lies? Not the individual rows — each is a correct evaluation of its own formula. The lie is the ORDER BY: the column is treated as a comparable series and it is not. And because both the value and the formula tag are frozen by trg_workout_set_records_immutable and trg_workout_log_sets_frozen, there is no repair path that does not involve voiding real training data.
fatalFlaws.fix: Separate the DISPLAY model from the COMPARISON model. Pin one canonical formula for PR detection forever (store it as e1rm_canonical_kg, always Epley, never changed) and let e1rm_kg + e1rm_formula be the presentational value that may evolve. Index and compare only the canonical column. If that is unacceptable, add e1rm_formula to workout_log_sets_e1rm_idx as the leading term after exercise_id and scope every PR comparison to a single formula — accepting that a switch resets everyone's bests, which at least is visible rather than silent. Also drop the `f <> 'epley'` escape from the arithmetic CHECK: give each formula its own verified branch, or the guarantee evaporates on the day it matters.

seriousFlaws.flaw: The migration filename is already taken. The repo is at user_version 9, not 8 — backend/src/db/migrations/009_language_roster.sql exists. A file named 009_workouts.sql is SILENTLY SKIPPED, with no error and no log line.
seriousFlaws.scenario: Replicated the exact loader logic from index.js:39-46 and worker.js:124-142. Files sort to [..., 009_language_roster.sql, 009_workouts.sql]. language_roster applies and bumps user_version to 9. workouts then hits `if (version <= current) continue;` → skipped. Final user_version = 9. server.js:31 runs migrate() before binding the port, gets {applied:[9]}, and boots healthy. /healthz and /readyz both pass. Every workout route then 500s with "no such table: workout_plans", and brain-gen.mjs generates an ERD with no workout tables in it — the generated docs will quietly agree that the feature does not exist.
seriousFlaws.fix: Name the file 010_workouts.sql and target user_version 10. Separately worth fixing in the loader: detect duplicate version numbers in index.js and throw at boot rather than silently skipping.

seriousFlaws.flaw: The derived exercise-visibility predicate is a FULL TABLE SCAN of the largest table in the database, once per exercise row. The design states it is "served by ... the (user_id, exercise_id) prefix of workout_log_sets_progress_idx" — that index is PARTIAL (WHERE voided_at IS NULL AND is_warmup = 0 AND completed_at IS NOT NULL) and the EXISTS repeats none of those terms, so SQLite cannot prove implication and will not use it. Verified with EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN.
seriousFlaws.scenario: Answering Q6. EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN on the design's own predicate returns `SCAN e / CORRELATED SCALAR SUBQUERY 1 / SCAN s`. Adding the partial predicate back flips it to `SEARCH s USING INDEX workout_log_sets_progress_idx (user_id=? AND exercise_id=?)` — proving the index exists and is simply unusable as written. Measured the miss case (a global exercise the user has never trained, so the scan runs to completion) at 500,000 rows: 18.8 ms per EXISTS. Six months × 200 clients × 4 sessions/week × 25 sets ≈ 520k rows, so that is today's number, not a projection. A client opening a 40-item plan evaluates this per item: ~750 ms of pure table scan on one page load, on a worker thread that holds a pool slot the whole time (pool is minThreads=maxThreads=cores−1). Two clients opening plans concurrently stall every other query in the app.
seriousFlaws.fix: Add a non-partial covering index: `CREATE INDEX workout_log_sets_seen_idx ON workout_log_sets (user_id, exercise_id);`. Or — better, since the predicate is about entitlement not history — repeat the partial terms in the EXISTS so the existing index applies, and accept that a client loses visibility of an exercise whose only sets were voided. Also note the plan half of the predicate IS correctly served by workout_plan_items_exercise_idx; only the log half is broken.

seriousFlaws.flaw: The celebrated double-conversion guard is opt-in by the client (entry_value is nullable, so the whole CHECK short-circuits when it is omitted), and on the occasions it does fire it produces an unmapped HTTP 500 in the middle of a workout. Verified both directions.
seriousFlaws.scenario: Bypass: the client POSTs {weight_kg: 225} with no entry_value. The CHECK is `entry_value IS NULL OR weight_kg IS NULL OR (...)` — first disjunct true, constraint satisfied, 225 kg stored for a 225 lb lift. The guard the design calls "THE double-conversion guard" is defeated by omitting a field. Misfire: verified that a client which rounds e1rm to one decimal before sending (119.1 vs the exact 119.0679) trips `abs(...) < 0.01` → SQLITE_CONSTRAINT_CHECK → per the repo's error handling (no typed mapping, lib/http.js:62-63) a generic 500. The user is mid-set, taps check, and gets an opaque server error with no retry path.
seriousFlaws.fix: Make entry_unit and entry_value NOT NULL and stop accepting weight_kg from the client entirely — the server computes weight_kg = entry_value × factor inside the named tx, which is what the project's "NEVER trust the client / all authoritative values computed on the backend" rule requires anyway. The CHECK then becomes a genuine backstop rather than the primary defence. Same treatment for e1rm_kg: compute it server-side from the server's own weight_kg and never round before storing.

seriousFlaws.flaw: Switching display units manufactures a round of fake PRs, because `CHECK (value > previous_value)` and the PR comparison use bare float `>` with no epsilon on a quantity the user only ever sees rounded.
seriousFlaws.scenario: Answering Q5. Metric user's bench best is exactly 100.0 kg for 5. They flip onboarding_profiles.units to imperial. The app renders 220.5 lb.
