Next session they load what the app tells them is the same weight and enter 221 lb (nobody loads 220.5). 221 × 0.45359237 = 100.244 kg > 100.0 → e1rm PR, rep_max PR, gold badge, coin. They flip back to metric and the app now shows their bench PR as 100.2 kg — a PR they never earned, from a settings toggle. Every exercise they train after the switch does this once. The reverse (imperial → metric) does the same in the other direction. The design correctly refuses a per-row unit discriminator but then compares raw REALs across the conversion boundary.
seriousFlaws.fix: Give the PR comparison a meaningful-progress threshold rather than a float epsilon: require `value > previous_value * 1.001` (or an absolute 0.25 kg, roughly the smallest real plate increment) in both the CHECK and the detection query. This also incidentally kills the float-noise class of spurious records.

seriousFlaws.flaw: `set_kind = 'warmup'` with `is_warmup = 0` is accepted, so a warmup can enter every PR index as a working set — precisely the failure the design names as "the single most common way a fitness app reports a fake PR". Verified: the CHECK is one-directional.
seriousFlaws.scenario: `CHECK (is_warmup = 0 OR set_kind = 'warmup')` constrains is_warmup=1 ⇒ kind='warmup', but permits kind='warmup' ∧ is_warmup=0. The player UI naturally models a single concept ("this row is a warmup") and a developer wiring it to set_kind — the more expressive column — while leaving is_warmup at its DEFAULT 0 produces rows that are semantically warmups and are indexed as working sets by all three partial PR indexes (WHERE ... is_warmup = 0). Concrete: a beginner's first session, warmup single at 60 kg tagged set_kind='warmup', is_warmup=0. e1rm 60 kg. No prior best. Gold e1RM PR, badge, coin — off a warmup.
seriousFlaws.fix: Make it biconditional: `CHECK ((is_warmup = 1) = (set_kind = 'warmup'))`. Better, delete is_warmup entirely and make set_kind the single source of truth, with the partial indexes reading `WHERE set_kind <> 'warmup'` — two columns for one fact is two chances to disagree, which is the design's own stated argument for omitting RIR.

seriousFlaws.flaw: The design asserts "day/week copying need no named transaction ... writeTx is sufficient and correct". It is not, and the only writeTx-shaped implementation duplicates items — because it must join on `position`, which another decision in this same design deliberately made non-unique. Verified: a 3-item day copies as 4 items.
seriousFlaws.scenario: writeTx takes a fixed array of {sql, params} and cannot feed step N's lastInsertRowid into step N+1's params, so copy-day cannot insert groups and then reference their new ids. The only single-call shape is INSERT..SELECT for groups, then INSERT..SELECT for items joining old group to new group on their shared `position`. Tested: a source day with two groups both at position 0 (legal and expected, since the design states duplicate positions are "cosmetically harmless") makes that join cartesian — 3 source items became 4 copied items, and the ratio grows with the collision count. The coach copies last week to this week and silently gets an extra set of exercises.
seriousFlaws.fix: Add copyDayTx / copyWeekTx to the named-transaction list (it already contains clonePlanTx, which is the same operation at a different grain — the inconsistency is the tell). Inside a named tx you can insert each group, read lastInsertRowid, and insert its items with the correct group_id and day_id.

seriousFlaws.flaw: The denormalisation triggers are INSERT-only, and the freeze trigger only covers sets with completed_at IS NOT NULL — so for the entire in-progress window the "guaranteed" columns are freely mutable with nothing checking them. The claim "a set whose user_id disagrees with its log cannot be inserted" is true; the implied claim that it cannot come to disagree is false. local_date is not covered by the parent trigger at all, in any state.
seriousFlaws.scenario: trg_workout_log_sets_parent is BEFORE INSERT only; there is no BEFORE UPDATE OF log_id, user_id, exercise_id counterpart (workout_plan_items got both, so the omission looks deliberate rather than accidental and nobody will question it). Every set in a live session has completed_at IS NULL, so trg_workout_log_sets_frozen does not fire either. Any UPDATE on the log path — the void path, a future appendSetTx, a correction, a data-repair script — can set user_id to another user with no error, and the row will then be returned by that user's `WHERE id = ? AND user_id = ?` ownership guard, which the design says is the whole point of the denormalisation. Separately: because local_date is in neither trigger, a set can carry a different local_date than its parent log, which puts it in one day on the progress graph and a different session in the rollup.
seriousFlaws.fix: Mirror the plan-items pattern exactly: add `BEFORE UPDATE OF log_exercise_id, log_id, user_id, exercise_id, local_date ON workout_log_sets` with the same NOT EXISTS body, and add local_date to the parent-match subquery. Do the same for workout_log_exercises.

seriousFlaws.flaw: workout_logs_one_active bricks the user with an unmapped 500 and there is no resume or abandon path in the design; workout_logs_occurrence_unique additionally forbids a legitimate second session on the same day.
seriousFlaws.scenario: Tail of the train scenario. The 4-minute outage ends, the OS has killed the backgrounded app, the user reopens it. The client has lost its local session state and offers "Start workout". startWorkoutTx INSERTs → SQLITE_CONSTRAINT_UNIQUE on workout_logs_one_active → wrapped by worker.js:61-67 → no typed mapping in lib/http.js → generic 500. The user cannot start and cannot resume, because no endpoint in this design returns "you already have a live session, here it is". They are locked out of training until someone touches the database. Second case: a client completes their prescribed Monday session, then does an extra evening session against the same plan day. workout_logs_occurrence_unique covers `status <> 'abandoned'`, so the completed row blocks the new in_progress row — another 500 for an entirely normal user action.
seriousFlaws.fix: Keep both indexes (they kill the two-phones bug, which is worth it) but make them reachable: add GET /workouts/active returning the live log so the client resumes rather than starts, POST /workouts/:id/abandon, and map SQLITE_CONSTRAINT_UNIQUE from these two indexes to 409 with a code the client can act on. For the occurrence index, add a nullable `attempt INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0` to the unique tuple so a deliberate second session is expressible.

seriousFlaws.flaw: workout_set_records is named and indexed as if it held current bests, but holds events — this is the piece that will be misused. Two lesser instances of the same problem: client_set_uid and the total_* rollups.
seriousFlaws.scenario: Answering Q7. In eighteen months someone builds the records screen and writes `SELECT * FROM workout_set_records WHERE user_id = ? AND exercise_id = ? AND invalidated_at IS NULL ORDER BY achieved_at DESC` — the exact shape workout_set_records_feed_idx and workout_set_records_current_idx (note: named _current_) invite. It returns every PR the user ever set: 80 kg, 85, 90, 95, 100 — all live rows, none invalidated, because superseding a PR correctly does NOT invalidate it. The screen shows five current bests for one exercise. The reviewer will not catch it, because the table name says "records" and the index name says "current". Secondary: client_set_uid is documented as "minted ONCE by the player" but is NOT NULL on rows the server creates in startWorkoutTx before any player has seen them, so the first implementer must invent a server-side uid and will reasonably conclude the column is decorative. Tertiary: workout_logs.total_* look like maintained aggregates but are pure code discipline — the design admits this, and the fourth transaction written next year will forget the recompute.
seriousFlaws.fix: Rename to workout_pr_events, and rename workout_set_records_current_idx to workout_pr_events_lookup_idx. If a current-bests read is a real screen, add a view (`CREATE VIEW workout_current_prs AS SELECT ... GROUP BY user_id, exercise_id, kind, rep_bucket HAVING value = MAX(value)`) so the obvious query is also the correct one. Make client_set_uid nullable, or move it to the correction/free-form path where it is genuinely client-minted. For the rollups, either accept the AFTER INSERT/UPDATE trigger cost or add a smoke assertion on rollup_at, as the design's own weakness note suggests.

seriousFlaws.flaw: The ICS token design puts a long-lived bearer credential in a URL, has no revocation column, and is attached to the plan rather than to a subscription — and the route carrying it must be mounted before the CSRF/auth middleware to work at all.
seriousFlaws.scenario: Calendar clients cannot send cookies, so /ics/:token must sit outside requireAuth — the token is the only credential. It lives in a URL that is stored in plaintext in the user's calendar app, synced to whatever cloud that app uses, sent as a Referer if any HTML is ever served from that path, and captured by every reverse-proxy access log. A coach who shares their screen or a client who exports their calendar leaks read access to a full training plan. There is ics_token_issued_at but no ics_token_revoked_at, so the only revocation is overwriting the hash — meaning revocation and rotation are the same operation and a user cannot kill a leaked feed without breaking every legitimate subscriber. Also, per the ground truth, anything mounted before backend/server.js:148 skips CSRF, and mounting this router carelessly puts the neighbouring plan routes outside CSRF too.
seriousFlaws.fix: Scope the token to a subscription, not the plan: a workout_ics_subscriptions(id, plan_id, token_hash, label, created_at, revoked_at, last_fetched_at) table lets a user revoke one leaked feed. Mount ONLY the ICS route before the CSRF middleware, in its own router, and rate-limit it. Never place the token in a query string — path segment only — and return 404 (not 401) on a bad token, consistent with the repo's enumeration policy.

strengths: ANSWER TO Q3 IS GENUINELY CORRECT AND SHOULD BE KEPT WHOLESALE. Deleting a plan, day or item does not damage history: workout_logs.plan_id / plan_day_id are ON DELETE SET NULL, workout_plan_days CASCADE from the plan, and plan_name_snapshot / day_name_snapshot / exercise_name_snapshot mean the session still renders its own identity after every FK has gone NULL. The prescription itself is snapshotted onto workout_log_sets, so "did the client hit the target?" survives the plan's deletion. This is the order-line price-snapshot pattern applied correctly, and it is the single best decision in the design.

THE MUTABLE-PLAN + SNAPSHOT-THE-PRESCRIPTION CHOICE IS RIGHT, and the rejected alternative (immutable versioned plans) is rejected for the right reasons. Coaches drag-reorder constantly; copy-on-write versioning would produce dozens of dead versions a week and still would not survive account deletion. Snapshotting targets onto the log achieves the actual integrity requirement at a fraction of the cost. Keep this, including plan_revision as the analytics tag (just enforce the bump).

LINK-ANCHORED OWNERSHIP IS EXACTLY RIGHT AND MATCHES THE REPO'S OWN PRECEDENT. Keying coach access on coach_clients.id rather than the client's user id, resolved live on every request with `status = 'active'`, reproduces the property documented at onboarding/routes.js:255-265: archiving ends access on the very next read, with the same access token, no refresh, no revocation list, no cache. The explicit decision to pick `= 'active'` over the roster's `<> 'archived'` — and to say WHY (an 'invited' link is a pending relationship; reading another user's DATA is stricter than listing relationship metadata) — resolves a real inconsistency in the existing codebase and should be adopted as the house rule.

THE CLIENT KEEPS FULL ACCESS TO THEIR OWN HISTORY AFTER BEING ARCHIVED. The deliberate absence of any coach_clients status filter on the client's own read/write path, plus ON DELETE SET NULL (never CASCADE) on coach_client_id in both workout_plans and workout_logs, means ending a coaching relationship never destroys or locks a client's training data. This is easy to get wrong and expensive to discover later.

NO CURRENT-BESTS CACHE TABLE. Deriving bests from partial DESC indexes instead of maintaining an exercise_bests upsert table is the correct call, and the rationale is the right one: the recompute path after a void is a full history scan anyway, so the cache buys nothing on the expensive path while adding drift risk on the cheap one. Keep this decision even after fixing the index that serves it.

THE volume_kg (STORED GENERATED) vs e1rm_kg (APP-WRITTEN) DISTINCTION IS THE RIGHT AXIS. Tonnage is a definition with no competing formula, so SQLite computing it makes drift and forgery structurally impossible; a 1RM estimate is a model with five competing formulas, so freezing it is correct. The reasoning is sound even though the PR-comparison consequence was not followed through — keep the axis, fix the comparison.

e1rm NULL OUTSIDE reps 1-12, AND weight ITSELF AT reps = 1. Refusing to manufacture a 1RM from a 30-rep bodyweight set, and refusing to inflate every single by naive Epley's 3.3%, are both correct and both enforced by CHECK rather than convention. The observation that making the column NULL outside the window is also what lets the PR query drop the reps term and keep its index is a genuinely good piece of engineering.

SERVER-COMPUTED local_date STORED AS TEXT, NEVER DERIVED FROM EPOCH AT READ TIME. The analysis is right: every analytic unit in the product is a user-local day, epoch seconds are UTC, SQLite has no IANA database so `date(started_at,'unixepoch')` cannot be made correct, and a 01:00 Budapest session lands in the previous UTC day and monthly in the previous UTC week. Storing it as an immutable historical fact (and identifying the missing onboarding_profiles.timezone column, with the correct note that ADD COLUMN forbids a non-constant default) is a real catch that most designs miss.

FREEZE-AND-VOID INSTEAD OF EDIT IS THE RIGHT INSTINCT FOR A LOG. Making measurements immutable at trigger level once completed, with corrections as appends carrying corrects_set_id and voids leaving a tombstone plus reason, is what makes the PR and reward story auditable at all. The idea is sound; it is the replay-detection layer above it that fails, not this.

PR EVENTS AS AN APPEND-ONLY FACT TABLE WITH invalidated_at. The distinction between "what is my best" (derivable, therefore not stored) and "a gold badge was shown to this user on 3 March and a coin was paid" (not derivable, therefore stored) is exactly right, as is refusing to delete the row on void so a future coin ledger keyed on the record id still finds its anchor. The deliberate omission of a BEFORE DELETE trigger — because it would abort the users CASCADE — shows the author actually traced the audit_log precedent rather than copying it.

body_area_muscle_map IS A REAL UNBLOCK NOBODY ELSE WOULD HAVE SPOTTED. onboarding_limitations.body_area is joint-centric and muscle_groups is muscle-centric, with nothing joining them, so T2.5.4's avoid-list filter is currently unimplementable. Copying the 13-code vocabulary verbatim (kebab-case included) rather than inventing a second spelling, seeding by slug rather than id, and splitting 'loads' from 'stabilises' so a knee complaint does not remove every exercise a calf stabilises, are all correct.

GROUPS AS A REAL TABLE, WITH EVERY ITEM IN ONE (INCLUDING kind='single'). The argument is right: a circuit repeats the GROUP while a straight set repeats the ITEM, so rounds / cap_seconds / inter-round rest genuinely belong to the group and a nullable group_key string on the item would have had nowhere to put them and would have made ordering between grouped and ungrouped items ambiguous.

THE NON-UNIQUE `position` REASONING IS CORRECT EVEN THOUGH IT HAS A CONSEQUENCE THE DESIGN MISSED. SQLite checks UNIQUE per statement rather than deferring to commit, so a unique (parent, position) really would abort a legal drag-reorder mid-transaction, and the id tie-break really does keep the order total. Keep the decision; just stop claiming copy-day can use writeTx.

EXPLICIT REST-DAY ROWS RATHER THAN CALENDAR GAPS, so "recover today" and "nothing scheduled" are different messages and adherence does not punish a prescribed rest. Small, cheap, and the kind of thing that is painful to retrofit once adherence numbers have been shipped to coaches.

THE RULE-BASED CALENDAR (cycle_days + starts_on) WITH A SPARSE EXCEPTIONS TABLE is the right shape — a year of a plan running normally costs zero rows, and materialised occurrences would need a job and would drift the moment starts_on moved.

CORRECT READ-BEFORE-WRITE ORDERING UNDER ADR-0005, AND CORRECT IDENTIFICATION OF WHY IMMEDIATE MATTERS. Putting every branch that can produce an error result strictly before the first write statement, and stating explicitly that the pattern is race-free only because tx.immediate() takes the write lock on the first statement (and would be a TOCTOU under DEFERRED), shows the author understood the repo's hardest-won lesson rather than pattern-matching it. The two-file named-worker-transaction mechanism (worker.js export + index.js facade, plain JSON-able args across the structured-clone boundary) is also spelled out correctly — these are the repo's first named transactions and the design does not hand-wave them.

THE WEAKNESSES SECTION IS HONEST AND MOSTLY ACCURATE — it self-reports the rep_max noise problem, the rollup discipline risk, the timezone gap, the one-live-session bluntness, the missing assisted/weighted-bodyweight model, the records-screen query, and the unanalyzed query plans. A reviewer can trust this document's self-assessment, which is rarer and more valuable than the design being right.

fatalFlaws.flaw: `workout_plan_days.plan_id` references a table that does not exist: `workout_plan_days_parent_guard_placeholder_removed_plan(id)`. This is in the submitted DDL, not a typo in prose.
fatalFlaws.scenario: I executed it. `CREATE TABLE` SUCCEEDS (SQLite resolves FK parents lazily), so the whole migration commits and `PRAGMA user_version` bumps. Then the first `INSERT INTO workout_plan_days (plan_id) VALUES (1)` fails with `SQLITE_ERROR: no such table: main.workout_plan_days_parent_guard_placeholder_removed_plan`. Per worker.js:131 the file is never re-run, and an FK cannot be changed by `ALTER TABLE`; the 12-step rebuild is unavailable because migrations run inside a transaction where `PRAGMA foreign_keys=OFF` is a no-op. Every plan in the product is uncreatable and the fix requires a second migration.
fatalFlaws.fix: `REFERENCES workout_plans(id) ON DELETE CASCADE`. Separately: the file must be numbered `010_workouts.sql` — `backend/src/db/migrations/009_language_roster.sql` already exists, so the ground-truth claim that user_version is 8 is stale and `009_workouts` collides.

fatalFlaws.flaw: Warm-up sets poison the record book and the progress graph. LAYER 4 (the PR insert) filters `s.set_kind <> 'warmup'`; LAYER 3 (`top_weight_kg`, `top_est_1rm_kg`, `total_reps`, `completed_sets`) and LAYER 5 (the `exercise_records` upsert) have no such filter. The design gives no gate tying LAYER 5 to a PR having fired.
fatalFlaws.scenario: Executed. Client's first ever squat session: heavy opener logged as `set_kind='warmup'` 140kg x1, then two working sets 100kg x8. Result: `workout_log_entries.top_weight_kg = 140`, `top_est_1rm_kg = 144.67`, `exercise_records.best_est_1rm_kg = 144.67`, and `SELECT * FROM workout_prs` returns ZERO ROWS. The progress graph (which the design says reads the entry rollups directly) plots a warm-up single. The record book is now set by a warm-up, so the client's PR badge never fires again until they beat a weight they never actually worked. Two screens show contradicting numbers for the same day.
fatalFlaws.fix: Append `AND set_kind <> 'warmup'` to every LAYER 3 subquery and gate LAYER 5 on the same predicate; or, better, make `counts_toward_records INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 1` an explicit column so 'warmup' is not the only excluded kind by accident and the filter is one condition everywhere.

fatalFlaws.flaw: `syncOfflineQueue` is specified as ONE all-or-nothing IMMEDIATE transaction, which contradicts its own promise of a per-op `{accepted|replayed}` array, and LAYER 1 `throw`s on any missing row. One bad op discards every good op in the batch.
fatalFlaws.scenario: Executed. Batch of ops arriving after the 4-minute dropout: two valid set-checks plus one 'create session' op (the player was force-restarted offline and minted a second session). The insert hits `idx_workout_logs_one_active`, throws SQLITE_CONSTRAINT_UNIQUE, and `tx.immediate()` rolls back — I measured 0 sets persisted, both good checks gone. A throw returns no per-op array, so the player cannot prune its queue; it retries the identical batch, hits the identical constraint, and per `lib/http.js:62-63` (no typed error mapping) gets a generic 500 forever. The 12-set workout is unrecoverable.
fatalFlaws.fix: Split the contract: `syncOfflineQueue` must never throw for a per-op failure. Apply each op with a guarded UPDATE, collect `{opId, outcome}` per op, and reserve `throw` for infrastructure failure only. Session adoption must be `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT(user_id, client_uid) DO NOTHING` plus a resolving `SELECT`, and the one-active-session rule must become an application-level resume/discard decision, not a UNIQUE index that turns a UX case into a 500.

fatalFlaws.flaw: The number of PR rows — and therefore the number of Phase-7 coins — depends on network delivery order, because LAYER 4 compares against `exercise_records`, which LAYER 5 advances within the same batch. The design explicitly accepts out-of-order queues.
fatalFlaws.scenario: Executed. Identical workout, three working sets: 100kg x5 (est 116.67), 110kg x5 (128.33), 120kg x5 (140). Delivery 1->2->3 produces 3 PR rows. Delivery 3->2->1 produces 1 PR row. Delivery 2->1->3 produces 2. `exercise_records.best_est_1rm_kg` converges to 140 in all three cases, so nothing detects the divergence and `needs_recompute` is never set. Client A on wifi earns 3 coins; client B doing the exact same session on the train earns 1. The design's own idempotency section calls this the mechanism that makes replay safe.
fatalFlaws.fix: Order the batch server-side before applying: sort ops by `client_completed_at` (or by the set's `(entry.position, set_number)`) inside the transaction, and set `achieved_at` from the set's `completed_at`, not `unixepoch()`. Better: stop deriving PRs per-op entirely — evaluate PRs once in `finishWorkoutSession` over the session's committed sets in chronological order, where order is knowable.

fatalFlaws.flaw: The `last_client_seq` guard silently discards legitimate writes and reports them as SUCCESS. `seq` is documented as per-session, but it is compared against a per-SET-ROW high-water mark, and any client that is not the original player instance has no access to that session's counter.
fatalFlaws.scenario: Client finishes leg day; the last in-session op carried seq 24, so set #7 now has `last_client_seq = 24`. Next morning they open the history screen on their laptop to fix a typo — they entered 100kg, it was 110kg. The web client never had that session's offline queue and mints seq 1. `1 > 24` is false, `changes = 0`, and the design maps zero changes here to `{replayed: true}`, which the UI renders as success. The set never changes. They try three times, give up, and the wrong value stays in `exercise_records` and in the `workout_prs` row derived from it. Every non-player write path (history edit, coach correction, admin repair) hits this. The design's `weaknesses` names the device-reset variant but not this one, and there is no schema affordance — `seq` has no scope column and no server-visible origin.
fatalFlaws.fix: Make the guard server-anchored: `WHERE id=? AND user_id=? AND :seq > last_client_seq` only for ops carrying `origin='player-queue'`, and give non-queue writers a separate unguarded path with optimistic concurrency on `updated_at`. Always return the current `last_client_seq` in the response so a client can fast-forward, and never report a zero-change guarded UPDATE as plain success — return `{applied:false, currentSeq}` so the UI can distinguish 'already done' from 'your edit was dropped'.

fatalFlaws.flaw: Unit conversion refutes the design's explicit claim that 'Epley on identical (weight, reps) inputs is bit-identical, so equality holds and no epsilon is needed'. lb->kg conversion guarantees the inputs are NOT bit-identical, and the PR comparison is a strict `>` on REAL.
fatalFlaws.scenario: Executed. Imperial client logs 225 lb x 5 twice. App v1 sends full precision: 102.05828325 kg -> est_1rm 119.067997125, PR row #1 (first ever, previous_value NULL). App v2 rounds to 2 decimals: 102.06 kg -> est_1rm 119.07000000000001 > 119.067997125 -> PR row #2, previous_value 119.067997125. The client gets a gold badge and (Phase 7) a coin for a +0.002 kg 'personal record' on an identical lift. A client-version bump, a second device, or a different rounding path in the web vs native client is all it takes; no forgery is involved. `distance_m INTEGER` has the same failure with miles (3.1 mi = 4988.97 m truncating to 4988 or 4989).
fatalFlaws.fix: Store the client's raw entry alongside the canonical metric value (`entered_value REAL`, `entered_unit TEXT CHECK (entered_unit IN ('kg','lb'))`) and quantise the canonical column — round `weight_kg` to 0.01 kg (or store integer grams) at the write boundary. Then compare PRs with a meaningful epsilon (`> best + 0.005`) rather than raw float `>`.

fatalFlaws.flaw: Changing the 1RM formula silently desynchronises the VIRTUAL column from every stored copy of it. `est_1rm_kg` recomputes on read under the new formula; `exercise_records.best_est_1rm_kg`, `workout_log_entries.top_est_1rm_kg` and `workout_prs.value` keep their Epley numbers. LAYER 4 then compares new-formula against old-formula, and nothing sets `needs_recompute`.
fatalFlaws.scenario: Computed. Swap Epley for Brzycki next year. A client whose stored best came from 100kg x5 has `best_est_1rm_kg = 116.67` (Epley). Under Brzycki they must now lift 103.70 kg x5 to 'beat' their own identical lift — their PRs freeze for months with no explanation. The sign flips at high reps: at 12 reps the required weight DROPS 2.78 kg, so deploy day produces a wave of unearned PR badges and coins for training already done. And at exactly 10 reps the two formulas are mathematically equal but differ in the last float bit — Brzycki 133.33333333333334 > Epley 133.33333333333331 — so repeating the identical lift fires a phantom PR. The design's own weakness section says the formula is 'hard to change'; the real problem is that changing it is easy and silently wrong.
fatalFlaws.fix: Take the formula out of the generated column. Keep VIRTUAL columns for the raw derivations that can never change (`volume_kg = weight_kg * reps`), and compute 1RM in the read layer or in a named worker tx that stamps `est_1rm_formula TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'epley'` on every stored 1RM value. Then a formula swap is a backfill keyed on that column, and mixed-formula comparisons are impossible by construction.

fatalFlaws.flaw: `workout_exercise_grants` revoke-on-archive misses any row whose `granted_by` is not the archiving coach — including NULL. `granted_by` is nullable, the PK is `(user_id, exercise_id)` so only the first writer's value sticks, and the archive DELETE is the ONLY revoke path in the design.
fatalFlaws.scenario: The design says a grant is written 'when the exercise enters the client's plan OR LOG'. Following the repo's universal `INSERT OR IGNORE` convention: client C logs coach A's private exercise X first (as `origin='substituted'` or a `source='repeat'` session), and the log-side writer has no coach in scope, so it writes `granted_by = NULL`. Coach A's later plan-side grant is IGNOREd by the PK. Coach A archives client C; `coaching/routes.js` runs `DELETE FROM workout_exercise_grants WHERE user_id = ? AND granted_by = ?`; `NULL = ?` is never true; zero rows deleted. C keeps permanent read access to A's private exercise — name, description, instructions, media — after the coaching relationship has ended. There is no `revoked_at`, no second revoke path, and `idx_workout_exercise_grants_by (granted_by, user_id)` cannot even find the orphans because they are NULL.
fatalFlaws.fix: `granted_by INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id)`, and revoke by re-deriving rather than by actor: on archive, `DELETE FROM workout_exercise_grants WHERE user_id = ? AND exercise_id IN (SELECT id FROM exercises WHERE owner_id = ?)`. Add a `source TEXT CHECK (source IN ('plan','log'))` column so a re-grant from a second path is a separate row (PK `(user_id, exercise_id, granted_by)`) and revoking one coach cannot leave another coach's grant dangling — or vice versa.

fatalFlaws.flaw: `ON DELETE SET NULL` on `workout_log_entries.exercise_id` combined with `ON DELETE CASCADE` on `exercise_records.exercise_id` strands history in an unqueryable state, while the design claims history 'renders forever'.
fatalFlaws.scenario: Executed. Coach (user 2) owns private exercise 'Bulgarian split squat'; client (user 1) has two sessions of it plus one of 'Coach curl'. `DELETE FROM users WHERE id = 2` -> exercises CASCADE -> all three of the client's entries get `exercise_id = NULL` (name snapshots survive) and `exercise_records` is emptied. Now `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM workout_log_entries WHERE user_id=1 AND exercise_id=10` returns 0: the progress graph is blank, `prev_entry_id` resolution finds nothing so 'previous performance' silently stops working, and `recomputeExerciseRecords()` cannot rebuild because the grouping key is gone. The rows exist and are visible in a flat list, which is exactly what makes the loss invisible until someone opens the graph. (Today `users` are soft-deleted via `disabled_at`, so this needs a real DELETE — but nothing in the design prevents one, and `exercises.owner_id` is already `ON DELETE CASCADE` in 003.)
fatalFlaws.fix: Never let a delete rewrite history's join key. Add `exercise_key TEXT NOT NULL` (or keep `exercise_id` and make the FK `ON DELETE RESTRICT`, forcing a soft delete). Also add `exercise_name_snapshot` to `workout_prs`, which has none — an orphaned PR row currently renders as a gold badge with a blank exercise name and no repair path.

seriousFlaws.flaw: `workout_plans.version` is never bumped by anything, so `workout_logs.plan_version` is a permanently false provenance claim.
seriousFlaws.scenario: The column's stated purpose is to let a log say 'the plan has changed since you did this'. But a structural edit is an INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE on `workout_plan_days` / `workout_plan_items` / `workout_plan_item_sets` — child tables — and `trg_workout_plans_touch` only writes `updated_at`. Coach adds a fourth exercise to day 3: `workout_plans.version` stays 1, the log's `plan_version` is 1, they match, and the UI confidently tells the client the plan is unchanged. This is scenario 2's whole answer and it is silently wrong.
seriousFlaws.fix: Add AFTER INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE triggers on all three child tables doing `UPDATE workout_plans SET version = version + 1 WHERE id = <resolved plan_id>`, or drop the column and compare `workout_logs.plan_version` against `workout_plans.updated_at` — but then the child edits must touch the parent anyway. Note the child tables have no `plan_id`, so the item-level trigger needs a join through `workout_plan_days`.

seriousFlaws.flaw: Reordering plan items with the repo's own documented delete-then-insert 'replace-in-place' pattern silently severs every historical log's plan linkage.
seriousFlaws.scenario: `onboarding/routes.js:189-199` establishes DELETE-then-INSERT inside one writeTx as THE way to save a set, with the reason written in a comment. A maintainer reorders day 3's exercises that way: all `workout_plan_items` for that day are deleted (CASCADE from nothing — a direct DELETE) and re-inserted with fresh rowids. Every `workout_log_entries.plan_item_id` pointing at them becomes NULL via SET NULL. The same pattern applied to days nulls `workout_logs.plan_day_id`, so `idx_workout_logs_plan_day` finds nothing and the week strip stops showing which prescribed sessions were completed — adherence history for the whole block evaporates from a drag-and-drop. Nothing warns, and `plan_id` still matches so the plan looks intact.
seriousFlaws.fix: Reordering must be `UPDATE ... SET position = ?` per row, never delete-and-recreate. Enforce it: add a `BEFORE DELETE ON workout_plan_items WHEN EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM workout_log_entries WHERE plan_item_id = OLD.id) SELECT RAISE(ABORT, ...)` guard, or give plan days/items a `deleted_at` so their lifecycle matches `workout_plans` (which is soft-deleted, meaning its CASCADE to days never fires anyway — the two halves of the plan tree have opposite delete semantics today).

seriousFlaws.flaw: The parent-consistency triggers are BEFORE INSERT only, so the denormalised `user_id` on entries and sets can be changed by any UPDATE. The design overclaims that 'the denormalisation cannot be used to forge a claim'.
seriousFlaws.scenario: Verified: the trigger correctly rejects `INSERT INTO workout_log_entries (log_id=1, user_id=2)` when log 1 belongs to user 1. But `UPDATE workout_log_entries SET user_id = 2 WHERE id = 3` is ACCEPTED — the row now claims to belong to user 2 while its log belongs to user 1. No current route does this, so it is not yet exploitable, but `user_id` is the sole ownership predicate for the hottest write in the product and the stated guarantee does not hold.
seriousFlaws.fix: Add matching `BEFORE UPDATE OF log_id, user_id` (and `entry_id, log_id, user_id` on sets) triggers with the same RAISE(ABORT), so the invariant is total rather than insert-only.

seriousFlaws.flaw: `workout_logs.total_sets / total_reps / total_volume_kg / exercise_count / pr_count` are `NOT NULL DEFAULT 0` and nothing in the described transactions writes them except `finishWorkoutSession`, so any session that is not cleanly finished reports zero forever.
seriousFlaws.scenario: Client trains 18 sets, forgets to tap Finish, and the stale-session sweeper marks the log `'abandoned'`. `finishWorkoutSession` never ran. The history list — which reads these columns — renders 'Leg day, 0 sets, 0 kg' while opening the session shows 18 completed sets and 4.2 tonnes of volume. Same for a session still `'active'`: the list shows zeros mid-workout.
seriousFlaws.fix: Either recompute the log rollups in the same LAYER 3 statement as the entry rollups (it is one more aggregate over `idx_workout_log_sets_log`), or drop the columns and compute them on read. Also: the sweeper's own input, `last_activity_at`, is never written by any statement in the design — LAYER 2 touches sets and LAYER 3 touches entries, neither touches `workout_logs` — so `idx_workout_logs_stale` measures time-since-start, not time-since-activity. If you do start writing it per set-check, that partial index gets rewritten on every single set write, which is pure churn on the hottest path for a sweeper that runs hourly.

seriousFlaws.flaw: `workout_plan_items.target_sets` and the rows of `workout_plan_item_sets` are two independent sources of truth for 'how many sets', with no constraint tying them and no stated precedence.
seriousFlaws.scenario: Coach builds a 5/3/1 wave as three `workout_plan_item_sets` rows; `target_sets` still holds its DEFAULT 3, so they agree by luck. The coach then adds a backoff set (4 rows) — `target_sets` stays 3. The materialiser now has two answers, and the plan editor UI, which naturally renders `target_sets`, tells the coach '3 sets' while the player produces 4. Nothing in the schema can detect the disagreement, and the design only specifies the absent-rows case.
seriousFlaws.fix: Make `target_sets` nullable and CHECK that exactly one of (`target_sets IS NOT NULL`, per-set rows exist) is used — which SQLite cannot express across tables, so instead: drop `target_sets` and always materialise from `workout_plan_item_sets`, generating the N identical rows at authoring time. One shape, one truth, and it matches the design's own 'the player only ever consumes one shape' goal.

seriousFlaws.flaw: `prev_entry_id` decays permanently and has no repair path. The design acknowledges backfilled sessions; it does not acknowledge deletion.
seriousFlaws.scenario: Verified: entry 2 points at entry 1 via `prev_entry_id = 1`. The client deletes the mis-logged session from three weeks ago (`DELETE FROM workout_logs WHERE id = 1`); CASCADE removes entry 1 and `ON DELETE SET NULL` blanks entry 2's pointer. The session that followed now shows an empty 'previous performance' column forever, and because the pointer is by design immutable there is nothing that recomputes it. Over two years of ordinary session deletions and Sunday catch-up logging, the prev column becomes progressively holed.
seriousFlaws.fix: Keep `prev_entry_id` as a materialised cache but make it repairable: add `prev_resolved_at INTEGER` and a `recomputePrevPointers(userId, exerciseId)` named tx triggered by any log delete or by an insert whose `performed_at` is older than an existing entry for the same (user, exercise). The window-function fallback the design rejected is the correct repair implementation even if it is the wrong read path.

seriousFlaws.flaw: The coach dashboard — the second most-loaded screen in a coaching product — has no supporting index and forces a dynamic `IN (?,?,...)` that leaks the never-evicted prepared-statement cache.
seriousFlaws.scenario: Scenario 6: 200 clients, 6 months. 'Recent activity across my clients' is `SELECT ... FROM workout_logs WHERE user_id IN (<47 ids>) ORDER BY started_at DESC LIMIT 24`. `idx_workout_logs_user_recent (user_id, started_at DESC)` forces 47 separate index scans plus a sort of the union; at ~78 sessions per client that is ~3,700 rows read to return 24, on every dashboard load. Worse, per `worker.js:43-51` the statement cache is keyed on the exact SQL string and never evicted: a coach with 47 clients, another with 48, another with 51 each mint a distinct cached statement, per worker thread. `workout_prs` (the 'recent PRs across my clients' strip) has the identical problem via `idx_workout_prs_user`. This is the first query that gets slow.
seriousFlaws.fix: Denormalise the coaching link onto the log: `coach_id INTEGER REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE SET NULL` stamped at session creation from the active `coach_clients` row, plus `CREATE INDEX idx_workout_logs_coach_recent ON workout_logs (coach_id, started_at DESC)`. One bound parameter, one index scan, one cached statement. Same for `workout_prs`. (Also: `idx_workout_prs_reward ON (reward_state) WHERE reward_state = 'pending'` currently indexes 100% of rows, because the column defaults to 'pending' and no coin worker exists — it is write amplification with zero readers until Phase 7 ships.)

seriousFlaws.flaw: Naming invites the wrong mental model in three specific places that will produce real bugs (scenario 7).
seriousFlaws.scenario: (a) `workout_plan_item_sets` vs `workout_log_sets` — near-identical names, opposite lifecycles, overlapping column names (`target_reps`, `target_weight_kg`, `rest_seconds`). A maintainer fixing a logged weight will write `UPDATE workout_plan_item_sets` and silently edit the prescription template for every future session instead of the one log row, with no error. (b) `exercise_records` is named like a durable record book and documented in `purpose` as 'the current record book', but is `ON DELETE CASCADE` from `exercises` and is a cache — a maintainer will read from it as history and be surprised when it empties (verified above). Its `needs_recompute` flag has no writer and no consumer specified. (c) `workout_plans.version` reads as an optimistic-concurrency token and will be used as one, but nothing increments it.
seriousFlaws.fix: Rename to `workout_prescription_sets` (or `plan_set_targets`) vs `workout_log_sets`; rename `exercise_records` to `exercise_records_cache` and put the CASCADE/rebuild contract in the table comment as the 004_translations.sql WITHOUT-ROWID comment does; either wire `version` or delete it.

seriousFlaws.flaw: Bodyweight training produces no volume, no 1RM and no PRs at all, because both generated columns require a non-null positive `weight_kg`.
seriousFlaws.scenario: `volume_kg` requires `weight_kg IS NOT NULL`; `est_1rm_kg` requires `weight_kg > 0`. A calisthenics client logging pull-ups, dips and push-ups gets `total_volume_kg = 0` on every entry and every session, an empty progress graph, and can never earn a PR of kind 'weight', 'est-1rm' or 'session-volume' — only 'reps'. The onboarding schema explicitly supports `training_location` and a bodyweight equipment slug, so this is a first-class user, not an edge case. The 12-rep Epley cap compounds it: high-rep bodyweight work is entirely outside the record system.
seriousFlaws.fix: Snapshot the client's `bodyweight_kg` onto `workout_logs` at materialisation (it is already in `onboarding_profiles`, and it must be snapshotted because it changes over time), add `load_kind TEXT CHECK (load_kind IN ('external','bodyweight','assisted','weighted-bodyweight'))` to the set, and make the generated volume expression `COALESCE(weight_kg,0) + CASE WHEN load_kind LIKE '%bodyweight%' THEN log_bodyweight_kg ELSE 0 END) * reps`. This also gives the imperial-switch case a stable historical anchor.

strengths: THE SNAPSHOT-AT-MATERIALISATION THESIS IS RIGHT AND SHOULD BE KEPT WHOLESALE. Materialising every set row with its own frozen prescription is the single best idea in this design: it makes scenario 2 (coach edits mid-session) a non-event by construction, makes history immune to retroactive rewriting, and gives the offline player everything it needs — including the rest-timer duration — without a separate plan cache. The rejected alternative (live join to workout_plan_items on render) really is wrong for the stated reason: it makes history a view of mutable data.

LAYER 0 — 'set rows exist as pending, so checking a set is an UPDATE, never an INSERT' — eliminates the entire class of double-tap duplicate rows before any guard logic runs. This is the structurally correct move and it is cheap. Keep it even if the rest of the idempotency stack is redesigned.

ROLLUPS BY RECOMPUTE, NEVER BY INCREMENT. Verified idempotent: the LAYER 3 aggregate subqueries produce identical numbers on repeated application, over ~5 rows. The stated reasoning — that two mechanisms failing independently is worth 5 extra row reads — is exactly the right instinct for a system whose only regression net is a smoke script.

THE VIRTUAL GENERATED COLUMN TECHNIQUE (not the formula choice) is a genuine improvement over convention-based backend computation: a generated column has no INSERT/UPDATE surface, so no forged, refactored, or hurried future write path can put a client-supplied derived value into the database. Keep it for volume_kg; just move the versionable 1RM formula out of it.

THE PARTIAL-UNIQUE PR BACKSTOP IS CORRECT SQLITE AND CORRECT ENGINEERING. I verified `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ... ON workout_prs (log_set_id, kind) WHERE log_set_id IS NOT NULL` plus `ON CONFLICT (log_set_id, kind) WHERE log_set_id IS NOT NULL DO NOTHING` prepares and executes. The two-partial-index split (set-scoped vs entry-scoped, because NULLs are distinct in a SQLite UNIQUE index) is right, the conflict target correctly repeats the partial WHERE clause, and the INSERT..SELECT form correctly carries a WHERE clause, avoiding SQLite's documented ON-CONFLICT-after-SELECT parse ambiguity. Enforcing 'one PR per set per kind' in the database rather than in transaction logic is the correct place for it, and it does correctly carry the Phase-7 double-award requirement on the same constraint.

THE OWNERSHIP SECTION IS THE STRONGEST PART OF THE DESIGN AND SHOULD BE LIFTED VERBATIM INTO THE SYNTHESIS. It correctly identifies that the ownership proof is the coach_clients LINK id, not the client's user id, and that the URL must therefore be /clients/:linkId/plans; it deliberately picks the stricter `status = 'active'` over `<> 'archived'` for cross-user reads and says why (an 'invited' link grants nothing); it puts the guard for the ownerless child tables in a correlated EXISTS INSIDE the UPDATE rather than a preceding SELECT; and it keeps 404-vs-403 straight (rows 404, endpoint role gates 403). It also correctly notes that archiving ends access on the very next request with the same access token, because there is no claim in the JWT to go stale.

IT CAUGHT THE ROLE-ENUM ERROR IN ITS OWN BRIEF AND CORRECTED IT IN WRITING — there is no role='client'; a client is role='user' appearing as coach_clients.client_id. A design that had silently accepted the brief would have been unwritable.

THE EXERCISE-VISIBILITY HOLE IS CORRECTLY DIAGNOSED AND THE CAPABILITY-TABLE APPROACH IS THE RIGHT SHAPE. The rejection of 'extend the VISIBLE predicate with an EXISTS over coach_clients' is correct for the stated reason: it would expose the coach's entire private library, drafts included, to any client who types into the search box. An explicit per-exercise grant is the right primitive; only its revoke path is broken.

CIVIL TEXT DATES FOR SCHEDULING, EPOCH INSTANTS FOR ORDERING, AND BOTH ON workout_logs. Deliberately breaking the epoch convention with a stated reason ('the epoch rule governs instants; a scheduled day is not an instant'), keeping scheduled_date vs local_date vs started_at as three distinct things, and rejecting epoch-of-local-midnight as 'a worse date that only works in one timezone' is correct and better reasoned than most schemas get. The 23:40-in-Sydney example is the right test case.

body_area_muscle_map IS SEEDED BY SLUG, NEVER BY ID, and I verified every one of the 20 slugs it references ('quads','hamstrings','adductors','abductors','neck','abs','obliques','lower-back','front-delts','side-delts','rear-delts', etc.) exists in the 003_exercises.sql seed — so the seed actually populates instead of silently inserting nothing. It also correctly identifies that onboarding's joint-centric body_area vocabulary and the exercises' muscle-group tagging were never connected, which is the real blocker on T2.5.4.

calendar_feed_tokens IS A REAL CATCH MOST DESIGNS WOULD MISS: 'ICS export' is meaningless without a bearer secret in the URL because Google Calendar cannot send an HttpOnly cookie, and modelling it hashed + revocable + optionally plan-scoped, shaped after the existing invite_codes table, is the correct answer rather than a download button or an unauthenticated URL.

exercise_name_snapshot ON ENTRIES IS THE RIGHT INSTINCT (history must render without read access to the exercise row), and origin ('plan'/'added'/'substituted') plus substituted_for_exercise_id makes off-plan and substitution first-class rather than bolted on. Freestyle being the same row with two NULLs is clean.

THE weaknesses SECTION IS HONEST AND SPECIFIC RATHER THAN HEDGED — it names the last_client_seq data-loss mode, the prev_entry_id backfill bug, the one-active-session UX cliff, the crude body-area map, and the fact that 13 tables and 6 named worker transactions are landing on a codebase with zero of either and no test suite. A design that self-reports at this resolution is far cheaper to fix than one that does not.

fatalFlaws.flaw: CROSS-TENANT IDOR: nothing ties `client_user_id` to the client of `coach_client_id`. The design asserts "the CHECK constraint `coach_client_id IS NOT NULL OR client_user_id IS NULL OR client_user_id = owner_user_id` makes it structurally impossible to assign a plan to an arbitrary user id". That is false: the moment `coach_client_id IS NOT NULL` the CHECK short-circuits and imposes NOTHING on `client_user_id`. The same hole exists on `workout_logs` (client_user_id + coach_client_id, zero relation between them). The route-level "validate the foreign id with an ownership SELECT" only proves the LINK belongs to the caller — never that the link's client_id equals the client_user_id being written.
fatalFlaws.scenario: REPRODUCED. Coach C (id 1) has one legitimate active link L=10 (C↔B). C posts `POST /plans {coach_client_id:10, client_user_id:3}` where 3 is victim V, a client C has never been linked to. The link-ownership SELECT passes (10 IS C's). The CHECK passes. Row written. Now: (a) V's own client predicate `WHERE client_user_id = 3` returns the plan — V sees a plan and a 2000-char `description` from a stranger in their app and on their Home "today" card (phishing / abuse surface); (b) when V trains it, `workout_logs.coach_client_id` is set to 10, and C's coach predicate `EXISTS (cc.id = l.coach_client_id AND cc.coach_id = 1 AND cc.status='active')` returns V's session — bodyweight_kg, notes, every set. Full cross-tenant read. Reverse direction also reproduced: attacker V posts a log with `coach_client_id = 20` (a link between coach X and client W that V has nothing to do with); coach X's dashboard query `JOIN coach_clients cc ON cc.id = l.coach_client_id WHERE cc.coach_id = 4 AND cc.status='active'` returns V's fabricated session. A client with ANY link (their own) can plant plans on any user id and inject sessions into any coach's feed.
fatalFlaws.fix: Add BEFORE INSERT and BEFORE UPDATE OF (coach_client_id, client_user_id) triggers on both workout_plans and workout_logs: `WHEN NEW.coach_client_id IS NOT NULL AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM coach_clients cc WHERE cc.id = NEW.coach_client_id AND cc.client_id = NEW.client_user_id) BEGIN SELECT RAISE(ABORT,'plan/log link must belong to the named client'); END;`. Do NOT rely on the route SELECT — this is exactly the class of invariant the design already trusts triggers for elsewhere (trg_workout_plan_items_parent).

fatalFlaws.flaw: THE e1RM FORGERY CHECK IS SELF-DISABLING, TWICE. `CHECK (e1rm_kg IS NULL OR e1rm_formula <> 'epley' OR abs(...) < 0.01)` is conditioned on a column the writer chooses, and `reps` has INTEGER *affinity*, not INTEGER type, so a REAL sails through `BETWEEN 1 AND 12`. The design claims "the forgery risk is closed by a CHECK that verifies the Epley arithmetic" and that "reps = 1 returns the weight itself; naive Epley would inflate every single by 3.3%". Both claims are defeated by a single field in the request body — and `trg_workout_log_sets_frozen` then makes the forged number PERMANENT (only a void, never a correction).
fatalFlaws.scenario: REPRODUCED, three payloads. (1) `{weight_kg:100, reps:5, e1rm_kg:1999, e1rm_formula:'lombardi'}` — accepted. Best-e1RM query now returns 1999 kg forever; the identical row with `e1rm_formula:'epley'` is correctly rejected. (2) `{weight_kg:200, reps:1.0001, e1rm_kg:206.6673, e1rm_formula:'epley'}` — accepted. `reps` stores as REAL 1.0001, so `CASE WHEN reps = 1` is false and the CHECK verifies the INFLATED branch: every single rep silently becomes a 3.33% e1RM PR, which is precisely the bug the design says it prevents. (3) `{weight_kg:100, reps:5.5}` — accepted, `typeof(reps)='real'`, `volume_kg` computed as 550. It also mints a permanent shadow rep-bucket: `workout_log_sets_repmax_idx` groups on `reps = ?`, and `reps=1.0001` has no competition, so every future 1.0001-rep set is an automatic rep_max PR. Once coins exist, that is an unbounded mint.
fatalFlaws.fix: (a) Never accept e1rm_kg/e1rm_formula/volume-relevant fields from the client — server-computed only, column allow-list per onboarding/routes.js:83-91. (b) Make the CHECK unconditional on the formula, or add a per-formula arithmetic branch for each enum value rather than an `<> 'epley'` escape. (c) Add `CHECK (reps IS NULL OR typeof(reps) = 'integer')` to reps, set_index, seconds, distance_m, rep_bucket, and every INTEGER-affinity measurement column — affinity is not a type.

fatalFlaws.flaw: THE DENORMALISATION GUARANTEE IS INSERT-ONLY. `trg_workout_log_sets_parent` and `trg_workout_log_exercises_parent` are `BEFORE INSERT` only. The design states "Enforced denormalisation is not drift: the trigger makes disagreement impossible" — but `workout_plan_items` got BOTH a parent trigger AND `trg_workout_plan_items_reparent` (BEFORE UPDATE OF group_id, day_id), and the log tables got only half of that pair. `log_exercise_id` is also absent from the freeze trigger's column list, so it is mutable even on a completed set.
fatalFlaws.scenario: REPRODUCED. Client B's completed set S (id 600, user_id=2, log_id=400) is re-parented with `UPDATE workout_log_sets SET log_exercise_id = 501 WHERE id = 600 AND user_id = 2` — 501 belongs to victim V (user 3). The ownership guard `AND user_id = ?` PASSES because the row really is B's. The freeze trigger does not fire because log_exercise_id is not in its list. V's session grid, which renders `WHERE log_exercise_id = ?`, now displays B's set. Also reproduced in the other direction: `UPDATE workout_log_exercises SET log_id = 400 WHERE id = 501 AND user_id = 3` moved V's exercise row into B's session — B's log now contains a row whose user_id is 3, and B's session render shows it. Third: `UPDATE workout_log_exercises SET exercise_id = 101, exercise_name_snapshot='Coach Secret Lift'` on a COMPLETED session succeeded (workout_log_exercises has no freeze trigger at all), so the parent now says "Coach Secret Lift" while its frozen child sets are indexed under Bench for every PR and progress query.
fatalFlaws.fix: Mirror the plan_items pattern exactly: add `BEFORE UPDATE OF log_exercise_id, log_id, user_id, exercise_id ON workout_log_sets` and `BEFORE UPDATE OF log_id, user_id ON workout_log_exercises` triggers with the same NOT EXISTS body. Add `log_exercise_id` to the freeze trigger, and give workout_log_exercises its own freeze trigger keyed on the parent log's status.

fatalFlaws.flaw: THE COMPLETED-LOG FREEZE TRIGGER OMITS `coach_client_id`, `plan_id`, `plan_day_id`, `occurrence_date`, `bodyweight_kg`, and every rollup. It guards only client_user_id / local_date / started_at / completed_at / status. So a "frozen" historical session can be re-attached to a different coach and have its authoritative aggregates rewritten, permanently, after it is closed.
fatalFlaws.scenario: REPRODUCED on a completed log (status='completed'). All of these succeeded: `SET coach_client_id = 20` (a link between coach X and client W — the attacker is neither), `SET total_volume_kg = 999999`, `SET total_sets = 9999`, `SET occurrence_date = '2030-01-01'`, `SET plan_name_snapshot = 'Elite Program'`, `SET bodyweight_kg = 399`. Coach X's client feed then returned `{id:400, client_user_id:2, total_volume_kg:999999}` — a session from a stranger, with a forged tonnage, that X can never remove (X does not own the row) and that the client can never take back (status is frozen, and see the deletion flaw below). Since the coach dashboard, adherence, and any future "coin velocity" metric read `total_volume_kg` rather than re-aggregating, this is a client-forgeable authoritative aggregate — a direct violation of "every authoritative value is computed on the BACKEND". The design carves the rollups out of the freeze deliberately ("Rollup columns and notes stay writable so a correction can recompute them"), which is exactly what opens it.
fatalFlaws.fix: Add coach_client_id, plan_id, plan_day_id, occurrence_date, plan_revision, bodyweight_kg and tz_offset_minutes to the freeze trigger. For the rollups, do not leave them plainly writable: either recompute them in an AFTER trigger on workout_log_sets, or gate them behind a sentinel the route cannot reach — and in every case exclude all six from the route's column allow-list.

fatalFlaws.flaw: ACCOUNT AND RELATIONSHIP DELETION HARD-FAIL. Three separate FK/CHECK collisions abort deletes that the design explicitly claims are safe. The design's own note — "A BEFORE DELETE trigger is deliberately absent — it would abort the ON DELETE CASCADE from users and make account deletion impossible" — describes precisely what the CHECK constraints do instead.
fatalFlaws.scenario: REPRODUCED, all three. (1) `DELETE FROM coach_clients WHERE id = 10` with one ordinary coach-assigned plan (owner=C, client=B, link=10): the `ON DELETE SET NULL` on workout_plans.coach_client_id fires, the row becomes (coach_client_id NULL, client_user_id=B, owner_user_id=C), and `CHECK (coach_client_id IS NOT NULL OR client_user_id IS NULL OR client_user_id = owner_user_id)` FAILS → SQLITE_CONSTRAINT_CHECK → whole delete aborts. The design states the exact opposite: "even hard-deleting the link leaves the client's plans and history intact and merely orphaned from the coach." The chosen ON DELETE action and the chosen CHECK are mutually exclusive. (2) `DELETE FROM users WHERE id = <coach>` after any client logged one of that coach's private exercises: exercises.owner_id CASCADEs into the exercise, workout_log_exercises.exercise_id RESTRICTs it → SQLITE_CONSTRAINT_TRIGGER FOREIGN KEY constraint failed. A coach can never delete their account, and there is no workaround short of manual DB surgery. That is a GDPR erasure request that returns 500. (3) `DELETE FROM workout_logs WHERE id = ?` once a session_volume PR exists: `workout_set_records.log_id ON DELETE SET NULL` collides with `CHECK (kind <> 'session_volume' OR log_id IS NOT NULL)` → abort. A single workout session is permanently undeletable.
fatalFlaws.fix: (1) Drop the `coach_client_id IS NOT NULL OR ...` CHECK and replace it with the client↔link trigger from the first finding, which enforces the real invariant without breaking SET NULL. (2) Change workout_log_sets/workout_log_exercises/workout_plan_items/workout_set_records `exercise_id` from ON DELETE RESTRICT to a null-able reference plus the existing name snapshot, or make exercises.owner_id ON DELETE SET NULL so a coach's deletion orphans rather than cascades. (3) Make `workout_set_records.log_id ON DELETE CASCADE` for session_volume rows, or drop `log_id IS NOT NULL` from that CHECK and enforce it on INSERT only.

seriousFlaws.flaw: NO OWNERSHIP PREDICATE EXISTS FOR A COACH'S OWN TEMPLATE, and the obvious fix reopens archived-client access. The ownership section gives the coach exactly one plan predicate, anchored on `p.coach_client_id`. The table CHECK forces `is_template = 1 AND coach_client_id IS NULL`. The two are contradictory.
seriousFlaws.scenario: REPRODUCED. Coach C creates template 201 (owner=1, is_template=1, coach_client_id NULL). The design's own coach predicate `EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM coach_clients cc WHERE cc.id = p.coach_client_id AND cc.coach_id = 1 AND cc.status='active')` returns `[]` — C cannot read their own template library. The design is not implementable as written, so an implementer adds the only obvious branch: `p.owner_user_id = ? OR EXISTS(active link)`. With the C↔B link archived, that predicate returned BOTH the template AND plan 200 (client_user_id = B) — because clone-to-client is described as `INSERT ... SELECT`, so `owner_user_id` stays the coach. Result: the archived coach reads the fired client's plan with the same access token, defeating the design's headline archive-ends-access property.
seriousFlaws.fix: State the template predicate explicitly and make it disjoint: `(p.is_template = 1 AND p.owner_user_id = ?)` for the library, and the link-anchored predicate for assigned plans — never an OR over both in one query. Better: null `owner_user_id` semantics for assigned plans (set owner_user_id = client_user_id on clone and keep authorship in `source_plan_id`), so `owner_user_id` can never grant cross-user reach.

seriousFlaws.flaw: THE COMPLETED-SET FREEZE OMITS `voided_at`, `target_*`, `set_index`, `set_kind`, `client_set_uid` and `created_at`. Voiding is presented as the one-way tombstone that keeps the record table from outliving its evidence; it is reversible.
seriousFlaws.scenario: REPRODUCED, all succeeded on a completed set: `SET voided_at = NULL` (un-void — the set re-enters workout_log_sets_progress_idx/repmax_idx/e1rm_idx while its PR row still carries `invalidated_at`, so the graph says best = 200 kg and the records screen says the old 150 kg PR is current, permanently divergent, with a stale `voided_reason` still attached); `SET target_reps = 1`, `SET target_weight_kg = 999` (the frozen prescription snapshot — the whole justification for keeping plans mutable — is forgeable after the fact, so "did the client hit the target?" becomes whatever they last wrote); `SET set_index = 99` (reorders history and moves the row inside the covering index); `SET client_set_uid = 'uid-99999'` (retroactively frees the idempotency key, so a later replay of the ORIGINAL request now inserts a duplicate row rather than colliding); `SET created_at = 1`. Also: `CHECK (is_warmup = 0 OR set_kind = 'warmup')` is one-directional — `set_kind='warmup'` with `is_warmup=0` is accepted, so a set labelled warmup in the UI still counts toward volume and PRs.
seriousFlaws.fix: Invert the freeze trigger: list the THREE columns that may change after completion (voided_at when going NULL→NOT NULL only, voided_reason, rest_taken_seconds) and RAISE on any other delta, rather than enumerating what is frozen. Add `CHECK ((is_warmup = 1) = (set_kind = 'warmup'))`.

seriousFlaws.flaw: THE UNIQUE INDEXES USED AS THE IDEMPOTENCY MECHANISM SURFACE AS HTTP 500, and one of them locks the user out permanently. The repo's errorHandler (lib/http.js:62-63) has no SQLITE_* branch — every raised UNIQUE becomes `{error:'internal server error'}` with a 500.
seriousFlaws.scenario: REPRODUCED. Double-tapped "Start workout" → `SQLITE_CONSTRAINT_UNIQUE: workout_logs.client_user_id, workout_logs.plan_day_id, workout_logs.occurrence_date` → 500. The design says this is where the double tap is "deduped ... rather than by a SELECT-then-INSERT in the route", and its own house rule (onboarding/routes.js:243) says a double-tapped submit "must not read as a failure". Worse: after the client mis-taps "Finish workout", `trg_workout_logs_frozen` blocks `status='abandoned'` (status is in the frozen list) and the delete is blocked by the session_volume CHECK — so the completed log is permanent, and `workout_logs_occurrence_unique` (WHERE status <> 'abandoned') then rejects every attempt to redo that plan day on that date, forever. Reproduced: second INSERT for the same (client, plan_day, date) after completion → UNIQUE violation → 500, with no recovery path.
seriousFlaws.fix: Either give completeSetTx/startWorkoutTx a read-before-write branch that returns `{deduped:true}` (legal under ADR-0005 because it precedes the first write), or add a SQLITE_CONSTRAINT_UNIQUE → 409/200 mapping in errorHandler. Separately, allow a completed log to be voided/abandoned by an explicit path, or scope the occurrence unique to `status = 'in_progress'` only.

seriousFlaws.flaw: `cycle_days` IS MUTABLE WITH NO GUARD AGAINST EXISTING `day_index` VALUES, and `day_index < cycle_days` is enforced nowhere in the database ("SQLite cannot express a CHECK against a parent row" — but a trigger can, and the design uses triggers for exactly this on plan_items).
seriousFlaws.scenario: REPRODUCED. Coach builds a 28-day block with days 0..27, then edits `cycle_days` to 7: 21 rows now satisfy `d.day_index >= p.cycle_days`. The occurrence generator (`starts_on + k*cycle_days + day_index`) either drops them or folds them into cycle k+1, where they collide with days 0..6 of the next cycle on the same calendar date. `workout_logs_occurrence_unique` does not catch the collision because plan_day_id differs, so the client's calendar shows two sessions on one date and the Home "today" card becomes nondeterministic. Also reproduced: `INSERT INTO workout_plan_days (plan_id, day_index) VALUES (200, 55)` on a cycle_days=7 plan — accepted, a ghost day that never renders.
seriousFlaws.fix: BEFORE INSERT/UPDATE trigger on workout_plan_days asserting `NEW.day_index < (SELECT cycle_days FROM workout_plans WHERE id = NEW.plan_id)`, plus a BEFORE UPDATE OF cycle_days trigger on workout_plans that RAISEs when any child day_index >= NEW.cycle_days.

seriousFlaws.flaw: UNBOUNDED GRID EXPANSION IN ONE IMMEDIATE TRANSACTION = SELF-SERVE WRITE-LOCK DoS. Nothing caps groups per day, items per group, or item_sets per item; `target_sets` allows 50. startWorkoutTx materialises the entire grid in a single IMMEDIATE transaction, which holds SQLite's one write lock for its whole duration.
seriousFlaws.scenario: A coach (or a self-coaching client — origin='client' is permitted) creates one day with 1,000 items × target_sets = 50, then taps Start. startWorkoutTx does 50,000 INSERTs into workout_log_sets — each firing trg_workout_log_sets_parent, which runs a correlated subquery, and each maintaining five indexes including three partial ones — inside one write-locked transaction. Every other writer in the whole application (any login, any set check by any other user) waits on `busy_timeout = 5000` and then gets SQLITE_BUSY, which errorHandler turns into a 500. There is no bound in the schema, no bound in the design, and the pool has only 2-N workers.
seriousFlaws.fix: CHECK-bound `target_sets` to something a human trains (already 50 — fine) and add hard caps enforced at write time on items per day (e.g. 60) and groups per day (e.g. 30), plus a total-set-count guard inside startWorkoutTx that throws before the first write if the expansion exceeds a few hundred rows.

seriousFlaws.flaw: A REPLAYED "set checked" WITH A CHANGED PAYLOAD SILENTLY DISCARDS THE NEW VALUE AND RETURNS 200. Layer 1's guard is `WHERE id = ? AND user_id = ? AND completed_at IS NULL`; Layer 2 returns `{applied:false, replayed:true}` before any write. Neither compares the incoming measurements with the stored ones.
seriousFlaws.scenario: The player POSTs set S as 100 kg × 5. The response is lost to a flaky connection. The user notices the typo in the still-optimistic UI, corrects it to 105 kg × 5, and the player retries the same set id. The server takes the replay branch and answers 200 `{applied:false}`. The client's own retry logic treats 200 as success and shows 105 kg. The database holds 100 kg, the e1RM and any PR are computed off 100, and `trg_workout_log_sets_frozen` makes it uncorrectable — the only remedy is a void that leaves a visible strikethrough. The user's screen and their history permanently disagree.
seriousFlaws.fix: In the replay branch, compare the submitted weight/reps/seconds against the stored row; when they differ, return a distinguishable result (`{applied:false, conflict:true, stored:{...}}` → HTTP 409) so the player can offer void-and-relog instead of silently claiming success.

seriousFlaws.flaw: AN ARCHIVED CLIENT KEEPS PERMANENT, UNREVOKABLE READ ACCESS TO THE COACH'S PRIVATE EXERCISE LIBRARY, and a soft-deleted exercise vanishes from plans entirely.
seriousFlaws.scenario: (a) Coach C prescribes private exercise E to client B. B is archived. The derived visibility predicate's branch `EXISTS (workout_plan_items i JOIN ... WHERE p.client_user_id = ?)` still matches, because the design deliberately lets B keep the plan row after archiving. So B reads E's name, description, instructions and media forever. C cannot revoke it: C cannot delete or edit the plan (the coach predicate requires an active link → 404), and cannot delete E (ON DELETE RESTRICT). For a coach whose custom library is their product, that is an unrevokable IP leak with no admin path. (b) REPRODUCED: once an admin soft-deletes an exercise, the derived predicate returned `[]` — because `e.deleted_at IS NULL` gates ALL branches including the plan/history ones. `workout_log_exercises` survives via `exercise_name_snapshot`, but `workout_plan_items` has no name snapshot at all, so every coach plan containing that exercise renders a nameless row and the client's today card shows a blank exercise.
seriousFlaws.fix: (a) Scope the plan branch of the derived predicate to plans whose link is still active, or add an explicit revoke path that strips the plan when a link is archived — and state which. (b) Relax `deleted_at IS NULL` to `(e.deleted_at IS NULL OR <prescribed/performed branch matched>)`, and add a `exercise_name_snapshot` to workout_plan_items the way workout_log_exercises has one.

seriousFlaws.flaw: ONE ASCENDING SESSION MINTS N e1RM PR EVENTS. Nothing in the schema or the transaction limits PR events to one per (user, exercise, session); the unique index is on `(set_id, kind, rep_bucket)`, and every set has a distinct set_id.
seriousFlaws.scenario: REPRODUCED. A lifter ramps 90/95/100/102/105 kg × 5 in one session, all above their previous best of 100 e1RM. Because tx.immediate serialises the writes, each set legitimately sees the previous one as the prior best, so `CHECK (previous_value IS NULL OR value > previous_value)` is satisfied every time: 5 e1rm PR rows minted from one session. The badge fires five times, the feed shows five PRs, and the design's own Layer 4 ("at most one coin can ever be granted per PR") then pays five coins for one session's progress. Combined with the acknowledged rep_max noise (any first-ever set at a novel rep count is a PR), the reward surface is far larger than the design's idempotency argument implies.
seriousFlaws.fix: Add a partial unique index `ON workout_set_records (user_id, exercise_id, kind, rep_bucket, local_date) WHERE invalidated_at IS NULL`, or have completeSetTx upsert the day's PR event rather than appending. Note the day-scoped index also makes 'best of the day' cheap.

seriousFlaws.flaw: `ics_token_hash` HAS NO EXPIRY, NO REVOCATION COLUMN AND NO SCOPE, and the feed it authenticates must sit outside cookie auth. The design ships the token but not its lifecycle.
seriousFlaws.scenario: A client subscribes their phone calendar to the ICS URL. The secret now lives in the URL, which is replayed on every sync and lands in reverse-proxy access logs, the calendar provider's fetch logs, and any Referer if the feed is ever rendered. There is `ics_token_issued_at` but no `ics_token_revoked_at` and no `ics_token_expires_at`, so the only revocation is to overwrite the hash — which silently breaks the user's calendar with no way to tell them why, and nothing records that a revocation ever happened. The feed exposes the full prescription: day names, 2000-char day `notes`, the coach's programming. The design also never states where the ICS router mounts, and server.js:146-148 makes that load-bearing — mounted before `csrfProtection` it is exempt (correct for a GET feed), mounted after it needs `X-CSRF: 1`, which a calendar client cannot send.
seriousFlaws.fix: Add `ics_token_revoked_at INTEGER` and `ics_token_expires_at INTEGER`, filter both in the feed lookup, and state the mount point explicitly (before csrfProtection, after a dedicated bearer-token middleware, read-only, its own rate-limit tier).

strengths: THE DDL IS REAL AND IT COMPILES. I applied the whole 009 body verbatim on SQLite 3.53.2 on top of a stand-in of user_version 8 and it created cleanly on the first attempt — subqueries inside trigger WHEN clauses, an index over a STORED generated column, DESC columns inside partial indexes, WITHOUT ROWID with a composite PK, and the ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN with a constant-free CHECK. That is not typical for a schema this size and it means the review can be about semantics rather than syntax. Keep the DDL as the drafting base.

`volume_kg` AS A STORED GENERATED COLUMN IS GENUINELY UNFORGEABLE, and it is the one place where the design's integrity claim survived every attack — I could not write a volume that disagreed with weight × reps, including on rows where I successfully forged the e1RM. The definition-vs-model distinction (tonnage is a definition and belongs to the engine; e1RM is a model and must carry `e1rm_formula` so a future formula does not retro-reshape an 18-month chart) is the right call and should be kept verbatim, with only the CHECK's formula escape closed.

THE PARTIAL-INDEX SHAPE IS EXACTLY RIGHT. `WHERE voided_at IS NULL AND is_warmup = 0 AND completed_at IS NOT NULL` on all three analytics indexes means voided rows and warmups are not merely filtered but absent from the B-tree, so a PR query cannot accidentally include them even if the WHERE clause forgets a term. The reasoning for dropping the reps range out of the e1rm index predicate (with the range there, the query must repeat it, and the planner then prefers repmax_idx plus a TEMP B-TREE) is the kind of thing that is only learned by running EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN, and it should be preserved along with its comment.

NO CURRENT-BESTS CACHE TABLE. The argument — a cache has to be invalidated on every void and every correction, the recompute after a void is a full scan anyway, and the query it saves is a single B-tree descent — is correct and is the highest-leverage decision in the document. Keep it. This is what makes the whole void-instead-of-edit story tractable.

`rep_bucket INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0` WITH A 0 SENTINEL INSTEAD OF NULL, justified by the fact that SQLite treats NULLs as distinct in a UNIQUE index — so a nullable rep_bucket would silently let two 'e1rm' rows coexist for one set and the idempotency backstop would not exist. This is a genuinely subtle, genuinely correct catch that most designs get wrong. The same instinct should be applied to the other partial uniques.

ANCHORING COACH ACCESS ON `coach_clients.id` RATHER THAN THE CLIENT'S USER ID, and requiring `status = 'active'` (the stricter of the repo's two inconsistent conventions, correctly identified and correctly chosen). Where the predicate is actually applied, I confirmed archiving ends access on the very next read with the same access token — no cache, no refresh, no denormalised coach_id to go stale. That property is worth protecting; my findings are about the places the design forgot to apply it, not about the mechanism.

THE IMMEDIATE-TRANSACTION ARGUMENT FOR THE REPLAY BRANCH IS CORRECT AND LOAD-BEARING: tx.immediate takes the write lock on the first statement, so the read in step 1 and the write in step 4 cannot be interleaved, and the same code in a DEFERRED transaction would be a TOCTOU. Concurrent identical set-checks are genuinely serialised. The step ordering (all reads and all error returns strictly before the first write, per ADR-0005's commit-on-return law) is right and should be copied into every named transaction.

IDEMPOTENCY VIA THE DOMAIN'S OWN NATURAL KEYS rather than a generic idempotency_keys table, with the correct justification that a generic table needs a TTL sweeper and a definition of 'the same request'. The three keys (client_set_uid per log, the occurrence per client, the PR per set+kind+bucket) are the right grain, and the reward-anchor idea — a future coin ledger keys on ('pr', workout_set_records.id) rather than a reward column on the set — is a clean way to leave room for the economy without inventing it.

`local_date` COMPUTED SERVER-SIDE FROM THE USER'S IANA ZONE AND NEVER RECOMPUTED. The reasoning (epoch seconds are UTC, SQLite has no tz database so it cannot be fixed in SQL, a 01:00 Budapest session lands in the previous UTC day and once a month in the previous UTC week, and the workout happened on that Tuesday forever) is correct, and denormalising it onto the sets table is what makes the progress graph a pure covering-index scan. The accompanying onboarding_profiles.timezone ALTER is the right minimal addition and correctly notes why it must be nullable.

`body_area_muscle_map` IS A REAL MISSING BRIDGE, correctly identified. onboarding_limitations.body_area is joint-centric and muscle_groups is muscle-centric, nothing joined them, and T2.5.4 is therefore not implementable today. Seeding by SLUG rather than id, copying the body_area vocabulary verbatim from 008 (kebab-case included), and splitting loads/stabilises so a knee complaint does not delete every exercise a calf stabilises are all correct choices. I verified all referenced slugs exist in the 003 seed.

NON-UNIQUE `position` WITH AN `id` TIE-BREAK, BECAUSE SQLITE CHECKS UNIQUE PER STATEMENT, SO A DRAG-REORDER THAT REWRITES 1..N INSIDE ONE TRANSACTION WOULD ABORT MID-WAY. Correct, non-obvious, and the contrast with UNIQUE on semantic coordinates (day_index+slot, set_index) that are replaced whole delete-then-insert is exactly the right distinction. Keep both halves and keep the comment explaining why.

THE GROUP TABLE OWNING `rounds`/`cap_seconds`/inter-round rest while the ITEM owns `target_sets`, with every item in a group including solos (kind='single'). This makes ordering total with no COALESCE and no 'is this grouped' branch in any renderer, and the observation that a `group_key TEXT` on the item would have had nowhere to put `rounds` is the correct reason to reject the cheaper option.

NAMING THE FIVE NAMED WORKER TRANSACTIONS AND THE TWO-FILE MECHANISM EXPLICITLY (worker export + index.js facade + the structured-clone constraint on arguments), and correctly identifying which operations do NOT need one (reordering and day/week copy, because each UPDATE carries its own ownership guard and the steps are independent). These are the repo's first named transactions and the design does not hand-wave the mechanism.
